Directly applying sparse attention does not fully solve this problem, because different queries can select different pages, inflating the block's collective read set, while repeated support construction adds overhead and permanent eviction can discard information needed later. We present RISA, a recoverable sparse-attention method with shared read plans for block-wise DLMs. RISA exploits the fact that historical KV remains fixed within a block while queries evolve across denoising steps. Newly generated history is organized into exact priority and recovery tiers; seed queries then build a protected, bounded read plan whose indices are reused across the block while attention is recomputed with fresh queries and current-block KV. This separates history preservation from repeated reading and amortizes sparse-support construction without changing the backbone or decoder. On DreamReasoner-8B, RISA retains comparable task performance. At 32K, the default configuration speeds up attention by $2.67\times$ and fixed-trajectory requests by $1.36\times$ over dense, and attention speedup reaches $5.53\times$ at 128K. Across eight settings on three models, RISA decodes faster than the tested MAGE, QUEST, and LoSA budgets at matched KL.

AI.tldr: The authors present RISA, a recoverable sparse-attention method with shared read plans for block-wise diffusion language models, achieving up to 5.53x attention speedup at 128K context while retaining comparable task performance.
AI.motivation: Long-context inference in block-wise diffusion language models is memory-bound because every denoising step repeatedly reads a growing historical KV cache, and naive sparse attention inflates read sets or permanently evicts needed history.
AI.method: RISA organizes newly generated history into exact priority and recovery tiers and uses seed queries to build a protected, bounded read plan whose indices are reused across denoising steps in a block while attention is recomputed with fresh queries and current-block KV.
AI.result: On DreamReasoner-8B, RISA retains comparable task performance while speeding up attention by 2.67x and fixed-trajectory requests by 1.36x at 32K, reaching 5.53x attention speedup at 128K, and decodes faster than MAGE, QUEST, and LoSA at matched KL across eight settings.
AI.conclusion: Separating history preservation from repeated reading via shared block-level read plans accelerates long-context block-diffusion inference without modifying the backbone or decoder.

title: EGS: A Complementary Safety Framework for Educational LLMs
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer strong potential for personalized education, but adolescent-facing deployment raises risks of toxic, biased, misleading, or developmentally inappropriate content. We argue that educational safety should move beyond binary refusal: student queries are often ambiguous or curiosity-driven, requiring contextual guidance rather than simple blocking. We introduce the Educational Guardrail System (EGS), a lightweight, model-agnostic runtime framework that complements intrinsic alignment through query moderation, scenario-aware pedagogical guidance, and response moderation. EGS triages inputs by risk level, redirects gray-zone queries with category-specific educational interventions, and audits outputs before delivery. Experiments across general and education-specific benchmarks show that EGS improves moderation performance, refusal quality, and jailbreak robustness across diverse LLMs. These findings suggest that defense-in-depth guardrails can strengthen safety while preserving the pedagogical utility required in educational LLMs. Our code and model weights will be publicly available to support community adoption.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce the Educational Guardrail System (EGS), a lightweight, model-agnostic runtime framework that replaces binary refusal with risk-based triage and pedagogical redirection, improving safety and jailbreak robustness across diverse LLMs.
AI.motivation: Adolescent-facing educational LLMs face safety risks, yet binary refusal is ill-suited for ambiguous or curiosity-driven student queries that require contextual guidance.
AI.method: EGS complements intrinsic alignment with three runtime stages: risk-level query moderation, scenario-aware pedagogical guidance for gray-zone queries, and pre-delivery response moderation.
AI.result: Experiments across general and education-specific benchmarks show that EGS improves moderation performance, refusal quality, and jailbreak robustness across diverse LLMs.
AI.conclusion: Defense-in-depth runtime guardrails can strengthen adolescent safety while preserving the pedagogical utility of educational LLMs.

title: Where Does Hindsight Enter Clinical Agent Benchmarks? An Audit of Simulators and Case Construction
comment: 8 pages main text, 20 pages in total, 6 figures, 11 tables
summary: Benchmarks for LLM diagnostic agents are built from retrospective records: the case an agent reads is rewritten from discharge summaries, and unrecorded test results are generated by a simulator that often sees the final diagnosis. HindAudit separates three hindsight channels (the diagnosis given to the simulator, the retrospective context it conditions on, and the agent-facing case text) and measures each with judges trained only on real data. On 27,489 emergency admissions from MIMIC-IV, five registered tests found no leakage into simulated laboratory results: providing the diagnosis to five simulators had a negligible effect, and prompted gatekeepers diluted the diagnostic signal, although exploratory results suggest they can raise agent scores. The largest effect lay in the case text. Against a presentation-time reconstruction from triage records, benchmark-style summaries raised the zero-shot accuracy of four LLMs from 25.4% to 39.7% and discharge histories to 45.3%, and raised six interactive agents' scores while barely changing their ranking. The exploratory gap was reproduced in a registered replication on held-out patients. Masking diagnosis names left it unchanged. Because MIMIC lacks a contemporaneous bedside history, the gap is an upper bound on hindsight. We report all registered outcomes and recommend construction practices.

AI.tldr: Auditing hindsight leakage in clinical diagnostic agent benchmarks on 27,489 MIMIC-IV admissions, the authors find negligible leakage into simulated lab results but a large artificial accuracy boost from retrospective case summaries.
AI.motivation: Clinical agent benchmarks are built from retrospective discharge summaries and simulators that often see the final diagnosis, raising concerns about hindsight leakage.
AI.method: HindAudit separates three hindsight channels—diagnosis given to the simulator, retrospective conditioning context, and agent-facing case text—and evaluates them with judges trained only on real data across 27,489 MIMIC-IV emergency admissions.
AI.result: Five registered tests found negligible leakage into simulated lab results; however, compared to presentation-time triage reconstructions, benchmark-style summaries raised zero-shot accuracy of four LLMs from 25.4% to 39.7% (and discharge histories to 45.3%) and raised six interactive agents' scores without changing their ranking.
AI.conclusion: Retrospective case text—rather than simulator lab generation—is the primary source of hindsight inflation in clinical agent benchmarks, motivating presentation-time case construction.

title: OfficePrism: Benchmarking Agents on Single-Domain Operations Across Enterprise Business Functions
summary: Broad workplace scores can mix competence within one business function with the extra cost of coordinating across functions and systems, making failures hard to localize. OfficePrism evaluates this prerequisite through 420 single-domain enterprise tasks spanning seven business functions under shared, benchmark-defined L1--L3 task-structure levels. Each task runs in a fresh environment combining a shared synthetic organization with one function-specific domain and yped state access. Our pipeline uses grounded records, business rules, and tool schemas to jointly construct a Chinese-language ticket, a hidden executable reference witness, and an expected response, followed by automated filtering and human curation. The same task set is evaluated through full-schema and search-and-dispatch packages. Across 124 model--harness--package configurations, the per-case joint natural-language-and-database pass rate ranges from 22.6% to 76.4%, with a median of 67.9%. L1 is highest in all 124 configurations, and L2 exceeds L3 in 122. Among 50 configurations sharing the same harness and model labels across both packages, search scores higher in 30, ties in one, and scores lower in 19.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce OfficePrism, a benchmark of 420 single-domain Chinese enterprise tasks across seven business functions, revealing pass rates from 22.6% to 76.4% across 124 configurations and consistent difficulty scaling across L1-L3 levels.
AI.motivation: Broad workplace benchmarks conflate single-function competence with cross-function coordination costs, making it hard to localize agent failures.
AI.method: OfficePrism evaluates single-domain operations across seven business functions and three task-structure levels (L1-L3) using synthetic organizations, Chinese-language tickets, hidden executable witnesses, and both full-schema and search-and-dispatch tool packages.
AI.result: Across 124 model-harness-package configurations, joint natural-language-and-database pass rates range from 22.6% to 76.4% (median 67.9%); L1 is highest in all 124 configurations, L2 exceeds L3 in 122, and search-and-dispatch outperforms full-schema in 30 of 50 matched configurations.
AI.conclusion: Isolating single-domain enterprise operations exposes clear capability gradients across task complexity and tool-discovery regimes.

title: Zero-Dimensional Attention Topology for Linguistic Acceptability
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Code and data are provided as ancillary files
summary: Topological summaries of Transformer attention provide sentence representations for linguistic acceptability classification. We examine a zero-dimensional persistent-homology ($H_0$) representation that summarizes minimum-spanning-tree merge values from 144 symmetrized BERT attention graphs into 1,440 features. The retrospective evaluation uses 8,517 downstream training sentences and 521 in-domain and 497 out-of-domain CoLA validation sentences after data-integrity filtering. The recorded out-of-domain Matthews correlation coefficients are 0.438 for the topological representation and 0.508 for attention statistics, compared with 0.545 for BERT. Attention-feature results are retained aggregate measurements; BERT predictions are rescored and length controls are refitted from the accompanying records. Analytical results show that the representation retains token-count information and discards a class of directional attention differences. Source resampling of BERT predictions also demonstrates the sensitivity of uncertainty estimates to the sampling unit. The reported results do not demonstrate a predictive advantage for this fixed topological representation over simpler attention summaries. They identify representation properties and evaluation controls relevant to subsequent studies of attention topology.

AI.tldr: Evaluating zero-dimensional persistent-homology (H0) summaries of BERT attention graphs on CoLA, the authors find no predictive advantage over simpler attention statistics (0.438 vs. 0.508 MCC) and show that H0 retains token-count information while discarding directional differences.
AI.motivation: Topological summaries of Transformer attention have been proposed for linguistic acceptability, but their actual predictive advantage and representation properties relative to simpler baselines remain unclear.
AI.method: The authors evaluate a 1,440-feature H0 minimum-spanning-tree representation from 144 symmetrized BERT attention graphs on 8,517 training and 521 in-domain / 497 out-of-domain CoLA validation sentences after data-integrity filtering, alongside analytical and resampling analyses.
AI.result: Out-of-domain Matthews correlation coefficients are 0.438 for the H0 topological representation and 0.508 for attention statistics, compared with 0.545 for BERT.
AI.conclusion: This fixed H0 attention topology representation does not outperform simpler attention summaries and highlights the need for length controls and appropriate sampling units in attention topology studies.

title: Comparing Implicit and Explicit Language Attitudes toward the Dutch multiethnolect Straattaal in Humans and Large Language Models
summary: While language attitudes have been extensively studied in humans, the extent to which large language models (LLMs) encode similar associations between language varieties and social attributes remains unclear. Contemporary sociolinguistic research distinguishes between explicit attitudes, which stem from deliberative processing, and implicit attitudes, which arise from automatic processing. This study investigates whether LLMs exhibit human-like implicit and explicit language attitudes toward the Dutch multiethnolect Straattaal, particularly its association with migrant communities. We use closely matched designs to assess attitudes in humans and LLMs. For humans, we use an Implicit Association Test (IAT) and an explicit rating task. For LLMs, we use the LLM Word Association Test (LLM WAT) and the same explicit rating task. Human participants strongly associate Straattaal with individuals with a migration background at both implicit and explicit levels. In the LLM WAT, Straattaal is consistently associated with individuals with a migration background, with stronger associations observed in larger and newer models. When presented with the same explicit rating task as human participants, LLMs produce comparable response patterns. Overall, the findings suggest that many LLMs encode language attitudes resembling those observed in humans, however we also highlight important questions about how concepts and measures developed to study human attitudes should be interpreted in LLMs. This highlights the relevance of incorporating sociolinguistic perspectives and language variation into NLP research to better identify and mitigate socially and linguistically embedded biases.

AI.tldr: Using matched implicit and explicit attitude tasks, the authors show that LLMs encode human-like associations linking the Dutch multiethnolect Straattaal with migrant communities, with stronger implicit associations in larger and newer models.
AI.motivation: While human language attitudes toward language varieties are well studied, it is unclear whether LLMs encode comparable implicit and explicit social associations.
AI.method: The authors compare human participants (Implicit Association Test and explicit rating task) with LLMs (LLM Word Association Test and the same explicit rating task) regarding the Dutch multiethnolect Straattaal and its association with migrant communities.
AI.result: Humans strongly associate Straattaal with migrant backgrounds both implicitly and explicitly; LLMs consistently show the same association in the LLM WAT—stronger in larger and newer models—and produce comparable explicit rating patterns.
AI.conclusion: LLMs encode sociolinguistic attitudes resembling human biases, underscoring the need to incorporate sociolinguistic perspectives to detect and mitigate language-variety biases.

title: Bad Apples in the Kitchen: How LLM Teams Detect, Correct, and Calibrate Against Their Misaligned Members
summary: What protects an LLM team when one teammate quietly goes wrong? Most multi-agent LLM work assumes cooperative partners and inspects chat between turns before acting. Real-time embodied cooperation does not allow this pause: chat runs alongside action, so a teammate whose words stay cooperative while behavior diverges can cause damage faster than the team can name what is happening. We study this case by injecting three theory-grounded misaligned agents into a custom four-player Overcooked environment, each stressing a different joint-action layer (speech-action mismatch, role invasion, and aggregate-progress disruption), and decompose robustness into three sequential gates of detection, correction, and calibration through a 3x4x2 design (n=720 episodes). Nearly all trolls are eventually named, but recovery follows only when attribution and situational diagnosis appear in the same utterance; direct source-attribution prompting improves the hardest case only by degrading the troll-free baseline by 37.5%. Robustness, then, depends less on detection alone than on whether team chat combines attribution with diagnosis in a single utterance, suggesting that sensitivity to misalignment should be targeted rather than uniformly raised.

AI.tldr: Studying four-player Overcooked LLM teams with misaligned teammates, the authors show that recovery requires combining source attribution and situational diagnosis in the same utterance, whereas uniform suspicion prompting degrades clean baselines by 37.5%.
AI.motivation: Real-time embodied multi-agent cooperation runs chat alongside action, allowing a teammate whose words stay cooperative while behavior diverges to cause damage before the team can respond.
AI.method: The authors inject three misaligned agent types (speech-action mismatch, role invasion, aggregate-progress disruption) into a four-player Overcooked environment and decompose robustness into detection, correction, and calibration across 720 episodes.
AI.result: Nearly all misaligned agents are eventually named, but recovery occurs only when attribution and situational diagnosis appear in the same utterance; direct source-attribution prompting improves the hardest case only by degrading the troll-free baseline by 37.5%.
AI.conclusion: Team robustness depends on targeted utterances that pair attribution with diagnosis rather than uniformly raising suspicion.

title: RICoT: Recurrent Interleaved Chain-of-Thought for Page Stream Segmentation
comment: 18 pages, 3 figures, 19 tables. Dataset and code to be released
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have renewed interest in Page Stream Segmentation (PSS), splitting a multi-page file into its constituent documents. Yet published LLM methods still frame the task as boundary classification over one or a few neighboring pages, and commercial document-splitting APIs do not disclose their methods. We reimagine PSS for LLMs as a sequential process over the whole stream and propose RICoT (Recurrent Interleaved Chain-of-Thought), a prompting framework that works through the pages as a reader would: within a sliding window it reasons about each page and commits its boundary decision before moving on, and across windows it carries forward a compact record of what it has read, keeping per-call cost bounded. We also introduce FinancePSS-205, a benchmark of 205 real-world, de-identified financial page streams, to be released publicly. On FinancePSS-205, RICoT matches or outperforms pairwise and windowed prompting with the same backbone for each of three open-weight LLMs; on a TABME test subset, RICoT with GLM-5 reaches document F1 0.847 and boundary F1 0.915, above published zero-shot results. A 2B-parameter student, trained on a larger teacher's decisions with and without the page-level reasoning, performs comparably in both modes and comes within 0.05 document F1 of the strongest prompted model on FinancePSS-205.

AI.tldr: The authors propose RICoT, a recurrent interleaved chain-of-thought prompting framework for Page Stream Segmentation, and introduce FinancePSS-205, achieving 0.847 document F1 on TABME and strong distillation into a 2B student.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM methods for Page Stream Segmentation frame the task as local boundary classification over a few neighboring pages rather than a sequential process over the full document stream.
AI.method: RICoT processes pages sequentially within a sliding window, reasoning and committing boundary decisions per page while carrying forward a compact summary across windows to bound per-call cost; the authors also release FinancePSS-205 (205 financial page streams).
AI.result: On FinancePSS-205, RICoT matches or outperforms pairwise and windowed prompting across three open-weight LLMs; on a TABME subset, RICoT with GLM-5 reaches 0.847 document F1 and 0.915 boundary F1, and a 2B student comes within 0.05 document F1 of the strongest prompted model.
AI.conclusion: Sequential sliding-window reasoning with compact state carry-forward provides an effective, cost-bounded framework for LLM-based Page Stream Segmentation.

title: LMMR: Learned Multigranular Memory Retrieval for Small Language Model Agents
comment: 18 pages, 11 figures. Code and experimental results: this https URL
summary: Small language model agents have limited space to read the memory needed for multi-hop questions. Relevant facts are often scattered across records whose surrounding text consumes much of that space. We propose LMMR, a learned multigranular memory retrieval method that selects both the next source and how much of it to read. LMMR links paragraphs and sentence fragments to their original sources and pairs views that supply the same missing support during training. Relevant distractors and repeated information provide contrasting examples. At inference, the reranker scores what each candidate adds to an anchor passage, and a selector chooses the evidence within a token budget. On 22,398 official validation questions from HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, and MuSiQue, a frozen 2B answer model reaches 61.47, 43.26, and 30.58 F1 under a 400-token budget. The gains over query expansion are 3.06, 2.14, and 4.55 points, while memory input decreases by 23.1-26.9%. LMMR also uses 23.5-27.7% fewer input tokens than a coarse retriever trained on the same questions. Against that retriever followed by LLMLingua-2 at comparable input lengths, F1 gains reach 3.99 points and are significant on HotpotQA and 2WikiMultihopQA after Holm correction. All eight small answer models evaluated on HotpotQA improve over query expansion and MMR in both F1 and exact match.

AI.tldr: The authors propose LMMR, a learned multigranular memory retrieval method for small language model agents that selects both sources and evidence granularity within a token budget, improving F1 by 2.14-4.55 points while cutting memory tokens by 23.1-26.9%.
AI.motivation: Small language model agents have limited context budgets for multi-hop QA, and retrieved records often contain surrounding text that wastes space.
AI.method: LMMR links paragraphs and sentence fragments to their sources, trains a reranker with contrasting distractors and repeated-info pairs to score marginal evidence value, and uses a selector to pack evidence within a token budget.
AI.result: Across 22,398 validation questions from HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, and MuSiQue, a frozen 2B model reaches 61.47, 43.26, and 30.58 F1 under a 400-token budget—gaining 3.06, 2.14, and 4.55 F1 over query expansion while reducing memory input by 23.1-26.9%—and improves all eight tested small models on HotpotQA.
AI.conclusion: Learned multigranular selection enables small language model agents to achieve higher multi-hop QA accuracy within tight token budgets.

title: Growing Clusters Lower the Bar: Profile Accretion in LLM-Based Incremental Entity Resolution
summary: Incremental entity resolution pipelines ask a large language model (LLM) whether a new record belongs to an existing cluster and show it the records already linked. Analyses of matching oracles assume that the answer depends only on the records compared. For the LLM matchers we test, it depends on cluster size, and the model lowers its bar for joining a cluster as the cluster grows. On French procurement suppliers from FOPPA, with SIREN identifiers as ground truth, we hold the new record fixed and vary only the number of verified members shown. Sixteen members instead of one raise the false match rate on similarly named companies by \dfmrMin--\dfmrMax{} percentage points in six open-weight models, while their area under the ROC curve rises by only \aucGainMin--\aucGainMax. In Claude Sonnet~5 and Haiku~5.5 the rise is \clSonD{} and \clHaiD{} points. The shift persists with street addresses, prompt variants and the BatchER and ComEM formats, and one false merge raises acceptance of the intruder's other records in every open model. It does not arise on Czech and Bulgarian TED notices, where one record with its full address already identifies the company. In online linking on confusable blocks, a single threshold set on labelled data raises recall by a factor of \fxRRmin--\fxRRmax{} for five models with no detectable loss of precision and no extra LLM calls.

AI.tldr: Testing LLM-based incremental entity resolution on French procurement suppliers, the authors show that larger existing clusters cause LLMs to lower their matching threshold and increase false merges, a bias mitigated by setting a single threshold on labeled data.
AI.motivation: Incremental entity resolution analyses assume matching decisions depend only on the records compared, ignoring how growing cluster context affects LLM matchers.
AI.method: Holding the new record fixed on FOPPA French procurement data (with SIREN ground truth) and Czech/Bulgarian TED notices, the authors vary the number of verified cluster members shown (1 vs. 16) across six open-weight models, Claude Sonnet 5, and Haiku 5.5.
AI.result: Showing 16 members instead of 1 substantially raises false match rates on confusable French companies with minimal AUROC gain, and one false merge increases acceptance of the intruder's other records; in online linking, a single threshold set on labeled data boosts recall across five models with no detectable precision loss or extra LLM calls.
AI.conclusion: Cluster size induces profile accretion bias in LLM entity resolution, which can be countered via calibrated thresholding on labeled data.

title: From syllable representation via gesture generation to articulation: A spiking neural model
comment: 47 pages, 9 figures. Submitted to the Journal of Neurolinguistics on 8 November 2026
summary: Speech production requires a transformation from phonological representations into coordinated vocal-tract movements. This paper presents a spiking neural sensorimotor model within the Neural Engineering Framework and Semantic Pointer Architecture. Each syllable occurrence has a neural oscillator whose evolving phase coordinates its gestures and initiates the next syllable. Phase-dependent commands recruit separate neural populations for vocalic, oral-constriction, velopharyngeal, and glottal actions (gestures). Neural ramp integrators shape the rise and fall of gesture activation. Together with articulatory targets, these trajectories determine the extent and time course of articulatory movements. Opponent neural populations provide control signals to a geometric articulatory model. Thirty reference recordings cover an input corpus of eight lexical words, an alternative realization of one word, a syllable sequence, and isolated syllables. Two additional paired simulation subcorpora of sixty runs each, covering two words and one syllable sequence, assess activation reliability across neural realizations. Adjusting gesture command amplitudes increased successful realizations from 57/60 to 60/60 under the specified criteria, with ramp rate factors held constant. The model demonstrates how neural oscillator and ramp dynamics generate articulatory timing under specified phasing rules. It complements a preceding mental-lexicon model through an ordered syllable interface. Continuous online execution across all components and connection to the acoustic extension remain further integration steps. Accessible code and synchronized visualization support inspection of the neural activation trajectories and resulting vocal-tract movements.

AI.tldr: The authors present a spiking neural sensorimotor model that translates syllable representations into coordinated vocal-tract movements via neural oscillators and ramp integrators, achieving 60/60 successful realizations after amplitude tuning.
AI.motivation: Speech production requires transforming phonological representations into coordinated vocal-tract movements, which the authors model within the Neural Engineering Framework and Semantic Pointer Architecture.
AI.method: Each syllable has a neural oscillator whose phase coordinates vocalic, oral-constriction, velopharyngeal, and glottal gesture populations, while neural ramp integrators shape gesture activation trajectories driving a geometric articulatory model.
AI.result: Evaluated on 30 reference recordings and two 60-run simulation subcorpora, adjusting gesture command amplitudes increased successful realizations from 57/60 to 60/60 under constant ramp rate factors.
AI.conclusion: Neural oscillator and ramp dynamics can generate articulatory timing under specified phasing rules, complementing a preceding mental-lexicon model toward continuous online speech production.

title: MM-ReportBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Multimodal Report Generation from Tables
summary: The ability to generate multimodal reports integrating fluent narratives with faithful visualizations from tabular data, has become a cornerstone capability for modern vision-language models in practical domains such as finance, healthcare, and policy making. However, existing benchmarks are limited by single-modality focus, simplistic metrics, novelty evaluation, and visualization quality. We address these limitations with MM-ReportBench, a multimodal report evaluation benchmark covering 386 tasks across 185 real-world tables. Each task is paired with an expert-curated reference report featuring standardized chapter structures and verifiable key insight points, constructed through a hybrid pipeline of multimodal reports generation based on Monte Carlo Tree Search and rigorous human quality control. For robust evaluation, we design a dual-judge evaluation framework: Text Judge Model assesses textual quality along structural completeness, grounded insight verification with numerical fact-checking against source tables, and novelty analysis that distinguishes genuine analytical discovery from trivial paraphrasing; Visualization Judge Model evaluates generated visualizations across data fidelity, expressiveness, aesthetics, and technical correctness. They also evaluate cross-modal consistency. Extensive experiments on 20 state-of-the-art models reveal critical weaknesses: even the strongest model achieves only 68.9 overall score, with numerical hallucination affecting 38.5% of reports and genuinely novel insights remaining rare. Our ablation studies further demonstrate that single-judge evaluation consistently inflates scores by 8-12 points compared to dual-judge assessment, confirming that rigorous and reliable benchmarking demands multi-faceted, complementary evaluation probes.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce MM-ReportBench, a benchmark of 386 multimodal report generation tasks from 185 tables with a dual-judge evaluation framework, showing that even the strongest of 20 models scores only 68.9 overall with 38.5% numerical hallucination.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for multimodal report generation from tables suffer from single-modality focus, simplistic metrics, and lack of novelty and visualization quality evaluation.
AI.method: MM-ReportBench pairs 386 tasks across 185 real-world tables with expert-curated reference reports (built via MCTS and human QC) and evaluates outputs using a Text Judge Model (structure, numerical fact-checking, novelty) and a Visualization Judge Model (fidelity, aesthetics, cross-modal consistency).
AI.result: Across 20 state-of-the-art models, the strongest achieves only 68.9 overall score, 38.5% of reports contain numerical hallucinations, genuinely novel insights are rare, and single-judge evaluation inflates scores by 8-12 points compared to dual-judge assessment.
AI.conclusion: Current vision-language models struggle with faithful, insightful multimodal report generation from tables, and rigorous evaluation requires complementary dual-judge probes.

title: JET: Just-Enough Exploration Tuning for Efficient Tool-Calling Agents in Repository-Level Question Answering
summary: In repository-level question answering (QA), an agent explores a code repository with tools and should answer a question once enough information is gathered. Nevertheless, we find that LLM agents often continue to invoke tools even after the gathered information is already sufficient to answer. We call this phenomenon over-exploration. Moreover, even though existing methods improve task performance through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on expert trajectories, SFT also propagates the over-exploration in the trajectories to the agent. To mitigate over-exploration, we propose Just-Enough Exploration Tuning (JET), a fine-tuning method that trains the agent to answer once the gathered information is sufficient. JET truncates each training trajectory at the step where the gathered information becomes sufficient, inserts a rationale that explains why the agent can answer at that step, and fine-tunes the agent with a higher loss weight on the rationale. Experiments on two repository-level QA benchmarks with two open-weight 8B models demonstrate that JET reduces tool calls by 11 to 33% on self-generated trajectories while largely preserving the score. On expert trajectories, JET makes 18 to 28% fewer tool calls than SFT while retaining most of the score gain of SFT. In both cases, JET also lowers the inference cost.

AI.tldr: The authors propose Just-Enough Exploration Tuning (JET), which truncates training trajectories at the point of sufficient information and weights an inserted stopping rationale, reducing tool calls by 11-33% in repository-level QA while preserving accuracy.
AI.motivation: LLM agents in repository-level QA often continue invoking tools after gathering sufficient information (over-exploration), and standard SFT on expert trajectories propagates this inefficiency.
AI.method: JET truncates each training trajectory at the step where gathered information becomes sufficient, inserts a rationale explaining why the agent can answer, and fine-tunes the agent with a higher loss weight on that rationale.
AI.result: On two repository-level QA benchmarks with two open-weight 8B models, JET reduces tool calls by 11-33% on self-generated trajectories while largely preserving scores, and makes 18-28% fewer tool calls than SFT on expert trajectories while retaining most of SFT's score gain.
AI.conclusion: Teaching agents to recognize information sufficiency during fine-tuning curbs over-exploration and lowers inference cost without sacrificing QA performance.

title: AfriNORM: An Evaluation Benchmark for Normative Reasoning of LLMs Across African Cultures
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed across various sectors. However, current evaluation benchmarks are insufficient to assess the applicability of these models in local African contexts, as most focus on linguistic fluency (grammar/translation) rather than cultural competence. The few existing benchmarks that measure general knowledge or social conventions do not capture the African deontic modality, i.e., the strict norms and taboos that govern diverse social interactions. In this paper, we introduce AfriNORM, a scenario-based, multiple-choice question dataset designed to measure and diagnose the normative reasoning limitations of LLMs when applied to African sociocultural contexts. We introduce two metrics: a Universal Commonsense Bias Score (UCBS) to quantify commonsense bias in LLM and a Distractor Bias Score (DBS) to quantify an LLM's limited understanding of African cultural norms. We also conduct a case study on the Yorùbá language, identifying confusion gaps in two closed-source LLMs, "Gemini 2.0 Flash" and "GPT-5", and one open-source LLM, "Llama 3.1 8B Instruct" when prompted in English versus Yorùbá. While their accuracy in English is high, their performance in Yorùbá is much lower, attributable to cultural confusion rather than simple bias, indicating that the models exhibit semantic confusion when reasoning about norms in Yorùbá.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce AfriNORM, a scenario-based multiple-choice benchmark for African normative reasoning, and show in a Yorùbá case study that Gemini 2.0 Flash, GPT-5, and Llama 3.1 8B Instruct perform much worse in Yorùbá than in English due to cultural confusion.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for LLMs in African contexts focus on linguistic fluency rather than cultural competence and the strict norms and taboos (deontic modality) governing social interactions.
AI.method: AfriNORM provides scenario-based multiple-choice questions paired with two new metrics—Universal Commonsense Bias Score (UCBS) and Distractor Bias Score (DBS)—and is applied to Gemini 2.0 Flash, GPT-5, and Llama 3.1 8B Instruct in English and Yorùbá.
AI.result: While all three models achieve high accuracy in English, their performance drops substantially in Yorùbá, driven by cultural and semantic confusion rather than simple bias.
AI.conclusion: High English performance on cultural norms does not transfer to African languages, highlighting the need for culturally grounded benchmarks like AfriNORM.

title: Understanding Cross-Modal Inconsistency through Representation Subspaces in Omni Models
summary: Omni Models process audio, vision, and text within a unified language backbone, yet often produce different answers for semantically equivalent inputs across modalities. Existing representation-level analyses do not distinguish between information that predicts whether disagreement will occur and the representation whose perturbation affects the model's answer. In this paper, we estimate a low-dimensional Answer Subspace from answer-position representations and use it to separate answer-related components from the remaining representation. Across three Omni Models and two multimodal reasoning tasks, information predictive of cross-modal inconsistency lies mainly outside the Answer Subspace, concentrating in a reproducible two-dimensional representation that is not explained by a fixed modality offset. Matched interventions reveal distinct behavioral roles: perturbing the Answer Subspace substantially changes the model's predictions, whereas perturbing the disagreement representation, like a random subspace of the same dimensionality, leaves them almost unchanged. Our key finding is that cross-modal disagreement can be induced by misaligning modality-specific answer representations: perturbing the Answer Subspace for only one modality induces disagreement, whereas applying the same perturbation to both largely preserves agreement. Thus, the representation that predicts disagreement is distinct from the answer-level representation through which disagreement can be induced, showing that linear decodability does not imply behavioral efficacy.

AI.tldr: By estimating a low-dimensional Answer Subspace in Omni Models, the authors show that information predicting cross-modal disagreement lies in a separate two-dimensional representation whose perturbation does not change answers, whereas misaligning modality-specific answer representations induces disagreement.
AI.motivation: Omni Models often produce different answers for semantically equivalent audio, vision, and text inputs, and existing analyses conflate representations that predict disagreement with those that causally affect model answers.
AI.method: The authors estimate a low-dimensional Answer Subspace from answer-position representations across three Omni Models and two multimodal reasoning tasks, and perform matched subspace interventions on both the Answer Subspace and the disagreement-predictive representation.
AI.result: Perturbing the Answer Subspace substantially changes predictions (and perturbing it for only one modality induces disagreement, whereas perturbing both preserves agreement), while perturbing the 2D disagreement-predictive representation leaves predictions almost unchanged.
AI.conclusion: Linear decodability of cross-modal disagreement does not imply behavioral efficacy; disagreement is causally governed by misalignment of modality-specific answer representations.

title: Contract-Explicit Evaluation: From Auditing Learned Readers to Scoped Certificates
comment: 50 pages, 4 figures. Supplementary material (Online Resource 1, 14 pages) included as ancillary file. Artifact repository: this https URL. Submitted to Applied Intelligence
summary: Evaluation readings of document-level relation extraction (DocRE) systems depend jointly on the model and the evaluation contract: gold version, scoring function, threshold. Rankings reverse across contracts, yet no existing method determines which comparisons survive the reversal. We address this gap with contract-explicit evaluation: a preregistered five-step protocol (Declare, Measure, Scope, Certify, Hedge), operationalizing the classical concordance decomposition of Kendall's rank correlation, that scopes certifiable regions and delivers distribution-free census certificates across two ecosystems. In the DocRE audit (44 training runs of one in-house architecture family), the scoring dimension scopes to a census certificate (three flagged instances, Clopper--Pearson upper bound 0.146); the confirmatory record includes registered negatives, and the audit prices its own simplification finding---the calibration dial's entire margin is one withdrawn commit. In an LLM-judge census (17 judges, 49,938 battles), 12.25% of leaderboard comparisons require hedging at the pre-declared split criterion (bound 0.124; panel-robust 0.143), with an exploratory two-tier reading certifying 69% at a bound \le 0.072 and a validity decomposition against released human labels (65% of contested battles are judge error, not ambiguity). The cross-model certificate is withdrawn on real confidence scores; the failure spectrum maps the boundary. The protocol, map, ledger, and per-instance artifacts are released.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces contract-explicit evaluation, a preregistered five-step protocol that scopes certifiable comparisons and provides distribution-free census certificates when evaluation rankings reverse across contracts.
AI.motivation: Evaluation readings in document-level relation extraction (DocRE) and LLM-judge leaderboards depend jointly on the model and the evaluation contract (gold version, scoring function, threshold), causing rankings to reverse without a method to determine which comparisons survive.
AI.method: They propose a preregistered five-step protocol (Declare, Measure, Scope, Certify, Hedge) operationalizing Kendall's rank correlation concordance decomposition to scope certifiable regions and produce distribution-free census certificates.
AI.result: In a DocRE audit (44 training runs), the scoring dimension scopes to a census certificate (3 flagged instances, Clopper-Pearson upper bound 0.146); in an LLM-judge census (17 judges, 49,938 battles), 12.25% of leaderboard comparisons require hedging (bound 0.124, panel-robust 0.143), an exploratory two-tier reading certifies 69% at bound <= 0.072, and 65% of contested battles are judge error rather than ambiguity, while the cross-model certificate is withdrawn on real confidence scores.
AI.conclusion: Contract-explicit evaluation provides a principled, reproducible way to separate certifiable model comparisons from contract-sensitive reversals and judge errors.

title: Visibility Graph Representations of Word Embeddings for Text Classification
summary: Text classifiers depend on representations that expose the distinctions between classes in a form the learning model can use, and a restricted vocabulary changes which representation is most effective. This paper studies natural visibility graphs as an intermediate representation for news topic classification under controlled vocabulary budgets. Word embeddings are averaged into a fixed-length document vector, the vector is read as an ordered numerical series, and its natural visibility graph is passed to a classifier either as an ordered node-degree vector or as an adjacency matrix. On the four-class AG News benchmark, chi-square selection retains 100 to 1,500 words, and the graph inputs are compared with direct embedding-based representations from continuous bag-of-words, skip-gram, GloVe, FastText and BERT. With a fully connected classifier, the degree representation is the most accurate configuration from 700 selected words onward; it reaches its highest accuracy of 91.24% at 1,000 words and exceeds the BERT-based baseline by 0.29 percentage points at 1,500 words. In a separate convolutional comparison, the adjacency input reaches 86.16% at 1,000 words, against 83.12% for the strongest static embedding. The results indicate that visibility-derived features can be competitive once the selected vocabulary provides adequate coverage. We discuss the roles of graph compression, coordinate ordering and classifier choice, and the controls needed to establish the reliability of the small differences observed.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates natural visibility graphs constructed from averaged word embeddings as intermediate representations for news topic classification under controlled vocabulary budgets.
AI.motivation: Text classifiers rely on representations that expose class distinctions, and restricting the vocabulary size alters which representation works best.
AI.method: Word embeddings are averaged into a fixed-length document vector, read as an ordered numerical series, and converted into a natural visibility graph passed to a classifier as either an ordered node-degree vector or an adjacency matrix, compared against CBOW, skip-gram, GloVe, FastText, and BERT on AG News with chi-square selection of 100 to 1,500 words.
AI.result: With a fully connected classifier, the degree representation is most accurate from 700 words onward, peaking at 91.24% at 1,000 words and exceeding the BERT baseline by 0.29 percentage points at 1,500 words; in a convolutional comparison, the adjacency input reaches 86.16% at 1,000 words versus 83.12% for the strongest static embedding.
AI.conclusion: Visibility-derived graph features can be competitive with standard embeddings for text classification once the selected vocabulary provides sufficient coverage.

title: Route Optimization under Port Congestion and Carbon Reduction: An NSGA-II Approach
summary: Maritime shipping simultaneously faces the dual challenges of escalating port congestion and increasingly stringent decarbonization mandates. Large-scale vessel anchorage at hub ports inflates unit transport costs while generating significant additional \(CO_2\) emissions from idling auxiliary engines. This study develops a multi-objective routing optimization framework that jointly incorporates time, transport, and carbon emission costs under congestion-dependent generalized cost functions. A variational inequality (VI) model is formulated to characterize network equilibrium in vessel route allocation, while the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II) is deployed to solve the resulting three-objective optimization problem. The model is empirically validated using China's coastal container network (Shanghai as the primary congested port, Ningbo-Zhoushan as the backup alternative), with sensitivity analyses conducted across congestion levels, carbon tax rates, and fuel price differentials. Key findings indicate that: (1) alternative ports effectively hedge congestion when diversion costs fall below waiting costs, with a diversion threshold at approximately 60 vessel calls; (2) a carbon tax of 80/t \(CO_2\) pushes clean fuel adoption above 50%; and (3) fuel prices primarily influence energy-type selection rather than port diversion decisions, confirming that the two decision dimensions operate independently. These findings offer actionable decision support for port authorities, regulators, and shipping operators seeking to balance economic efficiency with environmental sustainability.

AI.tldr: This study develops a multi-objective maritime routing optimization framework using variational inequality and NSGA-II to balance transport time, cost, and CO2 emissions under port congestion.
AI.motivation: Maritime shipping faces escalating port congestion and strict decarbonization mandates, where vessel anchorage at hub ports inflates transport costs and increases idling auxiliary engine CO2 emissions.
AI.method: A variational inequality (VI) model characterizes network equilibrium in vessel route allocation under congestion-dependent generalized cost functions, and NSGA-II solves the resulting three-objective optimization problem, validated on China's coastal container network (Shanghai as primary port, Ningbo-Zhoushan as backup).
AI.result: Alternative ports effectively hedge congestion when diversion costs fall below waiting costs with a diversion threshold around 60 vessel calls, a carbon tax of 80/t CO2 pushes clean fuel adoption above 50%, and fuel prices primarily affect energy-type selection rather than port diversion decisions.
AI.conclusion: Port diversion and fuel selection operate as independent decision dimensions, offering actionable guidance for port authorities, regulators, and shipping operators balancing economic efficiency and decarbonization.

title: Cross-cultural Adaptation of Recipes for Low-Resource Languages: A Benchmark and Multilingual Culinary Lexicon for Hausa, Yorùbá, and Igbo
summary: Recent multilingual large language models (LLMs) have improved machine translation, yet culturally adaptive translation for low-resource languages (LRLs) remains underexplored. This is particularly challenging for recipes, where ingredients, cooking tools, measurements, and procedures may require adaptation to the target cultural context. In this work, we introduce ReciLoReL, a benchmark of 600 expert-translated and culturally adapted recipes across Yorùbá, Hausa, and Igbo (three of the most prominent languages in Nigeria), and ReciLex, a multilingual culinary lexicon containing approximately 15,000 translated entities across ten recipe entity categories, including ingredients, tools, chef actions, state of tools, and durations. We evaluate state-of-the-art multilingual LLMs for English-to-LRL recipe translation under zero-shot and few-shot settings and investigate whether augmenting LLMs with ReciLex improves culturally adaptive recipe translation without requiring large target-language recipe corpora for training or fine-tuning. Beyond conventional reference-based translation evaluation using BLEU, chrF, and TER, we introduce five criteria for evaluating cultural adaptation, adapted from established cross-cultural adaptation methods. Across the selected LLMs and languages, ReciLex improves average BLEU from 13.57 to 14.51 and chrF from 37.89 to 38.74, while reducing TER from 77.14 to 75.12. Human evaluation further shows improvements ranging from 0.11 to 0.36 points across the five cultural adaptation evaluation criteria on a five-point scale. Overall, our work provides new resources, evaluation criteria, and empirical evaluation for studying culturally adaptive recipe translation in low-resource settings.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ReciLoReL, a benchmark of 600 culturally adapted recipes in Hausa, Yorùbá, and Igbo, and ReciLex, a 15,000-entity multilingual culinary lexicon, showing that lexicon augmentation improves culturally adaptive recipe translation by LLMs.
AI.motivation: Culturally adaptive machine translation for low-resource languages remains underexplored, especially for recipes where ingredients, tools, measurements, and procedures require cultural adaptation.
AI.method: They build ReciLoReL (600 expert-translated and culturally adapted recipes) and ReciLex (~15,000 translated entities across ten categories), and evaluate multilingual LLMs in zero-shot and few-shot English-to-LRL translation with and without ReciLex using BLEU, chrF, TER, and five human cultural adaptation criteria.
AI.result: Augmenting LLMs with ReciLex improves average BLEU from 13.57 to 14.51 and chrF from 37.89 to 38.74, reduces TER from 77.14 to 75.12, and yields human evaluation gains of 0.11 to 0.36 points across the five cultural adaptation criteria on a five-point scale.
AI.conclusion: ReciLoReL, ReciLex, and the proposed evaluation criteria establish resources and empirical baselines for culturally adaptive translation in low-resource settings without requiring large target-language training corpora.

title: StitchRAG: Constructing Compact and Evidence-Preserving Contexts for RAG with Diffusion-Based Stitching
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves factuality by grounding large language models (LLMs) in external evidence. However, long retrieved contexts incur computational overhead and can even hurt performance due to noisy or irrelevant content. We propose \textsc{StitchRAG}, a framework for constructing compact context in RAG. \textsc{StitchRAG} builds a faithful, information-dense context while dynamically compressing the retrieved passages. We adapt the size reduction ratio to each passage by formulating a utility maximization trading-off the retained information and computation costs. We then extract answer candidates and query-related keywords from passages as anchors and collect passage sentences containing anchors under the derived size constraint. Finally, we connect or stitch the collected sentences together using text diffusion to form a coherent and natural context. Experiments on five open-domain QA benchmarks show that \textsc{StitchRAG} consistently outperforms diverse multi-step and compression baselines. Extensive ablations show the effectiveness of dynamic size allocation, anchor preservation, and diffusion-based stitching.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes StitchRAG, a framework that compresses retrieved RAG passages dynamically and stitches anchor-containing sentences together using text diffusion to form compact, coherent contexts.
AI.motivation: Long retrieved contexts in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) incur high computational overhead and can degrade performance due to noisy or irrelevant content.
AI.method: StitchRAG formulates a utility maximization problem to adapt the size reduction ratio per passage, extracts answer candidates and query-related keywords as anchors to select sentences under the size budget, and connects the selected sentences via text diffusion.
AI.result: Experiments on five open-domain QA benchmarks show that StitchRAG consistently outperforms diverse multi-step and compression baselines, with ablations confirming the contributions of dynamic size allocation, anchor preservation, and diffusion-based stitching.
AI.conclusion: Combining utility-driven sentence selection with diffusion-based stitching yields compact, evidence-preserving contexts that improve RAG efficiency and accuracy.

title: Compact and Decodable Electrocardiogram Text for Large Language Models
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables. Preprint of a chapter submitted to "Advances in Artificial Intelligence and Data Science: Methods, Systems, and Applications" (Karabük University Press). Code: this https URL
summary: When a twelve-lead electrocardiogram is written as text for a large language model, the number of tokens has to be balanced against the information lost through compression. This paper presents a deterministic encoding that writes eight independent leads as amplitude letters and exact time gaps and recovers the remaining four limb leads algebraically. The key points are selected with a cardiac-cycle-dependent tolerance, the amplitudes are parameterized by a 26-letter logarithmic codebook learned from a training set, and a 10-step tolerance schedule keeps all records within a fixed token budget. The encoding was applied to 21,388 records from the public PTB-XL database and evaluated using an exact decode-and-re-encode round trip, waveform reconstruction error, and a paired comparison of convolutional classifiers trained with 5 different seeds on signals from the original and decoded databases. All records were contained in 4,080 tokens (average: 2,866 tokens, 64.3% fewer than a per-sample transcription), and all stored lead strings were exactly reproduced. The average correlation between the decoded and reference signals was 0.982. The macro-averaged area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.9167 for the reference signals and 0.9157 for the decoded signals (paired difference -0.0010; 95% patient-level bootstrap interval, -0.0028 to 0.0007), within the pre-specified non-inferiority margin of -0.010; this is not a confirmatory result, because the test fold had been used during encoder development. The diagnostic content of a compact text can therefore be preserved, while the language model's ability to read the text is yet another matter.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a deterministic text encoding for 12-lead electrocardiograms (ECGs) that compresses signals to fit within LLM token budgets while preserving diagnostic waveform information.
AI.motivation: Writing 12-lead ECGs as text for large language models requires balancing token count against information loss from compression.
AI.method: The encoding writes eight independent leads as amplitude letters (from a 26-letter logarithmic codebook) and exact time gaps using a cardiac-cycle-dependent tolerance and a 10-step tolerance schedule, while recovering the remaining four limb leads algebraically.
AI.result: Applied to 21,388 PTB-XL records, all records fit within 4,080 tokens (average 2,866 tokens, 64.3% fewer than per-sample transcription) with exact round-trip reproduction, 0.982 average decoded-reference correlation, and a convolutional classifier macro-AUROC of 0.9157 vs. 0.9167 for reference signals (paired difference -0.0010, within the -0.010 non-inferiority margin, though non-confirmatory due to test-fold use during development).
AI.conclusion: Compact deterministic text encoding can preserve the diagnostic content of 12-lead ECGs within tight token budgets, leaving LLM reading capability as a separate challenge.

title: When Passing Checks Do Not Establish Completion: Evidence Interpretation in Coding Agents
comment: 12 pages; supplementary material included as ancillary files
summary: Verification procedures in coding agents must preserve execution facts, interpret their scope and discharge checking obligations. We study these responsibilities through qualified repository checks, controlled evidence consumers and executable workflows. A prospective thirteen-task factorial study finds that correct reported facts need not yield the requested finite verdict. Conversely, all 122 delivered labels in a held-out receipt-supply study are correct, while sixteen responses misreport facts and eleven others exceed authorized scope. Production repair supplies successful controls and finite-supported preservation failures. Across 118 repair episodes on 31 tasks, source interventions separate startup reachability from repair and witness production from the claimed operation. Lifetime and resource controls delimit what passing validation establishes. Generated-note comparisons yield local repair differences but can state false explanations; strong ordinary baselines, new tasks and Skill-transfer studies supply no consistent overall advantage. These results characterize evidence interpretation, applicability and fulfilled actions while limiting claims of general diagnostic superiority, Skill deterioration or deployed folding effects.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how coding agents interpret verification evidence, finding that passing checks and correct reported facts do not reliably establish task completion or valid explanations.
AI.motivation: Verification procedures in coding agents must preserve execution facts, interpret their scope, and discharge checking obligations, yet how agents handle these responsibilities in practice is poorly understood.
AI.method: They conduct a 13-task factorial study, a held-out receipt-supply study (122 labels), and 118 production repair episodes across 31 tasks using qualified repository checks, controlled evidence consumers, source interventions, and lifetime/resource controls.
AI.result: Correct reported facts do not guarantee the requested finite verdict; in the receipt-supply study, all 122 labels are correct but 16 responses misreport facts and 11 exceed authorized scope; source interventions separate startup reachability from repair and witness production from claimed operations, while generated-note comparisons can state false explanations and Skill-transfer studies show no consistent overall advantage.
AI.conclusion: The findings delimit what passing validation establishes in coding agents and caution against broad claims of diagnostic superiority or Skill deterioration.

title: When Do Typed Decision Models Work in Transportation? Evidence from Travel Choice and Traffic Signal Control
summary: Typed decision models combine natural-language understanding with a structured interface that returns a selected action and an option-level probability distribution without generating lengthy textual responses. Their low inference cost and response latency make them attractive for transportation problems with predefined alternatives. This paper investigates their effectiveness, robustness, and efficiency in two representative transportation tasks: individual travel-mode choice prediction and sequential traffic signal control. We systematically evaluate TypeSafe Jev and GPT-6 Luna Decisions against conventional transportation methods, reinforcement learning algorithms, and four chat-based large language models. Experiments on the Swissmetro dataset show that typed decision models achieve lower prediction accuracy than traditional discrete choice models and the strongest chat-based baseline, while their performance varies substantially with input representation and question framing. In closed-loop traffic signal control experiments, typed decision models demonstrate competitive performance against established controllers in several scenarios, but exhibit performance degradation under more challenging network conditions. Furthermore, the typed models achieve lower inference latency and computational cost than the evaluated chat-based large language models, highlighting their potential for efficient, zero-shot transportation decision-making. Overall, these findings demonstrate both the potential and limitations of typed decision models, emphasizing the importance of input design, task characteristics, and robustness evaluation for their effective application in transportation systems.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates typed decision models in travel-mode choice prediction and traffic signal control, finding they offer lower latency and cost than chat LLMs but trail traditional methods in accuracy and degrade under challenging conditions.
AI.motivation: Typed decision models return structured actions and option-level probabilities with low latency and cost, but their effectiveness and robustness in transportation tasks with predefined alternatives remain unclear.
AI.method: They benchmark TypeSafe Jev and GPT-6 Luna Decisions against conventional transportation models, reinforcement learning algorithms, and four chat-based LLMs on Swissmetro travel-mode choice prediction and closed-loop sequential traffic signal control.
AI.result: On Swissmetro, typed decision models achieve lower prediction accuracy than traditional discrete choice models and the strongest chat-based baseline, with high sensitivity to input representation and framing; in traffic signal control, they are competitive in several scenarios but degrade under harder network conditions, while achieving lower latency and computational cost than chat LLMs.
AI.conclusion: Typed decision models show promise for efficient zero-shot transportation decision-making, but effective deployment requires careful input design and robustness evaluation.

title: The Shared Word: Evaluating Language Models on Dutch Word Puzzles
summary: Many LLM benchmarks for languages other than English are translated, multiple-choice, or difficult to score automatically. We introduce The Shared Word (TSW-NL), a Dutch benchmark built around four core principles: it is language-specific, open-vocabulary, human-curated, and deterministically scored. Each puzzle gives three clues that describe different senses or uses of the same Dutch word. The clues are individually ambiguous, requiring the solver to combine evidence across multiple clues. We construct the benchmark from Dutch Wikipedia disambiguation pages, followed by automatic filtering and extensive manual curation. The final dataset contains 222 instances, with three independent human answers per test item. The task is clearly challenging: scores in our human study range from 49.5% to 61.0% and the highest-scoring open-weight model we tested reaches only 39.3%. Many others even score below 20%. At the same time, closed-source models show great progress: GPT-4.1 (April 2025) scores 59.2%, whereas GPT-5.6 Sol with max reasoning scores 88.8%. We believe this task provides a useful addition to Dutch model evaluation, plus a clear recipe that can be applied to construct a similar benchmark for other languages.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces The Shared Word (TSW-NL), a human-curated, deterministically scored Dutch word puzzle benchmark of 222 instances, revealing a large gap between open-weight models and top closed-source models.
AI.motivation: Non-English LLM benchmarks are often translated, multiple-choice, or hard to score automatically, limiting language-specific evaluation.
AI.method: They construct TSW-NL from Dutch Wikipedia disambiguation pages via automatic filtering and manual curation, where each of 222 puzzles provides three ambiguous clues describing different senses of one Dutch word, evaluated against three independent human answers per item.
AI.result: Human scores range from 49.5% to 61.0%, the highest-scoring open-weight model reaches 39.3% (with many below 20%), GPT-4.1 scores 59.2%, and GPT-5.6 Sol with max reasoning reaches 88.8%.
AI.conclusion: TSW-NL provides a challenging, deterministically scored Dutch benchmark and a reproducible recipe for building language-specific word puzzle evaluations in other languages.

title: Can Decision Models Replace LLMs in Real-World Contact Center Classification and Judging Tasks?
summary: Contact center systems often need to make bounded decisions, such as identifying a caller's intent, retrieving the knowledge-base article that answers a query, assessing agent compliance, or judging the output of AI models used in production. Decision models return a typed answer and its probability directly, making them a promising cost-effective alternative to generative Large Language Models (LLMs) in such bounded conversational tasks. However, their effectiveness in real-world contact center applications remains unclear. In this paper, we compare nine decision models against thirteen generative LLMs in zero-shot settings across eight contact center use cases: six classification tasks and two judging tasks. Our experiments demonstrate that many decision models can match the performance of frontier LLMs on contact center classification, and API-based closed decision models achieve this at the lowest per-request cost among the API models we evaluate. We further observe that their confident predictions are more accurate, enabling selective routing in real-world production scenarios. Across classification tasks, the main weakness of most decision models is abstention: they rarely choose the no-answer option, which accounts for most of their gap to the strongest LLMs (although Gemini-Decision-1 is the notable exception in this regard). We also find that the judging quality of decision models drops sharply for smaller models, and they are also more prone to position bias. In short, our findings provide practical guidance for selecting decision models based on abstention behavior, confidence, and deployment cost, rather than overall accuracy alone.

AI.tldr: This paper compares nine decision models against thirteen generative LLMs across eight real-world contact center tasks, finding that decision models match frontier LLMs on classification at lower cost but struggle with abstention and smaller-model judging.
AI.motivation: Decision models return typed answers and probabilities directly, offering a potentially cheaper alternative to generative LLMs for bounded contact center decisions, but their real-world effectiveness is untested.
AI.method: They evaluate nine decision models and thirteen generative LLMs zero-shot across eight contact center use cases (six classification tasks and two judging tasks), analyzing accuracy, per-request cost, confidence calibration, abstention behavior, and position bias.
AI.result: Many decision models match frontier LLMs on classification, with API-based closed decision models achieving the lowest per-request cost and higher accuracy on confident predictions; however, most decision models (except Gemini-Decision-1) rarely abstain, and judging quality drops sharply for smaller models with greater position bias.
AI.conclusion: Selecting decision models for production contact centers should account for abstention behavior, confidence-based routing, and deployment cost rather than overall accuracy alone.

title: Large Language Models Have Not Yet Transformed Science
summary: The emergence of large language models (LLMs) in late 2022 has raised questions about the future of science, but assessing their impact requires understanding how scientific practices were already evolving. We analyze 2.5 million full-text papers across five disciplines from 2015 to 2025, tracing trends over a broad spectrum of lexical, structural, epistemological, and social dimensions. Aside from frequency shifts in some words, most pre-2023 trends continued with limited detectable breaks. Among the notable exceptions, growth in computer science coauthor teams accelerated significantly in Asia, while apparent declines in biomedical topic diversity largely reflected standardization in article formats. Our study establishes an empirical foundation for monitoring the health of global science as LLM adoption deepens.

AI.tldr: Analyzing 2.5 million full-text papers from 2015 to 2025 across five disciplines, this study finds that LLMs have not yet caused widespread structural or epistemological breaks in scientific practices.
AI.motivation: The rise of LLMs in late 2022 prompted claims about transforming science, but assessing their actual impact requires comparing post-2022 shifts against pre-existing trends.
AI.method: They trace lexical, structural, epistemological, and social dimensions across 2.5 million full-text papers spanning five disciplines from 2015 to 2025.
AI.result: Aside from frequency shifts in certain words, most pre-2023 trends continued with limited detectable breaks; notable exceptions include accelerated growth of computer science coauthor teams in Asia and apparent declines in biomedical topic diversity driven largely by article format standardization.
AI.conclusion: The study provides an empirical baseline showing limited structural transformation of science so far and a foundation for monitoring future LLM impact.

title: TPHC: Improving Hyper-Connections with Tensor-Parallel Grouped Updates
summary: Hyper-Connections (HC) expand the residual stream of a Transformer into $N$ parallel streams, and manifold-constrained HC (mHC) stabilizes them at scale. However, mHC benefits little from more than four streams, partly because each sublayer writes a single output to all streams, limiting how differently they can be updated. In this work, we propose TPHC, which integrates tensor-parallel (TP) shards with HC streams to promote greater independence across streams. Specifically, we route a separate mixture of the residual streams to each TP shard and keep the individual shard outputs separate during write-back, so each stream can receive a different mixture of those outputs. This design makes the residual-stream updates more expressive without adding parameters or FLOPs to the attention or FFN sublayers. With native support for stream sharding under TP, TPHC requires only 9% more training time than mHC on an 8B model when both use four streams. Increasing the number of streams from four to sixteen raises its training time by only 19%. On a 1.1B model trained on 100B tokens, TPHC reduces validation loss by 0.7-1.0% and raises average zero-shot accuracy across six commonsense reasoning benchmarks by 0.3-0.7 percentage points relative to mHC at matched stream counts $N\in\{4,8,16\}$. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes TPHC, which integrates tensor-parallel (TP) shards with Hyper-Connections (HC) residual streams to enable more expressive stream updates without adding parameters or FLOPs.
AI.motivation: Manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) gain little beyond four residual streams because each sublayer writes a single shared output to all streams, limiting update diversity.
AI.method: TPHC routes a separate mixture of residual streams to each TP shard and keeps individual shard outputs separate during write-back so each stream receives a distinct mixture of shard outputs, with native stream sharding under TP.
AI.result: On an 8B model with four streams, TPHC adds only 9% training time over mHC (and 19% when scaling from 4 to 16 streams); on a 1.1B model trained on 100B tokens, TPHC reduces validation loss by 0.7-1.0% and improves average zero-shot accuracy across six commonsense reasoning benchmarks by 0.3-0.7 percentage points over mHC at N in {4, 8, 16}.
AI.conclusion: Integrating tensor-parallel sharding with Hyper-Connections unlocks greater residual-stream expressivity at low overhead without increasing sublayer parameters or FLOPs.

title: Runtime Verification of Multiple Natural Language Criteria for Agent Governance
summary: AI agents are governed by hundreds of natural language criteria, yet existing verifiers cannot efficiently evaluate an agent's output against a large set of such criteria and report which are satisfied, violated, or inapplicable. We introduce the VFM, a tree-attention verifier that encodes the shared context and target text, and scores N natural language criteria in parallel, returning independent per-criterion ternary verdicts. The VFM is pretrained on CriteriaBank, a corpus of 394K (context, target, criterion, verdict) tuples spanning over 321K distinct criterion strings. A finetuned VFM-4B outperforms GPT-5.4 on a synthetic governance benchmark. On the DynaBench multi-criterion benchmark, it outperforms DynaGuard-4B on trace-level failure detection, and its per-criterion verdicts localize the violated rule and support focused escalation to a larger chain-of-thought judge. We show that CriteriaBank pretraining improves cross-domain transfer, particularly in the low-data regime, while matching a strong direct-finetuning control at full data. On a single H100, VFM-4B evaluates 1,000 criteria against a 4K-token context in under 2s at <11 GB VRAM, making it suitable for runtime verification.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces VFM, a tree-attention verifier pretrained on CriteriaBank (394K tuples), that evaluates an agent's output against 1,000 natural language criteria in parallel in under 2 seconds.
AI.motivation: AI agents are governed by hundreds of natural language criteria, but existing verifiers cannot efficiently evaluate outputs against large criterion sets and localize which rules are satisfied, violated, or inapplicable.
AI.method: VFM uses tree attention to encode the shared context and target text once and score N criteria in parallel with independent per-criterion ternary verdicts, pretrained on CriteriaBank (394K tuples across >321K distinct criteria).
AI.result: A finetuned VFM-4B outperforms GPT-5.4 on a synthetic governance benchmark and beats DynaGuard-4B on DynaBench trace-level failure detection while localizing violated rules; on one H100, VFM-4B evaluates 1,000 criteria against a 4K-token context in under 2s using <11 GB VRAM.
AI.conclusion: VFM enables fast, localized, and scalable runtime verification of natural language governance criteria for AI agents.

title: What's in a Tree ? Hierarchical $n$-gram models as controlled approximators of language
summary: Hierarchical models have been proposed as synthetic settings for studying language. However, their relevance to realistic language corpora remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce tree-grams, autoregressive generative $n$-gram models that build the conditional probability tensor $p(x_n \mid x_{1:n-1})$ through a hierarchical composition of order-2 and order-3 tensors. $n$ controls the maximal context window, whereas a rank hyperparameter $d$ controls model capacity, yielding an interpretable and systematically scalable family of approximators of language. We show how tree-grams outperform existing $n$-gram baselines, while remaining competitive with deep transformer-based language models. We demonstrate the utility of such controlled approximations by using tree-grams as generative models. In particular, we show that hyperparameter transfer under $\mu$P can be made more robust when narrower models are tuned on simpler data, generated by tree-grams with moderate $n$ and $d$. In addition, we show that entropy and effective range of correlations control performance gap after fine-tuning. This is because tree-grams allow us to explicitly control horizon and capacity. When allowed to route across candidate topologies, we observe emergent sparsity in tree-grams. Such concentrated routing permits pruning upto 95\% of topologies without significant change in performance.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces tree-grams, autoregressive hierarchical n-gram models built from order-2 and order-3 tensors, as interpretable and scalable language approximators that improve muP hyperparameter transfer.
AI.motivation: Hierarchical models are used as synthetic settings to study language, but their relevance and utility for realistic language corpora remain underexplored.
AI.method: Tree-grams construct the conditional probability tensor p(x_n | x_{1:n-1}) via hierarchical composition of order-2 and order-3 tensors, where n controls context window and rank d controls capacity, and can route across candidate topologies.
AI.result: Tree-grams outperform existing n-gram baselines while remaining competitive with deep transformers; tuning narrower models on tree-gram-generated data makes muP hyperparameter transfer more robust, and routing exhibits emergent sparsity allowing up to 95% topology pruning without significant performance loss.
AI.conclusion: Tree-grams provide a controlled, interpretable family of language approximators useful for studying correlation range, entropy, and hyperparameter transfer.

title: Natural Language Programming: Rethinking Language, Memory, and Cognition in the Era of Generative AI
summary: Generative Artificial Intelligence is transforming the role of natural language in computational systems. In classical Natural Language Processing (NLP), language was treated as an object of computation: something to analyse, classify, translate, or generate.
