summary: Large sign-language corpora benefit from temporal labels at two scales: subtitle spans for subtitle alignment and word spans for sign spotting. Sign spottings already locate words in time at corpus scale, but training subtitle alignment jointly on subtitle and word spans remains underexplored. We present SignAligner, a prompt-conditioned visual-language span generator that maps a sign-language video and a subtitle-sentence or target-word query to a textual start/end frame interval. It is first trained jointly on subtitle spans and word spans from sign spottings, then refined with overlap-based rewards while retaining auxiliary word examples. On the subtitle test set of the British Broadcasting Corporation-Oxford British Sign Language (BOBSL) corpus, the refined model reaches 66.68 F1@0.50 (F1 with a temporal intersection-over-union threshold of one half), the best among compared systems without external sign-video resources. This overlap-reward refinement outperforms cross-entropy continuation from the same jointly trained model. Joint training with word spans improves subtitle alignment in a pair of our generators matched in code, labels and maximum update budget. The advantage remains after both models of the pair are refined with overlap rewards. For word queries, the refined model follows the queried word, not a fixed position in the video: when the word's sign lies away from the video centre, it is far more accurate than predictions that use position alone. Together, these findings support one shared span generator refined with overlap rewards, aligning subtitles and producing word spans for human review.

AI.tldr: This paper presents SignAligner, a prompt-conditioned visual-language span generator trained jointly on subtitle and word spans and refined with overlap rewards, achieving 66.68 F1@0.50 on BOBSL subtitle alignment.
AI.motivation: Training sign-language subtitle alignment jointly with corpus-scale word spans from sign spottings remains underexplored despite the availability of temporal labels at both scales.
AI.method: SignAligner maps a sign-language video and a subtitle-sentence or target-word query to a textual start/end frame interval, trained first jointly on subtitle spans and word spans and then refined with overlap-based rewards while retaining auxiliary word examples.
AI.result: On the BOBSL subtitle test set, SignAligner reaches 66.68 F1@0.50, outperforming compared systems without external sign-video resources, beating cross-entropy continuation, and accurately localizing queried words even when they appear away from the video center.
AI.conclusion: A single shared span generator trained jointly on dual-granularity spans and refined with overlap rewards effectively supports both subtitle alignment and word-span generation for human review.

title: Surfacing Disagreement Beats Resolving It: A Gated Ablation Study of Provenance-Weighted Memory for Multi-Agent Debate
summary: Shared memory for multi-agent debate is usually built to resolve inconsistency: retrieval returns one winning fact and the disagreement disappears before any agent sees it. We ask whether that is correct. In DebateGraph, four backends share one contract (read/write/snapshot), so five mechanisms from the agent-memory literature can be removed independently under a fixed budget, each gated on a pre-declared threshold. Across 39 runs one survives: preserving contradictions and passing the ranked conflict set to the debate, rather than collapsing it to a winner, improves F1 by +0.340 (95% CI [+0.267, +0.414]) and cuts attack success from 22 to 7 of 122 poisoned items (McNemar exact p=0.0003), at equal cost. Reaching it meant fixing a bottleneck in our harness: conflict sets are built only over retrieved edges, and our pre-declared cap left three quarters of planted contradictions unretrievable, first measuring the mechanism at +0.084. The effect replicates on two retrieval substrates and directionally on HotpotQA documents. No other mechanism survives, and two are worse than inert: once contradictions reach the prompt, a write trust-gate and the router's provenance features each cost accuracy (-0.075 and -0.096 F1). The gate fails structurally: poisoned objects are always entities the graph already contains, against 53% of gold, so groundedness scores the lie above a truthful first mention. We release the harness, attack set, and logs, and argue that silently reconciling memory is the assumption worth abandoning.

AI.tldr: This paper conducts a gated ablation study in DebateGraph across 39 runs and shows that surfacing ranked contradictions to multi-agent debate beats resolving them in shared memory.
AI.motivation: Shared memory for multi-agent debate typically resolves inconsistencies before agents see them, returning a single winning fact without testing whether suppressing disagreement harms accuracy.
AI.method: Using DebateGraph across four backends sharing one read/write/snapshot contract, the authors independently ablate five agent-memory mechanisms under a fixed budget and pre-declared thresholds, evaluating on poisoned items, two retrieval substrates, and HotpotQA documents.
AI.result: Preserving contradictions and passing the ranked conflict set improves F1 by +0.340 (95% CI [+0.267, +0.414]) and cuts attack success from 22 to 7 of 122 poisoned items (p=0.0003) at equal cost, whereas a write trust-gate and router provenance features each reduce accuracy (-0.075 and -0.096 F1).
AI.conclusion: Silently reconciling contradictions in shared memory is counterproductive; surfacing ranked conflict sets to debate agents yields substantial accuracy and robustness gains.

title: LMLineage: Content Lineage and Context Governance for LLM Agents
summary: Interpretability for AI agents should not be confined to understanding the model's internal weights. It must also cover the agent's reasoning and decision-making process over multi-source context. We present LMLineage, an out-of-band system that attributes every output sentence of an agent session to its supporting input spans with calibrated confidences, without requiring white-box access to the model or any additional inference passes. On top of the lineage metadata, we build concept-drift micro compaction: instead of waiting for the context-length limit and summarizing everything, the system detects when previously used input documents have stopped being referenced ("drifted") and surgically compacts only those, preserving user instructions verbatim. We evaluate on a multi-tier corpus: 71 gold annotated sentences from 10 Chinese web-QA cases, plus 90 turns of independently collected multi-turn sessions across three generator models (gpt-4o-mini, qwen3.8-27b, deepseek-v4-flash). Results show that (i) window-level embedding similarity is far better aligned with LLM paraphrasing than whole document or lexical matching; (ii) the greedy-window fast path is both faster and more accurate on average than exhaustive line-matching (a multiple-comparisons bias in the latter inflates web recall at the cost of overall accuracy); (iii) per-turn attribution completes in 1s on a single GPU, remaining stable as context accumulates to 40 turns; and (iv) concept-drift detection is conservative (0% false compaction) with recall bounded by attribution accuracy. We further describe the concept-drift micro compaction design and an interactive incident-tracing/memory-cleaning case study. A companion patent application covers the lineage construction method.

AI.tldr: This paper presents LMLineage, an out-of-band system that attributes agent output sentences to supporting input spans and enables concept-drift micro compaction to manage multi-turn context.
AI.motivation: Agent interpretability requires tracing reasoning over multi-source context without white-box model access or extra inference passes, and standard context compaction waits until context limits are reached before summarizing everything.
AI.method: LMLineage computes calibrated sentence-to-span attributions out-of-band using window-level embedding similarity and a greedy-window fast path, and uses this lineage to detect drifted input documents for surgical compaction while preserving user instructions verbatim.
AI.result: Evaluated on 71 gold sentences from 10 Chinese web-QA cases and 90 multi-turn session turns across gpt-4o-mini, qwen3.8-27b, and deepseek-v4-flash, per-turn attribution completes in 1s on one GPU, greedy-window matching outperforms exhaustive line-matching, and concept-drift detection achieves 0% false compaction.
AI.conclusion: Out-of-band content lineage provides fast, model-agnostic attribution and enables safe, surgical context governance as agent sessions grow.

title: When Agent Skills Go Stale: Runtime Behavior and Selective Maintenance in Evolving Environments
summary: Agent skills use past experience and current observations to guide decisions and actions on related tasks. This experience is retained in skill state, whose reuse can amortize inference-time reasoning and environment interaction. When environment changes, parts of this state can become outdated while others remain useful. Across four task settings and two models, we compare skill reuse before and after environment changes. Previously beneficial skills can reduce task performance by over 10 percentage points or increase execution cost by nearly 40% relative to no skill. Task success can also remain unchanged while execution savings decline. These effects depend on which environment-specific details become outdated and the agent's ability to compensate using current observations. We introduce selective maintenance, which replays checks from successful executions without additional model calls. It verifies whether observed differences conflict with skill state, repairs affected content, and validates updates, rebuilding when local repair is insufficient. No description of the change is supplied. Relative to reusing stale state, maintenance improves task accuracy by up to 67pp and reduces execution steps by up to 37%. These results suggest that preserving a skill's inference time value as environments evolve requires selectively maintaining its state.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that stale agent skills can degrade performance in evolving environments and introduces selective maintenance to repair skill state without extra model calls.
AI.motivation: Agents reuse retained skill state to amortize reasoning and interaction, but when environments change, outdated skill details can harm performance or increase cost.
AI.method: The authors compare skill reuse before and after environment changes across four task settings and two models, and propose selective maintenance, which replays checks from successful executions without additional model calls to detect conflicts, repair affected content, validate updates, or rebuild when needed.
AI.result: Reusing stale skills can cut task performance by over 10 percentage points or raise execution cost by nearly 40%, whereas selective maintenance improves task accuracy by up to 67 percentage points and reduces execution steps by up to 37% relative to reusing stale state.
AI.conclusion: Preserving the inference-time benefits of agent skills in evolving environments requires selectively maintaining and validating their retained state.

title: From Perception to Simulation: Unveiling and Empowering Mental Spatial Dynamics in MLLMs
summary: Spatial reasoning is a fundamental component of world understanding for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). While existing research has advanced the perception of spatial relations in static scenes, the domain of dynamic spatial simulation remains relatively unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce MentalGrid, a benchmark focused on spatial reasoning tasks that require models to simulate evolving spatial states without intermediate visual feedback. Extensive evaluation on our benchmark reveals a significant deficiency in the spatial simulation capabilities of existing models. Specifically, we find that performance is constrained by perceptual limitations in simple simulation scenarios and hindered by inadequate multi-step reasoning as complexity increases. To address these challenges, we propose a three-stage curriculum learning framework utilizing 16k specialized spatial reasoning samples. This approach yields SpatialWalker, which achieves a 33.8% average improvement over its base model, surpassing proprietary models like Gemini-3-Flash in spatial simulation. Furthermore, SpatialWalker demonstrates robust generalization, maintaining a 4.9% average gain on out-of-domain benchmarks, demonstrating the pivotal role of spatial simulation as a fundamental building block for broader spatial intelligence.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the MentalGrid benchmark for dynamic spatial simulation in MLLMs and trains SpatialWalker via curriculum learning, achieving a 33.8% average improvement over its base model.
AI.motivation: While MLLMs have improved at perceiving static spatial relations, their ability to simulate evolving spatial states without intermediate visual feedback remains largely unexplored.
AI.method: The authors build MentalGrid to evaluate dynamic spatial simulation and propose a three-stage curriculum learning framework over 16k specialized spatial reasoning samples to train SpatialWalker.
AI.result: MentalGrid reveals perceptual bottlenecks in simple simulations and multi-step reasoning failures in complex ones; SpatialWalker improves over its base model by 33.8% on average, surpasses Gemini-3-Flash in spatial simulation, and retains a 4.9% average gain on out-of-domain benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic spatial simulation is a key weakness of current MLLMs that can be substantially improved with curriculum learning, yielding transferable gains for broader spatial intelligence.

title: Evolution Under Fire: Evolving Agent Safety Harnesses with Adaptive Injection Stressors
summary: Tool-using language-model agents must act on information from untrusted emails, webpages, and documents. This creates a central security challenge: malicious instructions and legitimate task directives can arrive through the same interaction channel. Existing defenses are largely hand-designed and static, making further improvements dependent on repeated manual redesign. We introduce Evolution Under Fire, a staged framework that couples safety-harness evolution with adaptive stressor evolution. Utility-constrained, Pareto-scheduled tree search evolves complete executable safety harnesses from execution evidence while keeping the task model, benchmark, tools, and evaluator fixed. Adaptive stressor evolution then discovers utility-preserving attacks that guide a subsequent stage of harness evolution. On AgentDyn with GPT-4o-mini, an evolved harness reduces attack success from 50.4% to 3.0%, improves clean and attacked utility over the initial harness, and offers a stronger security-utility trade-off than reproduced defenses. On Agent-SafetyBench with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, harness evolution reduces attack success from 82.6% to 62.0% while retaining helpfulness and runtime validity. Evolved harnesses also transfer without further evolution to Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, reducing attack success from 32.1% to 0.9% while improving attacked-task utility.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Evolution Under Fire, a staged framework that co-evolves executable agent safety harnesses and adaptive prompt-injection stressors, cutting attack success on AgentDyn from 50.4% to 3.0%.
AI.motivation: Tool-using agents receive untrusted external inputs alongside legitimate directives, and existing hand-designed static defenses require repeated manual redesign to keep pace with attacks.
AI.method: Utility-constrained, Pareto-scheduled tree search evolves executable safety harnesses from execution evidence with the task model, benchmark, tools, and evaluator fixed, while adaptive stressor evolution discovers utility-preserving attacks to guide further harness evolution.
AI.result: On AgentDyn with GPT-4o-mini, an evolved harness cuts attack success from 50.4% to 3.0% while improving clean and attacked utility; on Agent-SafetyBench with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct it cuts attack success from 82.6% to 62.0%, and evolved harnesses transfer to Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, reducing attack success from 32.1% to 0.9%.
AI.conclusion: Co-evolving executable safety harnesses against adaptive injection stressors produces stronger, transferable security-utility trade-offs than static manual defenses.

title: The Between-Round Decision in Autonomous Research: An LLM Controller That Reads the Whole Trajectory
summary: Executing an idea often changes how promising it looks, so the next step in autonomous research should rest on results, not on proposals. After each round of experiments, the system must decide whether to refine the best solution or start a new direction, which solution to build from, and what goal to set. We call this the between-round decision. Existing systems wrap it in machinery such as rules, scores, search trees, and schedules; where an LLM makes it, what the LLM needs to read is left open. We ask whether an LLM can make this decision from accumulated evidence, without a search structure around it, and how much of that evidence it needs to read. We present BRED (Between-Round Evidence-based Decision), an LLM-based controller that maintains the best verified solution so far (the Champion) and a log of past rounds, and makes one decision per round. On three widely used research-agent benchmark tasks, BRED improves on the task baselines by 4.80% in MAE on ETTh1 (to 0.4172) and by 3.44 and 3.43 points of accuracy on SST-2 (to 95.07%) and CIFAR-100 (to 84.63%), ahead of the published results. When the controller does not read the accumulated evidence, the same loop gains less: with no history it reaches 0.4299 on ETTh1 and 83.71% on CIFAR-100, whereas the full controller's MAE is 2.95% lower and its accuracy 0.92 points higher. On a new task, speech-based depression detection under a leakage-free protocol, it reaches a macro-F1 of 0.6164 on seeds held out from selection, 5.5 points above its baseline and 4.0 above the strongest published system. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper presents BRED, an LLM controller that makes between-round decisions in autonomous research by reading the full experiment log and Champion solution, outperforming baselines on four tasks.
AI.motivation: After each experimental round, autonomous research systems must decide whether to refine or pivot, but existing systems rely on rigid search machinery and leave open how much evidence an LLM controller needs to read.
AI.method: BRED maintains the best verified solution so far (the Champion) alongside a log of past rounds, and prompts an LLM controller to make one between-round decision per round directly from this accumulated evidence without an external search tree.
AI.result: BRED improves MAE on ETTh1 by 4.80% (to 0.4172) and accuracy on SST-2 and CIFAR-100 by 3.44 and 3.43 points (to 95.07% and 84.63%), outperforms ablations without history, and reaches 0.6164 macro-F1 on held-out seeds in leakage-free speech-based depression detection.
AI.conclusion: Reading the full trajectory of past experimental evidence enables an LLM controller to guide autonomous research effectively without complex surrounding search structures.

title: CrossEnv: Synthesizing Verifiable Cross-Environment Tasks for Long-Horizon Agent Training
summary: Executable synthetic environments provide scalable training tasks and verifiable feedback for long-horizon agents. Existing environment synthesis methods primarily generate tasks within individual environments. However, these tasks do not adequately capture real-world interactions across services, where actions in one service depend on information obtained from another. Synthesizing such tasks is challenging because data generated across environments must remain consistent to support executable and verifiable interactions. To address this challenge, we introduce CrossEnv, a framework that uses an entity-tool graph to identify connections between environments and aligns task-specific data to synthesize executable, verifiable cross-environment tasks. We further propose CrossEnv-Curriculum, which progresses from single-environment tool use to coordination across more environments and business domains, before introducing user interaction. Across four external benchmarks, combining cross-environment training data with this curriculum achieves competitive performance with fewer training examples. Further analyses support the benefits of cross-environment data and curriculum training, and provide evidence of transfer to new environment combinations, external tasks less similar to the training data, and longer workflows.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CrossEnv and CrossEnv-Curriculum to synthesize executable, verifiable cross-environment tasks for training long-horizon agents, achieving competitive performance with fewer examples.
AI.motivation: Existing synthetic environment methods generate single-environment tasks that miss real-world cross-service workflows where actions in one service depend on data from another and cross-environment consistency is hard to maintain.
AI.method: CrossEnv uses an entity-tool graph to identify connections across environments and align task data into executable, verifiable cross-environment tasks, paired with CrossEnv-Curriculum progressing from single-environment tool use to multi-environment coordination and user interaction.
AI.result: Across four external benchmarks, combining cross-environment training data with CrossEnv-Curriculum achieves competitive performance using fewer training examples, with evidence of transfer to new environment combinations, less similar external tasks, and longer workflows.
AI.conclusion: Graph-aligned cross-environment task synthesis and progressive curriculum training improve sample efficiency and generalization for long-horizon tool-using agents.

title: A Full-Ledger Counterfactual Audit of Adaptive Reasoning
summary: Adaptive reasoning must decide whether to answer now or spend more compute. Predicting that the current answer is wrong does not establish whether further reasoning will improve it. We introduce the Full-Ledger Counterfactual Value Audit (FLCVA), which compares an immediate answer with four fixed-length continuations from the same frozen prefix under one answer procedure and accounts for the cost of every signal used by a policy. On GSM8K and MATH-500, a random 256-token continuation recovers a wrong answer in 26.6% of Qwen3-8B cases and 18.9% of DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B cases, while damaging a correct answer in 1.4% and 1.9%. Correctness labels from independently sampled continuations predict a separate continuation's outcome in both primary models. In offline replay, using these labels to allocate compute improves performance on DeepSeek; the Qwen3 gain remains inconclusive. Under full cost accounting, the tested lightweight, myopic controllers mainly recognize current errors and add little continuation-specific value beyond that shortcut. A Llama-8B replication and action/cost ablations examine the robustness of these findings. FLCVA separates measuring local continuation value, predicting it from observable signals, and using those predictions to allocate computation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Full-Ledger Counterfactual Value Audit (FLCVA) to evaluate adaptive reasoning policies and finds that tested myopic controllers mainly detect current errors rather than continuation value.
AI.motivation: Adaptive reasoning policies must decide whether to answer immediately or spend more compute, but predicting that a current answer is wrong does not establish whether further reasoning will actually fix it.
AI.method: FLCVA compares an immediate answer against four fixed-length continuations from the same frozen prefix under a single answer procedure while accounting for the cost of every signal used by the policy, tested on GSM8K and MATH-500 with Qwen3-8B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, and Llama-8B.
AI.result: A random 256-token continuation recovers wrong answers in 26.6% of Qwen3-8B cases and 18.9% of DeepSeek cases while damaging 1.4% and 1.9% of correct ones; in offline replay, DeepSeek benefits from continuation-label allocation while Qwen3 gains are inconclusive, and lightweight myopic controllers add little continuation-specific value under full cost accounting.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling continuation value measurement, prediction, and cost-aware allocation reveals that current lightweight adaptive reasoning controllers rely largely on error-detection shortcuts.

title: When the tail is earned by its companions: measuring label dependence in long-tailed multi-label classification
comment: 27 pages, 3 figures, 13 tables. Submitted to Information Sciences
summary: A rare label seldom occurs alone, and a classifier can recover it from the frequent labels it co-occurs with, its companions, without having learned the label itself. Existing diagnostics of this need a trained model: none says before training whether a corpus admits the failure, or what the standard aggregate hides. Macro-F1, like any measure built from per-label confusion counts, is unchanged by how a label's recall divides between occurrences with and without a companion. We introduce a within-label estimand of that division, a reading rule under which a fall in dependence counts only if companion-free recall rises, and a statistic of training labels that bounds, before training, how far reported recall can exceed companion-free recall. Across 23 corpora, 7 training objectives and five families of label-correlation mechanisms, companion-free recall falls short on all six corpora where the estimand is defined. Up to 18.4% of the tail true positives macro-F1 credits would vanish at the companion-free rate, within the training-label bound on every corpus. No long-tail objective reduces the dependence, but architecture moves it. Models whose tail score is computed from other labels' predictions are strongly dependent.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a within-label estimand and a pre-training bound to measure how much rare-label recall in multi-label classification depends on frequent companion labels rather than the label itself.
AI.motivation: In long-tailed multi-label classification, classifiers can recover rare labels from co-occurring frequent companions, and standard metrics like macro-F1 cannot distinguish companion-driven recall from true label learning without a trained model.
AI.method: The authors define a within-label estimand splitting recall into occurrences with and without companions, a reading rule requiring companion-free recall to rise when dependence falls, and a training-label statistic that bounds the recall gap before training, evaluating across 23 corpora, 7 objectives, and 5 label-correlation mechanisms.
AI.result: Companion-free recall falls short on all six corpora where the estimand is defined, up to 18.4% of tail true positives credited by macro-F1 would vanish at the companion-free rate within the pre-training bound, and architecture rather than long-tail objectives drives dependence.
AI.conclusion: Pre-training label statistics can bound companion dependence ahead of training, and reducing this dependence requires architectural choices rather than specialized long-tail loss objectives.

title: Storing the Gemma 4 K=V Cache Once: Exact Global-KV Memory Savings in a Paged Serving Engine with Unchanged Attention Kernels
summary: In the global attention layers of Gemma 4 31B, the value is the normalized key projection, and the key is the value scaled by a fixed weight, with rotary position encoding on one quarter of its dimensions. The Gemma 4 report states that this design reduces the global KV cache by up to 37.5%, but the open serving engines that we checked still store a full key and a full value: 1,024 values per KV head and token. We store one 640-value row instead, exact in real arithmetic, and an unchanged paged attention kernel reads it through two overlapping strided views as its key cache and its value cache. In a vLLM prototype with the 16-bit 31B model, the outputs are bit-identical to an emulation of the same arithmetic on the stock cache, 2 of 432 final answers differ from the stock engine (within its run-to-run noise), and the steady decode KV memory per request falls by a factor of 1.34 to 1.40 at 32K to 64K tokens. On a prefill/decode pair of two A100 GPUs with NIXL transfer and CPU offload, a decode engine with a full 15 GiB pool ran 1.38 times the stock decode tokens per step for 16K-token prompts (repeated to 0.06%) and 1.24 times for 8K-token prompts; a model of the vLLM block pool predicted both ratios to within 1% (the engine was 0.7% to 0.9% higher) and matched the change between them. The eager decode throughput rose by 1.30 and 1.11 times, and on this path the compact engine gave the same output tokens as the emulation for 8 prompts at batch 1. The run-time prototype makes an eager step 4% to 9% slower at equal batch, and the method does not yet stack with an 8-bit KV cache at the default scale.

AI.tldr: This paper stores the shared K=V global attention cache of Gemma 4 31B once as a 640-value row read via strided views in vLLM, cutting steady decode KV memory by 1.34x to 1.40x.
AI.motivation: Gemma 4 31B's global attention design allows a 37.5% KV cache reduction in principle, yet open serving engines still store full separate key and value caches of 1,024 values per KV head and token.
AI.method: The authors store a single 640-value row per head and token and configure an unchanged paged attention kernel to read it through two overlapping strided views as both the key and value caches.
AI.result: In a vLLM prototype with 16-bit Gemma 4 31B, outputs are bit-identical to emulation, steady decode KV memory per request drops by 1.34x to 1.40x at 32K to 64K tokens, and on two A100 GPUs decode tokens per step rise 1.38x at 16K prompts and 1.24x at 8K prompts, with eager steps 4% to 9% slower.
AI.conclusion: Overlapping strided views unlock Gemma 4's theoretical global KV cache savings in paged serving engines without modifying attention kernels, though 8-bit KV cache stacking remains future work.

title: ForecastGym: A Live, Controlled, and Replayable Benchmark for Forecasting Agents
summary: Agents built on large language models (LLMs) increasingly forecast real-world events by searching the Web and reasoning over what they find. How well such an agent forecasts depends on both the retrieved evidence and the model, making control over that evidence essential for evaluation. Live evaluations can mix retrieval with reasoning when each system searches on its own, while retrospective search can leak later information through date filters or today's ranking of historical pages. Comparing models, search sources, and memory strategies requires both fixed evidence and a record of how it evolved before resolution. We introduce ForecastGym, which records what four commercial web search APIs return for open prediction-market questions every two days and replays this frozen evidence offline once outcomes are known, comparing models, memory, and captured search sources under a fixed evidence-acquisition policy. Its first release covers 150 questions, 614 evidence states, one per question and collection time, and 131k search results. Rerunning the same queries after settlement returns results that all but state the outcome for up to 92% of the questions, despite the tested date filters. On the frozen evidence, all tested LLMs trail the market in forecasting accuracy. Our diagnostic analysis suggests that missed public information contributes more to the gap in high-gap states than misreading does. Switching the search API changes a model's Brier score by up to 0.043, more than the spread across models, while persistent notes score similarly to rereading all evidence at half the input tokens. The evidence a forecaster sees can matter as much as the model that reads it.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ForecastGym, a live-captured and replayable benchmark of 150 prediction-market questions and 131k search results, showing that search evidence matters as much as the LLM forecaster.
AI.motivation: Evaluating LLM forecasting agents is confounded when live search mixes retrieval with reasoning or when retrospective search leaks post-resolution outcomes despite date filters.
AI.method: ForecastGym records outputs from four commercial web search APIs every two days for open prediction-market questions and replays the frozen evidence offline after resolution, covering 150 questions, 614 evidence states, and 131k search results.
AI.result: Post-settlement queries leak outcomes for up to 92% of questions despite date filters; on frozen evidence all tested LLMs trail the market, switching search APIs shifts Brier score by up to 0.043 (exceeding model spread), and persistent notes match full rereading at half the input tokens.
AI.conclusion: Controlling and replaying time-stamped search evidence prevents temporal leakage and reveals that evidence acquisition can impact forecasting accuracy as much as model choice.

title: The Resolution Hypothesis: Agent Evolution's Key Is Identifying Improvements
comment: 38 pages, 12 figures, 13 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: Agent evolution follows a simple loop: a proposer writes candidate artifacts (prompts, skills, memories) and selection accepts those that score higher. This loop has shown promise, yet practitioners face a puzzle: methods trade wins across papers, and evolution often fails to bootstrap on certain tasks. We trace this puzzle to the Resolution Hypothesis: agent evolution stalls not because methods fail to propose better artifacts, but because noisy evaluations cannot reliably identify them. Across seven evolution methods and six models (over 10M LLM calls), we find support for the hypothesis at both levels where evaluation scores are used. At the candidate level (choosing artifacts), helpful candidate artifacts exist, but selection is no better than random at telling them from harmful ones, so errors accumulate across rounds. At the method level (ranking methods), typical margins of a few percentage points are smaller than the difference between two independent runs of the same method, so published rankings often rest on luck. Together, these findings indicate that agent evolution is often bottlenecked by reliably identifying improvements. This calls for a shift in how we develop and evaluate self-improving agents, from designing ever more candidate improvement systems to making true improvements detectable and accumulable.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes the Resolution Hypothesis and shows across over 10M LLM calls that agent evolution stalls primarily because noisy evaluations cannot reliably distinguish helpful from harmful artifacts.
AI.motivation: Agent evolution methods trade wins across benchmarks and often fail to bootstrap, raising the question of whether the bottleneck lies in proposing candidate artifacts or in evaluating them.
AI.method: The authors evaluate seven evolution methods across six models using over 10M LLM calls, testing evaluation reliability at both the candidate-selection level and the method-ranking level.
AI.result: At the candidate level, helpful artifacts are proposed but selection performs no better than random at separating them from harmful ones, causing errors to accumulate; at the method level, typical margins of a few percentage points are smaller than run-to-run variance.
AI.conclusion: Self-improving agent research should shift focus from designing new artifact proposers to building low-noise evaluation mechanisms that can reliably detect and accumulate true improvements.

title: Large-scale Neuron Community Discovery Reveals Neuron-Sparse Behaviors in Language Models
summary: What reusable units of computation can we discover within a language model's neurons? Prior work has shown that individual forward passes can often be sparsified post-hoc to small groups of neurons, but it has been unclear whether these groups form coherent computational entities reused across inputs. We introduce neuron community discovery, an unsupervised method for finding neuron groups that recur across prompts and are causally necessary and sufficient, within the layers they span, for common computations. The method combines gradient-based attribution, a graph connecting neurons that are repeatedly attributed together, and community detection. Applied to Llama-3.1-8B using ten million prompts, it discovers thousands of candidate communities. We evaluate them on held-out prompts through three causal tests: community necessity, sufficiency within a layer subset, and layer necessity. These tests identify groups whose removal disrupts predictions and whose retention preserves predictions despite ablating the remaining MLP neurons in the tested layers. Discovered communities support functions like grammatical agreement, token-probability calibration, fixed phrases, in-context copying, addition, and multiplication. With communities capped at 128 neurons across all layers, 10.3% of held-out prompts have at least one layer's contribution explained on a neuron-sparse basis. Coverage remains 8.7% when requiring at least four layers and 3.3% when requiring at least twelve. These results show that small groups of existing neurons can provide reusable computational components across prompts, and that such groups can be discovered at scale.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces unsupervised neuron community discovery on Llama-3.1-8B using ten million prompts, finding small recurring neuron groups that are causally necessary and sufficient within their layers.
AI.motivation: While individual forward passes can be sparsified to small neuron sets post-hoc, it has remained unclear whether reusable, causally coherent neuron communities exist across prompts.
AI.method: The authors combine gradient-based attribution, a co-attribution graph, and community detection on Llama-3.1-8B over ten million prompts, then validate candidate communities on held-out prompts via community necessity, within-layer sufficiency, and layer necessity tests.
AI.result: Discovered communities support functions including grammatical agreement, calibration, fixed phrases, copying, and arithmetic; capping communities at 128 neurons across layers explains at least one layer's contribution for 10.3% of held-out prompts, 8.7% for at least four layers, and 3.3% for at least twelve.
AI.conclusion: Small groups of existing neurons form reusable computational components across prompts that can be discovered unsupervised at scale.

title: Nunchi: Ears Help Eyes in Multi-Party Conversations
summary: Identifying whom a person looks at is central to understanding multi-party conversations, yet gaze geometry alone becomes ambiguous as more people appear. Conversations offer cues that geometry lacks, such as who is speaking and what is said, but no gaze dataset provides them for many multi-party scenes. We introduce SORBET, a benchmark of 3,340 samples from 1,578 clips with synchronized speech, transcripts, and attended person labels, covering more multi-party scenes than existing gaze datasets. Prior gaze models struggle to use these cues, which come in different forms, must be linked to the right person, and can conflict with gaze geometry. We propose Nunchi, a framework that constructs a text prompt from the transcript and the outputs of gaze and speaker models, links every cue to the candidates with shared labels, and lets a vision-language model (VLM) weigh gaze geometry against conversational cues to identify the attended person. Nunchi outperforms the strongest existing method by 4.8 percentage points. On SORBET, conversational cues help whereas additional visual cues do not, and the gains hold across three VLMs, with automatic transcripts, and on two existing datasets.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the SORBET multi-party gaze benchmark and the Nunchi framework, which uses a VLM to weigh gaze geometry against conversational cues and improves attended-person accuracy by 4.8 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Gaze geometry becomes ambiguous in multi-party conversations as participant counts grow, yet existing gaze datasets lack synchronized speech and transcripts and prior models struggle to reconcile conflicting conversational cues.
AI.method: The authors construct SORBET (3,340 samples from 1,578 clips with synchronized speech, transcripts, and attended-person labels) and propose Nunchi, which formats transcript, gaze, and speaker-model outputs with shared candidate labels into a text prompt for a VLM.
AI.result: Nunchi outperforms the strongest existing method by 4.8 percentage points on SORBET, with gains holding across three VLMs, automatic transcripts, and two existing datasets, while additional visual cues do not help.
AI.conclusion: Integrating conversational cues with gaze geometry through shared candidate labeling in a VLM effectively resolves multi-party gaze ambiguity.

title: The Illusion of Grounding: Do Vision-Language Models Weigh Retrieved Text and Images Like an Ideal Observer?
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures, 11 tables. Code and data: this https URL (archived at this https URL)
summary: Retrieval-augmented vision-language models (VLMs) answer from two sources of evidence that can each fail: the retrieved text can be wrong or noisy, and the image can be degraded or contradicted. We introduce GIB-200K, 200,000 image-question items built from COCO and Visual Genome, each expanded into controlled stress conditions: hard-negative retrieval noise (1-20 documents), visual ambiguity (Gaussian and motion blur, low-resource crops) and cross-modal conflict with counterfactual flip pairs. Instead of only measuring degradation, we ask how models combine the two modalities. From ideal Bayesian cue combination we derive a testable prediction that yields formal definitions of Knowledge Inertia (text over-weighted relative to the model's own image evidence) and Sensory Capture (the reverse), and we estimate the weights with a measurement-error-corrected regression whose recovery of known weights we verify. A counterfactual flip decomposition separates modality bias from concept priors, and a Grounding Illusion Score measures how much clean accuracy is not grounded in the image. We evaluate 4 open models on one frozen, seeded evaluation split of 2,000 GIB-200K items. All models are accurate on clean inputs (92.5%-94.2%) but adverse accuracy falls to 41.3%-59.9%. The two LLaVA models over-weight the text (Knowledge Inertia, w_T/w_I = 1.229 and 1.322), whereas InternVL3 favours the image (w_T/w_I = 0.680); between 34.8% and 71.4% of the clean answers that are correct are abandoned when the document lies. A training-free consistency check that compares the answer with and without retrieval trades coverage for accuracy under misleading documents, while falling back to the image fails when the image is heavily degraded. All per-instance outputs, code, and an audit that recomputes every reported open-model number are released.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the GIB-200K benchmark and a Bayesian cue-combination audit, showing that open retrieval-augmented VLMs exhibit strong modality biases and lose substantial accuracy under retrieval or visual stress.
AI.motivation: Retrieval-augmented VLMs must weigh retrieved text against visual evidence when either can fail, yet how they combine these modalities relative to an ideal observer has not been formally quantified.
AI.method: The authors build GIB-200K (200,000 items from COCO and Visual Genome) with retrieval noise, visual degradation, and counterfactual flip pairs, and derive formal measures of Knowledge Inertia, Sensory Capture, and Grounding Illusion Score using measurement-error-corrected regression.
AI.result: Across four open models on a 2,000-item split, clean accuracy (92.5%-94.2%) drops to 41.3%-59.9% under stress; LLaVA models over-weight text (w_T/w_I = 1.229 and 1.322) while InternVL3 favors images (0.680), and 34.8%-71.4% of clean correct answers are abandoned when retrieved text lies.
AI.conclusion: Open retrieval-augmented VLMs deviate markedly from ideal Bayesian cue combination, and simple training-free consistency checks face fundamental coverage-accuracy trade-offs when images are degraded.

title: Mind the Gap: A Deployed Multi-Agent System for Documentation Maintenance
comment: Accepted at IAAI-27 (Innovative Applications of AI, co-located with AAAI 2027), Emerging Applications track. 12 pages (6 pages + references and appendix), 2 figures, 6 tables
summary: The "AI revolution" has enabled teams across the technology industry to deliver software features at unprecedented velocity. While code evolves faster than ever, customer-facing documentation often struggles to stay up to speed. As users increasingly rely on LLM-based agents that consume documentation as their primary interface, the impact of this documentation gap worsens: stale information propagates and is treated as authoritative. Signals for identifying where documentation has fallen behind already exist in abundance, both explicit (e.g., resolved support tickets revealing what documentation lacks) and implicit (e.g., code-documentation discrepancies detectable from automated loops). We deploy a multi-agent system, built around a triage agent we call "TriAgent," that continuously extracts these signals and repairs documentation drift. Over 43 days of shadow-mode operation, our system triaged 499 tickets and surfaced 92 gaps in the documentation. Using a panel of LLM judges from independent model families, 81.1% of TriAgent's verifiable assertions were correct (245 of the 302 assertions the human resolution addresses; majority of three judges); on length-comparable pairs the panel preferred TriAgent's response in 70.5% of pairs and the human engineer's in 23.2% (the rest had no judge majority). Importantly, agent- and human-sourced replies tended to be complementary, with the human often surfacing insights that were either buried within the existing documentation or missing from it entirely; our system turns each such insight into a documentation gap and, after human review, a fix. Repairing a gap measurably improved the agent's later answer: when the agent re-answered the same ticket after the repair, blinded judges preferred the post-repair answer over its own pre-repair answer 71.4% of the time (n=35). A blinded human audit confirms strong alignment on self-improvement.

AI.tldr: This paper deploys TriAgent, a multi-agent system that extracts documentation gaps from support tickets and code discrepancies over 43 days, improving post-repair agent answers in 71.4% of re-evaluated cases.
AI.motivation: Rapid software evolution causes customer-facing documentation to drift, which increasingly harms users and LLM agents that rely on documentation as an authoritative interface.
AI.method: The authors deploy a multi-agent system centered on TriAgent in 43 days of shadow-mode operation to triage support tickets, surface explicit and implicit documentation gaps, and feed human-reviewed insights back into documentation repairs.
AI.result: TriAgent triaged 499 tickets and surfaced 92 documentation gaps; 81.1% of its verifiable assertions were judged correct by an LLM panel, judges preferred its length-comparable replies over human engineers 70.5% to 23.2%, and blinded judges preferred post-repair over pre-repair agent answers 71.4% of the time (n=35).
AI.conclusion: Continuously mining support tickets and code discrepancies with a triage agent closes documentation drift and measurably improves downstream agent support quality.

title: TextSphere: Efficient Text-to-Image Generation via Shared Hyperspherical Alignment and Uniformity
summary: Recent advances in text-to-image generation have substantially improved image quality, particularly through diffusion-based methods that require multiple inference steps. In contrast, Sphere Encoder offers an efficient generative framework capable of producing images with fewer forward steps. However, extending it to free-form text is nontrivial, because its class-conditioned design lacks cross-modal alignment. To address this challenge, we propose TextSphere, an efficient text-to-image generative framework that extends Sphere Encoder with language conditioning and cross-modal alignment. We incorporate pretrained CLIP text embeddings through adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN) to guide image generation while retaining the original spherical sampling mechanism. To bridge the cross-modal representation gap, we introduce a Spherical Semantic Alignment and Uniformity (SSAU) objective that jointly promotes semantic alignment and representation uniformity on the hypersphere. Experiments on CUB-200-2011, MS-COCO-2014, and Flickr30k demonstrate that TextSphere consistently reduces generation FID (gFID) over the text-conditioned baseline while achieving reconstruction FID (rFID) below 1.0. With only 4 and 6 sampling steps, TextSphere achieves lower gFID than the compared diffusion- and GAN-based models trained from scratch on CUB-200-2011 and MS-COCO-2014, respectively. We further observe that improved reconstruction fidelity does not necessarily yield better generation quality. In addition, we use Partial Least Squares Singular Value Decomposition (PLS-SVD) to analyze cross-modal alignment and modality gap, offering insight into the effectiveness of our approach.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes TextSphere, extending Sphere Encoder to text-to-image generation via CLIP AdaLN conditioning and a Spherical Semantic Alignment and Uniformity objective, outperforming diffusion and GAN baselines in 4 to 6 steps.
AI.motivation: Sphere Encoder generates images in few forward steps, but its class-conditioned design lacks cross-modal alignment for free-form text-to-image generation.
AI.method: TextSphere injects pretrained CLIP text embeddings via adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN) while preserving spherical sampling, and introduces a Spherical Semantic Alignment and Uniformity (SSAU) loss alongside PLS-SVD analysis of the modality gap.
AI.result: On CUB-200-2011, MS-COCO-2014, and Flickr30k, TextSphere lowers generation FID over the text-conditioned baseline, achieves reconstruction FID below 1.0, and outperforms compared diffusion and GAN models trained from scratch using only 4 and 6 sampling steps.
AI.conclusion: Aligning and uniformly distributing cross-modal representations on the hypersphere enables fast few-step text-to-image generation without multi-step diffusion sampling.

title: Ambient LLMs: Data-Efficient Supervised Fine-tuning via Temperature Matching
summary: Collecting large-scale, diverse, and high-quality post-training datasets for autoregressive language models is challenging. Consequently, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is typically applied to datasets significantly smaller than those used for pre-training, which leads to overfitting and the catastrophic forgetting of the tails of the data distribution. To prevent this collapse, we introduce Ambient SFT, a principled framework for leveraging imperfect predictions to augment the fine-tuning set. In our method, a "frozen" version of the pre-trained model serves as a noisy teacher that the fine-tuned model must match at a coarse level. In particular, we require that the high-temperature versions of the conditional distributions produced by the post-training model should match the high-temperature versions of the pre-training ones. The temperature hyperparameter controls the level of trust in the pre-trained model, with the limit $T\to \infty$ reverting back to regular SFT and $T=1$ to knowledge distillation. We demonstrate that our approach outperforms standard SFT across domain adaptation, instruction-tuning, and reasoning, leading for up to $21\%$ average relative improvement to standard SFT.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Ambient SFT, which regularizes supervised fine-tuning by matching high-temperature conditional distributions of a frozen pretrained teacher, yielding up to 21% average relative improvement over standard SFT.
AI.motivation: Standard supervised fine-tuning uses datasets much smaller than pre-training corpora, causing overfitting and catastrophic forgetting of distribution tails.
AI.method: Ambient SFT uses a frozen pretrained model as a noisy teacher and requires the fine-tuned model's high-temperature conditional distributions to match those of the pretrained model, smoothly interpolating between knowledge distillation (T=1) and standard SFT (T->infinity).
AI.result: Across domain adaptation, instruction-tuning, and reasoning tasks, Ambient SFT outperforms standard SFT with up to 21% average relative improvement.
AI.conclusion: Temperature-matched regularization against a frozen pretrained model prevents tail forgetting and improves data efficiency in LLM post-training.

title: Bandit Online Submodular Minimisation Using Zeroth-Order Oracles
summary: We consider online submodular minimisation under bandit feedback, where at each round a decision maker plays a subset and observes only its cost, while the cost functions, and hence their minimiser, change over time. Existing bandit methods only guarantee static regret, which compares against a single fixed subset and is a weak benchmark when the minimiser moves. This paper provides, to the best of our knowledge, the first method with guarantees for tracking a moving minimiser in this setting. We propose a zeroth-order method built on a two-point oracle for the Lovász extension whose two evaluations are both subsets that can be played. The perturbed and base points are rounded by a common random threshold, and drawing the smoothing direction from the unit sphere makes the base evaluation a zero-mean control variate, so the oracle is an unbiased estimator of the smoothed gradient. We establish dynamic regret bounds of order $O\big((1+\sqrt{P^\ast_N})N^{3/4}\big)$ in general and $O\big((1+\sqrt{P^\ast_N})N^{2/3}\big)$ under a sufficiently small drift, where $P^\ast_N$ is the path length of the minimiser sequence, together with the corresponding $O(N^{3/4})$ and $O(N^{2/3})$ static regret bounds. Numerically, the method attains lower regret than the algorithm of (Hazan and Kale (2012)), with the advantage growing with the path length.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a zeroth-order two-point oracle algorithm for bandit online submodular minimization with dynamic regret guarantees for tracking a moving minimizer.
AI.motivation: Existing bandit online submodular minimization methods only bound static regret against a fixed subset, which is inadequate when cost functions and their minimizers change over time.
AI.method: The authors design a two-point oracle on the Lovasz extension that evaluates two playable subsets rounded by a common random threshold with a unit-sphere smoothing direction, making the base evaluation a zero-mean control variate for an unbiased smoothed gradient estimator.
AI.result: The method achieves dynamic regret bounds of O((1+sqrt(P*_N)) N^{3/4}) in general and O((1+sqrt(P*_N)) N^{2/3}) under small drift, matching O(N^{3/4}) and O(N^{2/3}) static bounds, and numerically outperforms Hazan and Kale (2012) with growing advantage as path length P*_N increases.
AI.conclusion: Common-threshold two-point rounding enables unbiased zeroth-order gradient estimation and the first dynamic regret guarantees for bandit online submodular minimization.

title: Robust Actor-Critic Learning under Transport and Divergence Uncertainty
summary: Learning reliable control policies requires accounting for uncertainty in transition dynamics and errors introduced by function estimation and action generation. We develop an actor--critic method for discounted robust Markov decision processes with continuous states and actions and an unknown nominal transition law. We consider transition uncertainty sets defined by Wasserstein distance, total variation, Kullback--Leibler divergence, or Pearson chi-square divergence. A conditional diffusion model is fitted once to offline transitions. At each subsequent iteration, we estimate the robust action-value function from current-policy observations using a shared-target minimax criterion, then update a generative actor through exponentially weighted score matching. Regularization preserves exploration and provides the density regularity needed for conditional distribution estimation. Under coverage and regularity conditions, we establish finite-sample bounds for critic estimation, the learned conditional action law, and the robust return of the implemented policy. The bounds distinguish critic estimation error, uncertainty in the nominal transition model, and policy regularization, and characterize how the four robustness radii affect the resulting guarantees.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a generative actor-critic algorithm for continuous-state-action robust MDPs under four transition uncertainty sets and establishes finite-sample bounds on critic, actor, and robust return errors.
AI.motivation: Reliable control requires handling both transition dynamics uncertainty and errors from function approximation and action generation in continuous spaces with unknown nominal transitions.
AI.method: The method fits a conditional diffusion model once to offline transitions, estimates the robust action-value function via a shared-target minimax criterion under Wasserstein, total variation, KL, or Pearson chi-square uncertainty sets, and updates a generative actor via exponentially weighted score matching.
AI.result: Under coverage and regularity assumptions, the authors derive finite-sample bounds for critic estimation, the learned conditional action law, and the implemented policy's robust return, separating estimation error, nominal model uncertainty, policy regularization, and robustness radii.
AI.conclusion: Combining offline diffusion transition modeling with minimax critic estimation and score-matching actors provides finite-sample theoretical guarantees for continuous robust reinforcement learning.

title: Symmetries of Counterfactuals: Identification and Testability of Counterfactual Maps from Covariate Heterogeneity
summary: In general, counterfactuals are not identified from data alone, because many causal models produce the same observed distributions but different counterfactuals. A common approach to circumvent this problem is to restrict the mechanism to a class in which it becomes unique, such as triangular monotone maps or optimal transport maps. However, whether the assumed class is correct is usually not examined. In this work, we study what the data can tell us when covariates are available that influence the outcome only through its latent cause. First, we characterise all counterfactual maps that are consistent with the data. They differ from the true map by a group of symmetries that preserve the conditional outcome distributions given the covariates. The more these distributions vary across covariate values, the smaller the group. Second, we show that for the classes above, consistency with the data is equivalent to a single conditional independence, which yields a test of the assumed class. We illustrate both results on synthetic data and on the ACTG 175 HIV trial.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes counterfactual map identifiability up to outcome-distribution-preserving symmetries given auxiliary covariates and derives a conditional-independence test for common structural assumptions.
AI.motivation: Counterfactuals are generally unidentifiable from observational data without restricting mechanisms to classes like triangular monotone or optimal transport maps, and those assumed classes are rarely tested.
AI.method: When covariates affect the outcome only through its latent cause, the authors characterize all data-consistent counterfactual maps via symmetry groups preserving conditional outcome distributions, and show that membership in triangular monotone or optimal transport classes reduces to a single conditional independence.
AI.result: Theoretical results establish that greater variation in conditional outcome distributions across covariates shrinks the ambiguity symmetry group, and the resulting conditional-independence test is demonstrated on synthetic data and the ACTG 175 HIV trial.
AI.conclusion: Covariate heterogeneity both narrows counterfactual ambiguity and makes standard structural mechanism assumptions empirically testable.

title: Amortizing Tempered Sampling with Corrected Self-Training
summary: Learning a neural sampler can reduce the cost of repeated sampling from an un-normalized distribution, but obtaining good training data remains difficult. We develop a corrected self-training scheme across a sequence of tempered targets, making use of importance sampling and Markov chain Monte Carlo to correct the samples and replay buffers to store them. We introduce Sequential Score Sampler (SSS) as a particular case. In SSS, the proposal is a score-based diffusion trained by regression on energy gradients; and the samples are corrected by importance weights on the path space. After training, samples can be collected directly from the model, from its importance-corrected proposals, or from the final-temperature buffer. The method amortizes repeated sampling by encoding the global structure of the target in the model. SSS achieves competitive sampling accuracy across the benchmarks and, on several targets, uses shorter runtimes with fewer energy evaluations than competing samplers.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a corrected self-training scheme and Sequential Score Sampler (SSS) for amortizing tempered sampling, achieving competitive accuracy with fewer energy evaluations and shorter runtimes.
AI.motivation: Training neural samplers for un-normalized target distributions reduces repeated sampling cost, but acquiring high-quality training data remains challenging.
AI.method: The authors propose corrected self-training across a sequence of tempered targets using importance sampling and MCMC for sample correction and replay buffers for storage; in SSS, a score-based diffusion proposal is trained by regression on energy gradients and corrected via path-space importance weights.
AI.result: Across benchmark targets, SSS achieves competitive sampling accuracy and uses shorter runtimes with fewer energy evaluations than competing samplers on several targets.
AI.conclusion: Combining tempered self-training with path-space importance correction enables accurate, amortized neural sampling at lower computational cost.

title: Bias-Reduced and Parallel Heavy-Tailed Stochastic Convex Optimization in $\ell_p$ Geometries
summary: We consider the fundamental problem of parallel stochastic convex optimization (SCO), whose aim is to approximately minimize a convex objective when given the ability to query a moment-bounded stochastic gradient oracle multiple times in parallel per round. Whereas most previous results have focused on the variance-bounded Euclidean ($\ell_2$-norm) setting, meaning the objective is Lipschitz with respect to the $\ell_2$-norm over an $\ell_2$-bounded feasible set in $\mathbb{R}^d$, in this work we study parallel SCO in $\ell_p$ settings for $2 \le p < \infty$ under a heavy-tailed noise model. We begin by introducing a new class of $\ell_p$-optimal-distance-convergence (ODC$_p$) algorithms, drawing on prior stochastic bias-reduced techniques [ACJ+21], which combine with multilevel Monte Carlo methods to efficiently estimate the optimum of uniformly convex objectives. As a consequence of our ODC$_p$ algorithms, we first establish rates for projection-efficient $\ell_p$-Lipschitz optimization, composite convex minimization, and efficient $\ell_p$-proximal point estimation. Combining our ODC$_p$ algorithms with a new $\ell_p$-generalized Gaussian-based stochastic gradient estimator ($p$-GREG), we provide two efficient $\ell_p$ parallel algorithms, EpochDA and $\ell_p$-AC-SA, which achieve optimization error $\epsilon > 0$ with at most $\tilde{O}(d^{\frac{p}{2p + 2}} \epsilon^{-\frac{p}{p + 1}})$ query depth, improving upon the sequential heavy-tailed stochastic query depth of $O(\epsilon^{-p})$ for $\epsilon \leq \tilde{O}(d^{-1/(2p)})$. We also establish dimension-dependent lower bounds of $\Omega\bigl(\min\{\epsilon^{-p},d^{p/(3p-2)}\}\bigr)$ adaptive rounds for nonsmooth convex optimization over a subset of the unit $\ell_p$ ball. Our results improve upon the $\Omega(\min\{\epsilon^{-p},\epsilon^{2/3}d^{1/3}\})$ bounds of [DG19], when adapted to the same feasible set.

AI.tldr: This paper develops parallel heavy-tailed stochastic convex optimization algorithms in l_p geometries (2 <= p < infinity) with improved query-depth upper bounds and matching-regime lower bounds.
AI.motivation: Prior parallel stochastic convex optimization focused on variance-bounded Euclidean (l_2) settings, leaving heavy-tailed noise in general l_p geometries underexplored.
AI.method: The authors introduce l_p-optimal-distance-convergence (ODC_p) algorithms combining stochastic bias reduction with multilevel Monte Carlo, and pair them with a new l_p-generalized Gaussian gradient estimator (p-GREG) to form EpochDA and l_p-AC-SA.
AI.result: EpochDA and l_p-AC-SA achieve query depth O_tilde(d^{p/(2p+2)} epsilon^{-p/(p+1)}), improving on sequential O(epsilon^{-p}) depth for epsilon <= O_tilde(d^{-1/(2p)}), alongside new adaptive-round lower bounds of Omega(min{epsilon^{-p}, d^{p/(3p-2)}}) over the unit l_p ball.
AI.conclusion: Bias-reduced ODC_p methods and generalized Gaussian estimators extend parallel heavy-tailed stochastic convex optimization to non-Euclidean l_p geometries with provable depth improvements.

title: Adaptive Memory for Online Reinforcement Learning under Sparse Model Changes
summary: We study the discounted reinforcement learning (RL) problem in a setting where the underlying environment changes between deployments. Each deployment provides $H$ observations from a fixed MDP. The reward function and transition kernel are fixed within each deployment. Across deployments, at most an $\epsilon >0$ fraction of the reward and transition kernel entries may change. In this setting, learning each model to deploy from scratch may discard useful observations from past deployments, whereas pooling all past observations can bias the estimates of entries that have already changed. We then propose an algorithm that for each state and action pair, selects how much history to reuse to estimate the reward and probabilities of the next state. We start with observations from the current deployment and add earlier deployment observations one at a time, the most recent first. After each addition, we check whether a single average reward agrees with the estimates from all histories considered until that point. We apply the same check to the distribution of next states. For each estimate, we leverage the last history that passes these aforementioned checks. The optimal control policy is then computed on top of the fitted MDP. We characterize the average gap between the optimal return and the return of the learner's policies over a finite number of deployments. We demonstrate that when $0< |S|\epsilon \leq 2$, with $|S|$ being the cardinality of the state space, our algorithm needs only the observations from the most recent $O(1/\epsilon)$ deployments, and achieves a long-run average gap of at most $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{\epsilon/H})$.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an adaptive history-selection algorithm for online RL across deployments with sparse MDP changes, achieving an O_tilde(sqrt(epsilon/H)) long-run average suboptimality gap.
AI.motivation: When at most an epsilon fraction of reward and transition entries change between H-step deployments, learning from scratch wastes past data while pooling all history introduces bias.
AI.method: For each state-action pair, the algorithm incrementally adds past deployments from most recent to oldest, testing whether a single average reward and next-state distribution agree across the considered histories, and fits an optimal control policy on the longest passing history.
AI.result: When 0 < |S| epsilon <= 2, the algorithm requires only the most recent O(1/epsilon) deployments and achieves a long-run average return gap of at most O_tilde(sqrt(epsilon/H)) relative to the optimal policy.
AI.conclusion: Per-pair statistical consistency checks allow RL agents to selectively reuse past deployment data under sparse non-stationarity without sacrificing asymptotic accuracy.

title: Cancellation-Free Constrained SquareCB for Safe Controller Selection
summary: We study constrained contextual bandits, in which a learner chooses one of $K$ actions in each round to minimize loss while keeping the expected cost of its play below a budget. Existing reductions to online regression weight the cost by a Lagrange multiplier learned from past constraint residuals, so slack in some rounds can offset violations in others. We instead run SquareCB proposed in \citep{foster2020beyond} with a rectified weight on the cost: it is zero when the estimated cost is within the budget, and otherwise just large enough to bring it back to the budget. Under realizability and Slater's condition with margin $\delta$, the algorithm attains regret $O(\sqrt{KT\,\mathrm{Reg}_{\mathsf{Sq}}(T)}/\delta)$ and cancellation-free violation $\sum_t(V_c^{p_t}-b)^+=O(\sqrt{KT\,\mathrm{Reg}_{\mathsf{Sq}}(T)})$, where $\mathrm{Reg}_{\mathsf{Sq}}$ is the error of the regression oracle. The same bounds hold when the budget must be met in every context, potentially adversarially chosen contexts. In controller selection for a safe-control-gym quadrotor and a BOPTEST building, the violation is 6 to 9 times lower than that of primal-dual and virtual-queue baselines, with a lower or comparable regret.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a rectified-weight version of SquareCB for constrained contextual bandits, achieving cancellation-free violation bounds and 6x to 9x lower violations in control benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing reductions for constrained contextual bandits use Lagrange multipliers that allow slack in some rounds to cancel out constraint violations in others.
AI.method: The authors run SquareCB with a rectified cost weight that is zero when estimated cost is within budget and otherwise just large enough to restore the budget, analyzed under realizability and Slater's condition with margin delta.
AI.result: The algorithm attains regret O(sqrt(KT Reg_Sq(T))/delta) and cancellation-free violation O(sqrt(KT Reg_Sq(T))) even under adversarial contexts, and cuts violations by 6x to 9x versus primal-dual and virtual-queue baselines on safe-control-gym quadrotor and BOPTEST building tasks.
AI.conclusion: Rectified cost weighting eliminates inter-round violation cancellation in constrained contextual bandits while maintaining competitive regret.

title: DEFTS: Data-Efficient, Training-Free Few-Shot Learning for CLIP in the Text Subspace
summary: Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) achieves impressive zero-shot image classification performance by comparing image embeddings against class-specific text embeddings. While recent few-shot methods leverage labeled training samples to improve upon this zero-shot baseline, they often predominantly rely on image embeddings and underutilize the semantic structure of the text embeddings. In this paper, we introduce DEFTS, a data-efficient, training-free few-shot classification method strictly in the text subspace. We first demonstrate empirically that while raw text embeddings can be suboptimal as direct classifiers, the linear subspace they span remains highly discriminative. DEFTS therefore proposes to reduce the image-text modality gap by projecting estimated image prototypes directly into this subspace. Importantly, by expressing these prototypes as linear combinations of text embeddings, DEFTS reduces a high-dimensional estimation problem to the derivation of just a few coefficients. These coefficients are then computed via a Bayesian posterior mean, using a prior naturally centered on the original text embedding coordinates. Extensive experiments across 12 image classification benchmarks demonstrate that DEFTS significantly improves upon existing training-free methods.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces DEFTS, a training-free few-shot CLIP classifier that projects image prototypes into the linear text subspace via Bayesian posterior mean estimation, improving across 12 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing few-shot CLIP methods rely heavily on image embeddings and underutilize the discriminative linear subspace spanned by class text embeddings.
AI.method: DEFTS reduces the image-text modality gap by expressing estimated image prototypes as linear combinations of text embeddings, computing the low-dimensional coefficients via a Bayesian posterior mean with a prior centered on the original text embedding coordinates.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across 12 image classification benchmarks show that DEFTS significantly outperforms existing training-free few-shot CLIP methods.
AI.conclusion: Restricting few-shot prototype estimation to the text subspace via a Bayesian posterior mean provides a data-efficient, training-free way to adapt CLIP.

title: Locally Linear Generalized Single Index Regression
summary: In this work we propose and analyze a procedure for estimating a generalized single-index regression model. This generalized single-index regression framework models the conditional mean of the responses $Y$ as a function of the covariates $X$ where the mapping is assumed to have the form $f \circ g$, where $g$ is $\beta$-Hölder with $\beta \geq 2$ and $f$ can be a discontinuous function of bounded variation. We propose a general procedure that operates under minimal assumptions about the distribution of covariates $X$, requiring only boundedness, sufficient smoothness and absolute continuity with respect to Lebesgue. Our procedure jointly estimates the gradient vector $\hat v(x) \approx \nabla g(x)$ and the conditional mean $\mu(x) = f(g(x))$ by solving a localized weighted linear least squares problem. We derive central limit theorems for gradient vector estimates $\hat{v}_x$ and regression estimates $\hat{\mu}(x)$, and we derive rates of convergence for our approach, illustrating that it indeed achieves a stochastic convergence rate matching the minimax mean squared error rate when $\beta = 2$ and $f$ has a locally Lipschitz derivative. Unlike prior approaches our velocity estimation results accommodate link functions in the local bounded-variation class, allowing for nonsmooth and even discontinuous links while retaining consistency and asymptotic normality at almost every inference point. Finally, we instantiate this model in the situation where $g = \Pi$ is a closest point projection onto a compact and regular embedded $C^3$ curve $\gamma$, a setting recently studied in the literature. We also supplement our theoretical results with experiments on real and synthetic data to demonstrate the utility of our procedure.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a localized weighted linear least squares estimator for generalized single-index regression f(g(x)) with nonsmooth links f, establishing central limit theorems and minimax-optimal rates.
AI.motivation: Existing single-index regression methods struggle to accommodate nonsmooth or discontinuous link functions f while maintaining asymptotic normality and minimax rates for both gradient and mean estimation.
AI.method: Assuming g is beta-Holder (beta >= 2) and f has bounded variation, the procedure jointly estimates the gradient nabla g(x) and conditional mean f(g(x)) via localized weighted linear least squares, including instantiation for closest-point projection onto a C^3 curve.
AI.result: The authors derive central limit theorems for both gradient and regression estimates, match the minimax MSE rate when beta=2 and f has a locally Lipschitz derivative, and demonstrate utility on synthetic and real data.
AI.conclusion: Localized weighted linear least squares enables valid asymptotic inference and minimax-optimal estimation in generalized single-index models even with discontinuous link functions.

title: Two Counterexamples for e-means
summary: e-means (Bessa et al., 2026) combines exponential averaging and cluster revival. We give two counterexamples to its published recipe with higher final loss than standard k-means (Lloyd, 1982) from identical initial centers. Mass-based revival can destroy a global optimum and make the ratio of expected losses unbounded even with k-means++ seeding.

AI.tldr: This paper presents two counterexamples showing that e-means clustering can produce higher final loss than standard k-means and unbounded expected loss ratios even with k-means++ seeding.
AI.motivation: e-means (Bessa et al., 2026) combines exponential averaging and cluster revival, but its convergence properties relative to Lloyd's k-means had not been refuted.
AI.method: The authors construct two explicit counterexamples comparing the published e-means recipe against standard k-means starting from identical initial centers.
AI.result: In the counterexamples, e-means yields higher final loss than k-means, and mass-based cluster revival can destroy a global optimum and cause an unbounded ratio of expected losses even under k-means++ seeding.
AI.conclusion: The published e-means mass-based revival mechanism can catastrophically degrade clustering quality compared to standard k-means.

title: COSI: A Framework for Robustly Valid Inference
comment: Slides based on this paper can be found at this https URL (These slides includes more examples and sometime more simulations. The discussion in some of these slides is also informal.)
summary: We introduce COSI (COnfidence from Scale Invariance), a framework for constructing confidence sets for statistical functionals. COSI builds on the HulC (Hull-based Confidence), which uses median unbiasedness to construct confidence sets from batch estimates. COSI uses scale-invariance properties shared by many common estimators. We divide the data into batches, compute an estimate in each batch, and retain each candidate parameter value for which the batch estimates pass a test of scale invariance. The resulting confidence sets are asymptotically valid under weaker assumptions than classical Wald and bootstrap procedures require, and their coverage can be closer to the nominal level in small samples. Applications include robust inference for the mean, regression coefficients in misspecified linear models, tensor norms, and Fréchet means.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces COSI, a batch-based confidence-set framework using scale-invariance tests that achieves asymptotic validity under weaker assumptions than Wald and bootstrap methods.
AI.motivation: Classical Wald and bootstrap confidence sets rely on strong regularity assumptions and can suffer poor small-sample coverage for general statistical functionals.
AI.method: Extending HulC, COSI splits data into batches, computes an estimator per batch, and retains candidate parameter values for which the batch estimates pass a scale-invariance test.
AI.result: COSI confidence sets are asymptotically valid under weaker assumptions than Wald and bootstrap procedures, can yield closer-to-nominal small-sample coverage, and apply to means, misspecified linear regression, tensor norms, and Frechet means.
