With simulated feedback, both models repaired the trained network in single sessions and wrote a working controller from zero weights, whereas from zero the evolution strategy found none. The controllers written from zero were sparse and in a classical cascaded structure; one model edited the trained network while the other replaced it. Gradient descent reached higher accuracy with far more simulation, and all language model controllers steered the real tractor without intervention, with errors of the same order as pure pursuit. Language models can program the weights of a neural controller directly, much as control engineers design one. We call this Weight-Space Engineering.

AI.tldr: This study applies weight-space programming—where LLMs directly read and edit neural network weights without gradient descent—to adapt and synthesize a 253-parameter tractor guidance controller. Both GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1/5.2 produce controllers that steer a real tractor without intervention.
AI.motivation: Adapting small neural controllers to physical hardware changes typically relies on gradient descent or evolution strategies rather than direct analytical editing.
AI.method: Using a small budget of simulated evaluations, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1/5.2 read and directly modify a 253-parameter guidance network's weights—both repairing a pretrained network and writing a controller from zero weights—and are compared against evolution strategies, gradient descent, and pure pursuit.
AI.result: With simulated feedback, both LLMs repaired the trained network in single sessions and wrote sparse, cascaded controllers from zero weights (where evolution strategy failed); all LLM-written controllers steered the real tractor without intervention with errors comparable to pure pursuit, though gradient descent achieved higher accuracy with far more simulation.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can directly program neural controller weights in a manner akin to control engineering, demonstrating the feasibility of Weight-Space Engineering on real hardware.

title: How Much Distribution Shift Can a Clustering Withstand? Exact Split and Merge Certificates for Structured Transports
summary: In clustering, the distribution of the population being clustered is often uncertain or changes over time, so the true distribution may shift away from the nominal distribution used to form the clustering. Once the clustering is committed and each member is assigned to a cluster, such shifts may change the distribution of each cluster. They can make a cluster too spread out for one representative at a given resolution, motivating a split, or bring distinct clusters close enough to share a representative at that resolution, motivating a merge. We make these split and merge events precise using a local stability criterion built on the phase-transition analysis in deterministic annealing. This notion of stability enables us to quantify how robust a clustering is against such events. Furthermore, motivated by applications in which uncertainty and population change are structured, we study shifts whose displacements are restricted to a prescribed subspace. The smallest structured shifts that reach the respective thresholds define the split and merge radii, for which we obtain exact semidefinite programming (SDP) reformulations. The split SDP has only two scalar decision variables. These convex reformulations enable us to combine the radii into a robustness certificate for the full clustering that gives the size of the smallest structured shift that reaches any monitored split or merge threshold.

AI.tldr: This paper derives exact semidefinite programming (SDP) certificates for cluster split and merge stability under structured distribution shifts. Combining these split and merge radii yields a robustness certificate for the full clustering.
AI.motivation: Distribution shifts can invalidate committed clusterings by spreading a cluster enough to warrant a split or bringing clusters close enough to merge, yet exact stability certificates for structured shifts were lacking.
AI.method: Building on deterministic annealing phase-transition analysis, the authors define split and merge radii for shifts restricted to a prescribed subspace and derive exact SDP reformulations (with only two scalar decision variables for the split SDP).
AI.result: The convex SDP reformulations compute exact split and merge radii and combine into a single robustness certificate giving the smallest structured shift that reaches any monitored split or merge threshold.
AI.conclusion: Exact SDP reformulations provide a tractable, rigorous way to certify clustering stability under structured distribution shifts.

title: An AI-Based OSSE Framework to Evaluate Learned Physical Consistency: A Multi-Model Study Using FourCastNet, Aurora, Prithvi WxC, and GraphCast
summary: Observing System Simulation Experiments (OSSEs) are a central methodology for evaluating future atmospheric observing systems. We present the first AI-based OSSE framework to test whether different AI weather models can reproduce comparable physical impact from new observations that traditional physics based models generate. We evaluate four distinct architectural AI models on the Charney conjecture that incomplete historical observations can infer the present state of the atmospheric. We considner- FourCastNet V2, GraphCast, Aurora and Prithvi WxC and integrate each autoregressively over a 60-day forecast horizon. After a 30-day spin-up, we insert ERA5 temperature fields to infer winds and related atmospheric fields. Similar OSSE experiments are conducted for wind insertion. We measure the performance of each model's response to observational information on a 30-day data assimilation cycle forecast with and without data insertion. Distinct architectural AI weather models respond differently to the same OSSE observations. Foundation models (i.e. Prithvi WxC and Aurora), produce the strongest impact. For example, while GraphCast is the weakest, all three of the four models capture the temperature-to-geopotential height response. The two foundational models retain a positive, non-trivial, tropical zonal wind at 500 hPa response to temperature insertion. Various data insertion experiments can vary significantly even within a given architecture. We identify an architecture-specific numerical instability in GraphCast's full 37-level configuration that produces a runaway feedback concentrated at the uppermost levels with ERA5 temperature insertion correctable by excluding levels at or below 100 hPa.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an AI-based Observing System Simulation Experiment (OSSE) framework to evaluate physical consistency across FourCastNet V2, GraphCast, Aurora, and Prithvi WxC. Foundation models show the strongest observational impact, while GraphCast exhibits a correctable upper-level numerical instability.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether AI weather models reproduce the physical impact of new observations in the same way traditional physics-based models do in OSSEs.
AI.method: The authors run 60-day autoregressive forecasts with a 30-day spin-up, inserting ERA5 temperature or wind fields into a 30-day data assimilation cycle across FourCastNet V2, GraphCast, Aurora, and Prithvi WxC.
AI.result: Foundation models (Prithvi WxC and Aurora) produce the strongest observational impact and retain positive tropical 500 hPa zonal wind responses to temperature insertion, while three of four models capture the temperature-to-geopotential height response; GraphCast's full 37-level setup exhibits a runaway upper-level feedback under temperature insertion that is resolved by excluding levels at or below 100 hPa.
AI.conclusion: AI-based OSSEs effectively reveal architectural differences in physical consistency and diagnose numerical instabilities in learned weather models.

title: GP--RL--MPC: Uncertainty-Aware Reinforcement Learning-Augmented Model Predictive Control with Gaussian Process Postdecision State-Value Functions
comment: 19 pages including references and appendices, 3 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to L4DC 2027
summary: We propose Gaussian Process Reinforcement Learning-Augmented Model Predictive Control (GP--RL--MPC), which uses a learned critic as the MPC terminal penalty to account for costs beyond the prediction horizon. Gaussian process regression (GPR) enables data-efficient critic learning from limited, noisy rollouts within optimistic approximate policy iteration (OAPI), with soft updates mitigating policy chattering. A tunable risk coefficient weights GP epistemic uncertainty in the terminal cost, regulating sensitivity to uncertain critic predictions. The postdecision state formulation shifts disturbance averaging offline to account for aleatoric uncertainty from the terminal transition onward. Under matching objectives and admissible actions, a one-step horizon recovers greedy value-space RL. After fitting GP hyperparameters by exact marginal likelihood, we construct a sparse deterministic training conditional (DTC) posterior using inducing points selected by pivoted Cholesky (PC), reducing online evaluation costs as the training dataset grows. In a continuous stirred-tank reactor (CSTR) subject to exogenous disturbances, GP--RL--MPC with an appropriately selected risk coefficient and policy screening reduces the sum of squared errors (SSE) by an average of 80.52% relative to an otherwise matched baseline MPC across five random seeds (sample standard deviation: 3.48%).

AI.tldr: GP--RL--MPC augments model predictive control with a Gaussian process postdecision state-value critic to account for costs beyond the prediction horizon. On a disturbed CSTR benchmark, it reduces sum of squared errors by an average of 80.52% over a matched baseline MPC.
AI.motivation: Standard MPC ignores costs beyond its finite prediction horizon, while learning-based critics need data efficiency, uncertainty awareness, and low online evaluation cost.
AI.method: GP--RL--MPC learns a postdecision state-value critic via Gaussian process regression within optimistic approximate policy iteration with soft updates, weights GP epistemic uncertainty via a tunable risk coefficient, and uses a sparse deterministic training conditional posterior with pivoted Cholesky inducing points.
AI.result: On a continuous stirred-tank reactor (CSTR) with exogenous disturbances across five random seeds, GP--RL--MPC reduces the sum of squared errors by an average of 80.52% (standard deviation 3.48%) relative to a matched baseline MPC.
AI.conclusion: Combining sparse GP critics with postdecision state-value MPC enables data-efficient, uncertainty-aware control under disturbances.

title: DSADiff: Data Structure-Aware Diffusion for Crystal Structure Prediction via Mitigating Complexity- and Imbalance-Induced Biases
summary: Crystal Structure Prediction (CSP) is an important step in accelerating the generation and discovery of new materials. In recent years, diffusion-based CSP methods have made significant progress. However, existing models still suffer from generation bias when facing diverse materials spaces, while systematic approaches for tracing the sources of such performance variations remain limited. To address this issue, we propose LAS (Layered Analysis Strategy), a mechanism analysis framework that identifies crystal complexity and elemental composition imbalance as two key factors affecting generation difficulty and further reveals their relationships with model generation performance. Building on these findings, we further propose DSADiff (Data Structure-Aware Diffusion), a data structure-aware diffusion model that transforms the key factors identified by LAS into a unified generation difficulty representation and uses it to jointly drive feature modeling and training strategy optimization. This enables the model to adapt its representation and generation capability to samples with different data structures and difficulty levels, thereby mitigating learning bias across samples. Experiments on three CSP benchmark datasets, including Carbon-24, demonstrate that DSADiff consistently improves both Match Rate and RMSE, with a maximum Match Rate improvement of 9%, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods and achieving new state-of-the-art performance. This work deepens the understanding of diffusion-based CSP models from the perspective of generation bias and provides a new direction for designing less biased generative models for complex materials spaces.

AI.tldr: DSADiff diagnoses and mitigates generation bias in diffusion-based crystal structure prediction (CSP) caused by crystal complexity and elemental composition imbalance. It achieves new state-of-the-art Match Rate and RMSE across three CSP benchmarks, improving Match Rate by up to 9%.
AI.motivation: Diffusion-based CSP models suffer from generation bias across diverse materials spaces, and systematic ways to trace its sources are limited.
AI.method: The authors propose LAS (Layered Analysis Strategy) to identify crystal complexity and elemental imbalance as key bias drivers, and build DSADiff, which converts these factors into a unified generation difficulty representation to guide feature modeling and training strategy optimization.
AI.result: Across three CSP benchmark datasets including Carbon-24, DSADiff consistently improves both Match Rate and RMSE over existing state-of-the-art methods, with up to a 9% Match Rate gain.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling data-structure difficulty mitigates learning bias and advances diffusion-based crystal structure prediction.

title: RiDEx: Reward-Informed Directional Exploration for Diffusion Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reward-based diffusion post-training updates model parameters from task rewards. While existing approaches improve sampling and policy optimization, they still rely largely on isotropic random perturbations in a high-dimensional latent space for exploration. Such variation often spends the perturbation budget on changes with little influence on the target reward, making exploration inefficient. We study where diffusion models should explore and how to learn from that exploration. We introduce Reward-Informed Directional Exploration (RiDEx), which concentrates local exploration in reward-relevant subspaces of the denoising velocity field. Conditional residuals or differentiable reward gradients propose the subspace, and equal-and-opposite perturbations at the same generation state measure its terminal reward response. The reward difference supplies signed local supervision in the explored coordinates, while all generated images contribute to global DiffusionNFT learning. RiDEx thereby couples exploration-space selection with feedback about the changes it produces. On Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium, RiDEx attains the highest peak rewards among the evaluated methods on four alignment and preference tasks. Its gradient-direction instantiation achieves 15x and 29x target-attainment speedups over DiffusionNFT on HPSv2 and PickScore, measured in H200 GPU hours. Controlled experiments confirm that reward-aligned directions elicit stronger responses at equal perturbation magnitude, and that applying their measured credit improves curve-average reward across all four tasks.

AI.tldr: RiDEx accelerates diffusion reinforcement learning by focusing exploration in reward-relevant subspaces of the denoising velocity field rather than isotropic random perturbations. On Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium, it achieves the highest peak rewards and 15x-29x speedups over DiffusionNFT.
AI.motivation: Existing reward-based diffusion post-training relies on isotropic latent perturbations, wasting exploration budget on directions with little impact on the target reward.
AI.method: RiDEx proposes reward-relevant subspaces via conditional residuals or differentiable reward gradients, measures terminal reward responses using equal-and-opposite perturbations for signed local supervision, and feeds all generated images into global DiffusionNFT learning.
AI.result: On Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium across four alignment and preference tasks, RiDEx achieves the highest peak rewards, and its gradient-direction variant reaches target rewards 15x faster on HPSv2 and 29x faster on PickScore than DiffusionNFT in H200 GPU hours.
AI.conclusion: Coupling reward-informed directional exploration with signed local feedback substantially improves sample and compute efficiency in diffusion post-training.

title: BernBRS: Certified Backward Reachability for Deep Bernstein Neural Networks
summary: Ensuring the safety of complex neural network systems requires mathematically rigorous verification. While backward reachability analysis is a critical tool for identifying safe initial states, computing tight, formal bounds remains notoriously difficult to scale. Recent advancements have demonstrated that DeepBern-Nets neural networks utilizing Bernstein polynomial activation functions possess advantageous mathematical properties that enable exceptionally fast and tight forward reachability analysis. Building upon this efficiency, this paper introduces BernBRS, a highly accurate and scalable framework for the backward reachability analysis of DeepBern-Nets. BernBRS simultaneously computes certified inner and outer approximations of the Backward Reachable Set (BRS). Rather than relying on single convex bounding, our method intelligently refines a cover of the input space by analyzing activation patterns, splitting the input domain precisely where an exact decomposition of the relaxation gap predicts the most significant reduction in error. This targeted refinement enables high levels of scalability to highly complex and massive architectures that remain intractable for existing certified methods. We demonstrate the efficacy of our framework on high-dimensional models, including a linearized closed-loop approximation of the Half-Cheetah controller and a distilled Bernstein student of a Transformer block and we empirically study how these model-level guarantees relate to the original Half-Cheetah and TinyBERT classifier, respectively.

AI.tldr: BernBRS is a scalable framework for computing certified inner and outer backward reachable sets (BRS) of DeepBern-Nets. It scales to high-dimensional models such as a Half-Cheetah controller and a distilled Transformer block.
AI.motivation: Computing tight, formal backward reachability bounds for neural network safety verification is notoriously difficult to scale to large architectures.
AI.method: Building on DeepBern-Nets (neural networks with Bernstein polynomial activations), BernBRS simultaneously computes certified inner and outer BRS approximations by refining an input-space cover based on activation patterns and splitting where an exact relaxation-gap decomposition predicts the largest error reduction.
AI.result: BernBRS scales to high-dimensional models including a linearized closed-loop Half-Cheetah controller and a distilled Bernstein student of a Transformer block, where its model-level guarantees are compared against the original Half-Cheetah and TinyBERT classifier.
AI.conclusion: Targeted input-space refinement on Bernstein polynomial networks makes certified backward reachability tractable for complex neural architectures.

title: Every Measurement, Every Direction, All at Once: Multimodal Flow Matching for Molecules and Spectra
summary: Generative modeling in science is often data-limited, where experiments are expensive. However, each experiment may yield several coupled measurements of the same physical entity. Standard generative models often train only on a single direction, discarding supervision from the rest. We argue that each experiment contains more training signal than this asymmetry allows the model to exploit: random masking enables measurements to serve as either conditioning inputs or prediction targets, yielding multiple supervised denoising tasks from a single experiment. We investigate this premise with MOSAIC, a multimodal flow matching transformer over molecular 3D structure and UV, IR, and Raman spectra. MOSAIC is a single model that is capable of any-to-any generation: generating any subset of modalities from any disjoint subset of the others. On QM9S, MOSAIC achieves 88.8% molecular graph recovery, outperforming the strongest spectra-to-structure baseline by 23.2% in structure generation, while simultaneously outperforming a structure-to-spectra specialist model in spectral generation. Ablations show that the any-to-any objective improves structure generation over structure-only training across model sizes. Furthermore, MOSAIC supports arbitrary subsets of available measurements and enables molecular identification by matching generated spectra to experimental references.

AI.tldr: MOSAIC is a single multimodal flow matching transformer for any-to-any generation across molecular 3D structures and UV, IR, and Raman spectra. On QM9S, it achieves 88.8% molecular graph recovery, beating specialist baselines in both structure and spectral generation.
AI.motivation: Standard scientific generative models typically train in a single direction, discarding supervision from other coupled experimental measurements of the same entity.
AI.method: MOSAIC uses random masking during training so any disjoint subset of modalities (3D structure, UV, IR, Raman spectra) can serve as conditioning inputs or denoising targets within a unified flow matching transformer.
AI.result: On QM9S, MOSAIC achieves 88.8% molecular graph recovery (outperforming the strongest spectra-to-structure baseline by 23.2%), outperforms a structure-to-spectra specialist in spectral generation, and improves structure generation over structure-only training across model sizes.
AI.conclusion: Any-to-any multimodal flow matching extracts richer supervision from coupled experimental data, enabling unified molecular generation and spectral identification.

title: VTT: Reading Vehicle Size and Powertrain Type from Motion Trajectory Across Unseen Car Models
summary: Vehicle size and powertrain information can enrich trajectory data for traffic analysis and simulation. We present VTT, a dataset and benchmark for identifying these attributes from motion and controller area network (CAN) signals across unseen car models. The dataset contains 9,062 drives, about 3,950 h, from 1,431 vehicles and 174 car models. It provides three footprint-based size classes, powertrain labels, and evaluation on unseen car models and unseen drivers. Using 60-s windows, we compare four sequence architectures, statistical features and physical features proposed by large language models. Training with auxiliary physical targets, data augmentation and task-specific weighting raises drive-level macro-F1 to 92.6-93.0% for battery-electric versus combustion vehicles and from 62.9% to 67.1% for size classification. On public logs from 4,061 additional drivers, the full-input model identifies powertrain correctly for 86 of 88 car models; size accuracy is 63.2%, close to the internal vehicle-level result of 63.5%. Physical-feature analysis links powertrain recognition to deceleration behaviour and size recognition to steering response. Errors near size-class boundaries and limited gains from longer observations highlight the importance of label resolution and training-fleet coverage for cross-model generalisation.

AI.tldr: VTT is a 9,062-drive dataset and benchmark for classifying vehicle size and powertrain type from motion and CAN signals across unseen car models. Auxiliary physical targets and augmentation raise drive-level macro-F1 to 92.6-93.0% for powertrain and 67.1% for size.
AI.motivation: Identifying vehicle size and powertrain from trajectory data can enrich traffic analysis and simulation, but cross-model generalization to unseen cars is underexplored.
AI.method: The authors introduce VTT (3,950 hours, 1,431 vehicles, 174 car models) with 60-second windows, comparing four sequence architectures, statistical features, and LLM-proposed physical features, trained with auxiliary physical targets, augmentation, and task-specific weighting.
AI.result: Training improvements raise drive-level macro-F1 to 92.6-93.0% for battery-electric versus combustion powertrains and from 62.9% to 67.1% for three-class size classification; on public logs from 4,061 drivers, the full model identifies powertrain for 86 of 88 car models and achieves 63.2% size accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Deceleration behavior drives powertrain recognition while steering response drives size recognition, though label resolution and fleet coverage remain key for cross-model generalization.

title: TempQuant: Learning Adaptive Temperatures for Quantized Language Models
summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed at low precision, yet quantization can degrade their performance. We study how quantization interacts with decoding settings such as the sampling temperature and top-p by examining how it distorts the model's next-token probabilities. Measuring entropy during generation across deployed temperatures, we find that quantization warms the model on average, and that temperature matters much more for the performance of a quantized model than for its full-precision counterpart. Because quantization and temperature both shape the next-token distribution, we investigate how much the sampling settings can undo what quantization changes, through our method TempQuant, which learns the quantized model's temperature and top-p to bring its next-token probabilities closer to the full-precision model's. We learn these settings at two granularities. The first is a single global setting per requested temperature, which finds nearly the same temperatures that tuning on labeled answers would, without any labels. Model cards typically recommend sampling a quantized model with the same settings as its full-precision counterpart, while we find that different settings can substantially improve its accuracy. On 3-bit Qwen3-4B, for example, global TempQuant raises MATH accuracy from 34% under the configuration recommended for Qwen's quantized releases to 51%. The second sets the temperature and top-p for every token, motivated by our finding that tokens whose rankings flip under quantization tend to need warming, while tokens whose rankings are preserved tend to need cooling. When quantization degrades accuracy substantially, TempQuant recovers much of it, and when degradation is lighter, it still brings the quantized model's behavior closer to the full-precision model's.

AI.tldr: TempQuant learns adaptive sampling temperature and top-p settings to align a quantized LLM's next-token probabilities with its full-precision counterpart. Global TempQuant raises 3-bit Qwen3-4B MATH accuracy from 34% to 51% without labeled data.
AI.motivation: Quantization warms an LLM's next-token distribution on average, yet model cards typically recommend reusing full-precision decoding settings, degrading quantized performance.
AI.method: TempQuant learns temperature and top-p without labels by matching the quantized model's next-token probabilities to the full-precision model, either as a single global setting per requested temperature or per-token (warming rank-flipped tokens and cooling rank-preserved tokens).
AI.result: Global TempQuant recovers nearly the same temperatures as tuning on labeled answers, raising 3-bit Qwen3-4B MATH accuracy from 34% to 51%, while per-token TempQuant further aligns quantized and full-precision behavior.
AI.conclusion: Adapting decoding hyperparameters to counteract quantization-induced probability distortion substantially recovers lost accuracy without retraining or labels.

title: ReMoE: An Interpretable Mixture-of-Experts Framework for Human Mobility Recovery Forecasting Across Disasters
summary: Human mobility often declines sharply following disasters and subsequently exhibits complex recovery dynamics. Effective forecasting of this recovery is critical for timely assessment and resource allocation. However, existing approaches are often developed for individual events and operate as black boxes, limiting their transferability and interpretability beyond the events they were trained on. Recent studies have identified recurring post-disaster mobility recovery types across disasters, suggesting that recovery knowledge may be transferable. Motivated by this, we propose ReMoE, an interpretable mixture-of-experts framework for cross-disaster mobility recovery forecasting. ReMoE uses a feature-guided router to adaptively combine specialized experts that learn these heterogeneous yet reusable recovery types, producing a region-specific recovery pattern. It further refines this pattern through residual correction informed by forecasts of future hazard conditions. We evaluate ReMoE on a large-scale mobility dataset covering 18 disaster events spanning hurricanes, floods, winter storms, and wildfires. ReMoE is competitive in-distribution and achieves the strongest performance on unseen events and hazard types, with larger gains under greater distribution shifts. Further analyses show that ReMoE yields interpretable learning outcomes and maintains robust performance under uncertainty. Broadly, ReMoE offers a transferable and traceable forecaster that can support anticipatory post-disaster assessment.

AI.tldr: ReMoE is an interpretable mixture-of-experts framework for cross-disaster human mobility recovery forecasting. Evaluated across 18 disaster events, it achieves the strongest performance on unseen events and hazard types while offering interpretable recovery patterns.
AI.motivation: Existing post-disaster mobility forecasters are typically event-specific black boxes that fail to transfer or provide interpretability across different disasters.
AI.method: ReMoE uses a feature-guided router to combine specialized experts representing recurring post-disaster recovery types into a region-specific pattern, then applies residual correction informed by future hazard forecasts.
AI.result: Evaluated on a large-scale dataset of 18 disasters (hurricanes, floods, winter storms, wildfires), ReMoE is competitive in-distribution and achieves the strongest performance on unseen events and hazard types, with larger gains under stronger distribution shifts.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing recovery into reusable, interpretable expert patterns enables transferable and traceable post-disaster mobility forecasting.

title: Synthetic Crystal Data Generation for Diffusion Pretraining in Material Property Prediction
comment: 14 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. Accepted at the AI4Mat Workshop at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Diffusion-based pretraining has emerged as a powerful strategy for learning transferable representations in graph neural networks for materials property prediction without requiring quantum-mechanical labels such as energies, forces, and stresses for every pretraining structure. However, the method retains a critical dependency: it requires structures residing near local minima of a potential energy surface, which have traditionally been obtained through costly DFT relaxations of known or physically synthesized compounds. This reliance constrains both the scale and the structural diversity of available pretraining data, leaving large regions of crystal structure space unexplored. In this work, we connect diffusion-based pretraining with synthetic structure generation to reduce this bottleneck. We introduce a synthetic data generation pipeline combining three complementary strategies: perturb-and-relax, generative sampling via MatterGen, and protostructure enumeration. Where structural relaxation is required, we use fast machine-learned interatomic potentials instead of performing a new DFT relaxation for each generated structure. We further compare a coordinate-denoising control with continuous-time variance-preserving (VP) and sub-VP diffusion objectives using a randomly initialized Orb-v2 backbone. The source comparison covers seven MatBench property-prediction tasks, and an eighth task, \texttt{mp\_gap}, is included in the protostructure scaling study. Every synthetic-pretraining condition numerically outperforms random initialization on all seven source-comparison tasks. Scaling the protostructure corpus from 20k to 165k under a fixed 400-epoch schedule numerically matches or exceeds MP-20k pretraining on most tasks; because this protocol increases both data diversity and optimization updates, the result reflects joint data-and-compute scaling.

AI.tldr: This paper pairs diffusion-based pretraining for material property prediction with synthetic crystal structure generation relaxed by machine-learned interatomic potentials. Synthetic pretraining outperforms random initialization on all seven MatBench tasks and matches MP-20k pretraining when scaled to 165k structures.
AI.motivation: Diffusion pretraining for materials GNNs relies on structures near potential energy minima, traditionally requiring costly DFT relaxations that limit data scale and diversity.
AI.method: The authors build a synthetic pipeline combining perturb-and-relax, MatterGen generative sampling, and protostructure enumeration—using fast machine-learned interatomic potentials for relaxation—and compare coordinate-denoising, VP, and sub-VP diffusion objectives on an Orb-v2 backbone.
AI.result: Every synthetic-pretraining condition numerically outperforms random initialization across all seven MatBench source-comparison tasks, and scaling the protostructure corpus from 20k to 165k under a fixed 400-epoch schedule matches or exceeds MP-20k pretraining on most tasks.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic crystal generation with ML-potential relaxation provides a scalable, DFT-free path to pretraining materials property predictors.

title: When does deep reinforcement learning pay off in HVAC supervisory control? Four small Modelica case studies trained directly on FMUs
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Code, models and trained agents: this https URL
summary: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) is often proposed for the supervisory control of heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC) systems. The reported gains are, however, difficult to interpret, because the baselines are often weak and the attainable optimum is seldom known. This paper examines four small, reproducible case studies based on an office building in Brisbane, Australia: pre-cooling under a time-of-use tariff; chiller staging with condenser water reset; chilled water supply temperature reset with a wet cooling coil; and chilled water storage under time-of-use prices and a demand charge. The plants were modelled with the Modelica Buildings library, and in three of the cases a soft actor-critic agent was trained directly on the exported functional mock-up unit (FMU). Each agent was compared with tuned rule-based controllers and, where practicable, with a near-optimal reference from hourly exhaustive search or dynamic programming with perfect foresight. In the two cases without storage the agent reached the near-optimal reference, but the margin above a well-chosen rule was small: 1.3% for condenser water reset and 0.18% for chilled water reset. In the latter case two common reset rules consumed more energy than a fixed set point. With a chilled water storage tank the margin was considerably larger. The agent outperformed both rules (-7.8%, compared with -3.9% and -6.3%) and adopted midday charging during the solar off-peak period, yet it obtained only about 45% of the saving achieved by the perfect-foresight schedule and did little to limit the demand peak. In the pre-cooling case a hand-tuned rule remained superior (-12.0% compared with -5.6%). These results suggest that studies of DRL for HVAC control should state the margin between the best rule and a near-optimal reference. Some practical difficulties encountered in training on co-simulation FMUs are also reported.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates soft actor-critic (SAC) deep reinforcement learning directly on Modelica FMUs across four HVAC supervisory control case studies against tuned rules and near-optimal references. DRL yields large gains only with thermal storage, while well-tuned rules remain competitive or superior without storage.
AI.motivation: Reported DRL gains in HVAC control are often hard to interpret because baselines are weak and the attainable optimum is rarely known.
AI.method: Four Brisbane office building cases (pre-cooling, chiller staging with condenser water reset, chilled water supply reset, and chilled water storage) are modeled in Modelica, with SAC trained directly on exported FMUs and compared against tuned rule-based controllers and exhaustive/DP near-optimal references.
AI.result: Without storage, SAC reached near-optimal references but beat tuned rules by only 1.3% (condenser water reset) and 0.18% (chilled water reset); with chilled water storage, SAC beat rules (-7.8% vs. -3.9% and -6.3%) yet captured only ~45% of perfect-foresight savings, and in pre-cooling a hand-tuned rule remained superior (-12.0% vs. -5.6%).
AI.conclusion: HVAC DRL studies should report the margin between strong rule-based baselines and near-optimal references, as DRL's payoff depends heavily on storage and problem structure.

title: Towards Optimism-Pessimism Trade-off in Model-based Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning
summary: Model-based offline-to-online reinforcement learning (RL) enables sample-efficient adaptation by leveraging offline pre-training for online fine-tuning. However, the distribution shifts between offline and online stages often hinder fine-tuning performance. Many existing methods encode the optimism-pessimism trade-off through a single-objective formulation. Selecting its trade-off coefficient through online fine-tuning can require costly bi-level optimization. We identify the balance established during offline training as a key challenge: in our motivating experiments, optimistic policies adapt better to novel tasks, whereas pessimistic policies perform better on the same online tasks. To address this challenge, we propose a bi-objective formulation that captures this trade-off, yielding a Pareto policy pool during offline training. This policy pool enables adaptive selection during online fine-tuning across diverse online tasks. To generate the pool, we introduce Multi-Objective Soft Actor-critIC (MOSAIC), which solves bi-objective problems and constructs diverse Pareto policies. After offline training, a contextual bandit algorithm hierarchically selects the most suitable policy for fine-tuning at each online interaction step. Empirically, our pipeline, Hierarchical Pareto Policy Pool (HiP3), achieves the strongest aggregate performance across both same and novel online tasks and maintains its advantage under stronger distribution shifts. Comprehensive ablations further clarify the roles of the policy pool, MOSAIC-based pool construction, and the online selection mechanism.

AI.tldr: HiP3 addresses the optimism-pessimism trade-off in model-based offline-to-online RL by constructing a Pareto policy pool offline and selecting policies hierarchically online. It achieves the strongest aggregate performance across both same and novel online tasks.
AI.motivation: Single-objective offline-to-online RL encodings of optimism versus pessimism struggle because pessimistic policies favor same-task fine-tuning while optimistic policies adapt better to novel tasks.
AI.method: The authors introduce Multi-Objective Soft Actor-critIC (MOSAIC) to solve a bi-objective formulation and build a diverse Pareto policy pool offline, then use a contextual bandit online to hierarchically select the best policy at each step.
AI.result: HiP3 achieves the strongest aggregate performance across both same and novel online tasks and maintains its advantage under stronger distribution shifts, with ablations confirming the value of the pool and bandit selection.
AI.conclusion: Maintaining a Pareto pool of optimistic-to-pessimistic policies enables adaptive, sample-efficient offline-to-online RL across diverse task shifts.

title: An Optimization Framework for Denoising Generation
summary: Noise-unconditioned denoising learns a single score, so generation can be viewed as gradient ascent on a fixed log-density landscape. This optimization interpretation leaves two questions: do trajectories approach meaningful data, and do different initializations retain diverse outcomes? We establish both phenomena for empirical and population multi-scale Gaussian-mixture objectives. Under explicit posterior and landscape conditions, ascent converges almost surely within $O(m\sigma_{\min}^2/\tau)$ of an $m$-dimensional reference manifold with reach at least $\tau$. We derive a source--sink identity for the same fixed field and use it to prove finite-resolution regional coverage. In an affine construction, we further identify a positive-bandwidth regime where even empirical-score optimization can avoid training-sample memorization while preserving diversity at the training resolution. The same fixed objective naturally supports penalty-guided controllable generation. Experiments support our predicted mechanisms, show improved robustness under large-step guidance, and demonstrate downstream gains consistent with finite-data generative generalization.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes noise-unconditioned denoising generation as gradient ascent on a fixed log-density landscape, proving manifold convergence, finite-resolution regional coverage, and a non-memorization regime.
AI.motivation: Viewing noise-unconditioned denoising as optimization on a fixed landscape leaves open whether trajectories reach meaningful data and preserve diversity across initializations.
AI.method: For empirical and population multi-scale Gaussian-mixture objectives, the authors prove almost-sure convergence within O(m sigma_min^2 / tau) of an m-dimensional manifold, derive a source-sink identity for regional coverage, and analyze an affine construction for bandwidth-dependent memorization.
AI.result: The theory identifies a positive-bandwidth regime where empirical-score optimization avoids training-sample memorization while preserving diversity, and experiments confirm the predicted mechanisms, large-step guidance robustness, and downstream generalization gains.
AI.conclusion: Fixed-landscape optimization theory explains how denoising generation achieves manifold convergence, diversity, and controllable generation without memorization.

title: Sample-efficient Personalization of Large Language Model Alignment with Multidimensional User Preference Data
summary: Preference alignment has become a central tool to align large language models (LLMs) with human values and desired behavior, and its online variant can further advance their capabilities beyond what static data alone offer by repeatedly generating and labeling new responses with human feedback. But costly, time-consuming annotations limit its scalability, making sample efficiency essential, and existing methods typically seek to improve it by expanding coverage of the response space or selecting pairs with the highest uncertainty for comparison. Although they are effective, these methods quantify uncertainty from the perspective of the LLM, which may differ from the uncertainty perceived by the user: a pair can appear highly uncertain to the LLM even when past comparisons from the user already imply a clear ordering. In this paper, we propose multidimensional preference-guided online direct preference optimization (MPG-DPO), which leverages low-cost multidimensional evaluations from automated verifiers on the user historical comparisons to construct a personalized preference cone guiding response selection for online preference alignment. Specifically, it first discards responses that are confidently dominated under the estimated user preference, then selects two responses that are competitive under the retained preference cone yet exhibit the strongest unresolved disagreement. Theoretical analysis shows that, with high probability, the fraction of queries spent on cone-dominated responses vanishes as learning progresses. Experiments across multiple LLM families show that MPG-DPO outperforms strong contenders under matched query budgets.

AI.tldr: MPG-DPO improves sample efficiency in online personalized LLM alignment by using multidimensional automated verifier scores to build a user preference cone for query selection. It outperforms strong baselines under matched query budgets across multiple LLM families.
AI.motivation: Online preference alignment is bottlenecked by costly human annotations, and existing uncertainty-based query selection ignores that pairs uncertain to the LLM may already be ordered by a user's past comparisons.
AI.method: MPG-DPO uses low-cost multidimensional automated verifier evaluations on historical user comparisons to construct a personalized preference cone, discarding cone-dominated responses and querying pairs that are competitive yet have the strongest unresolved disagreement.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis shows the fraction of queries spent on cone-dominated responses vanishes with high probability, and experiments across multiple LLM families demonstrate that MPG-DPO outperforms strong contenders under matched query budgets.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging multidimensional verifier feedback to model user preference cones significantly reduces annotation waste in online personalized alignment.

title: Communicate the Change: Efficient Expert Parallelism via Activation Compression
summary: Scaling has driven the success of large language models (LLM), with sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures enabling greater parameter capacity without a proportional increase in computation. At large scales, MoE models rely on expert parallelism to distribute experts across devices. Each MoE layer requires two synchronous collective communication steps during inference: dispatching hidden states to the activated experts and combining the resulting expert outputs. As compute throughput has outpaced interconnect bandwidth, these synchronous collectives have become a major bottleneck to MoE scaling and efficiency. We address this challenge with EchoMoE, a lightweight architecture modification that retrofits existing MoE models, requiring approximately 8,500x fewer training tokens than full pretraining. Motivated by the observation that transformer blocks update the residual stream incrementally, we use a hidden state from an earlier layer as a reference and communicate only the compressed difference between it and the current state, rather than communicating each hidden state in full. EchoMoE periodically refreshes these reference states and transmits only the compressed differences synchronously, reducing the traffic on latency-critical paths without significant computational overhead. EchoMoE reduces inter-node communication volume by 58% and improves throughput by 22.6%, while preserving average performance within 3.8 percentage points across 18 benchmarks. EchoMoE further improves inference throughput by up to 2.38x over bandwidth-constrained Ethernet, paving the way for wide-area distributed inference. EchoMoE also tolerates quantization of the communicated representations without measurable quality loss. We release an efficient implementation for applying EchoMoE to pretrained MoE models, together with an inference integration for vLLM.

AI.tldr: EchoMoE reduces inter-node collective communication in MoE inference by transmitting compressed differences from earlier-layer reference hidden states rather than full states. It cuts inter-node communication by 58% and boosts throughput by 22.6% (up to 2.38x over Ethernet) with minimal accuracy loss.
AI.motivation: Synchronous dispatch and combine collectives in expert-parallel MoE inference have become a major scaling bottleneck as compute outpaces interconnect bandwidth.
AI.method: EchoMoE retrofits existing MoE models (using ~8,500x fewer tokens than full pretraining) to periodically refresh reference hidden states from earlier layers and communicate only compressed residual differences synchronously, with vLLM integration.
AI.result: EchoMoE reduces inter-node communication volume by 58% and improves throughput by 22.6% (up to 2.38x over bandwidth-constrained Ethernet) while keeping average performance within 3.8 percentage points across 18 benchmarks and tolerating representation quantization.
AI.conclusion: Communicating compressed residual changes makes distributed MoE inference viable even over bandwidth-constrained interconnects.

title: Learning Optimal Transport Plans Via Autoregressive Token Regression
summary: Optimal Transport (OT) provides a principled framework for finding the minimum cost coupling between probability distributions. Classical solvers remain the gold standard for this task. At the same time, OT is an ideal testbed for studying whether learning-based amortized models can internalize the structure of OT type problems. Here, ground-truth solutions are available and marginal constraints are explicitly defined. Also, exact discrete solutions have well-characterized sparsity. We describe ToR-OT, a transformer-based model that learns to predict discrete OT plans through autoregressive token regression. We reframe OT into a structured sequence generation task. ToR-OT decodes sparse transport plans as sequences instead of solving an optimization task at test time. We focus on three properties: (a) Zero-shot generalization: pretraining on a large synthetic corpus of OT instances allows a single model to generalize to unseen distribution pairs and heterogeneous cost metrics without retraining, (b) Sparse primal decoding: by exploiting the inherent sparsity in exact discrete OT solutions, the decoder predicts only nonzero entries (avoids dense coupling outputs), (c) Amortized inference: on low-dimensional discrete problems, ToR-OT gives accurate approximate plans and compares favorably with per-instance neural OT baselines. Overall, ToR-OT is not yet a replacement for classical solvers, but a step toward understanding how autoregressive transformers can learn structure of constrained optimization problems like OT.

AI.tldr: ToR-OT frames discrete Optimal Transport (OT) as autoregressive sequence generation, predicting only nonzero entries of sparse transport plans. Pretrained on synthetic OT instances, it generalizes zero-shot to unseen distributions and cost metrics on low-dimensional problems.
AI.motivation: Classical OT solvers remain the gold standard, making OT a clean testbed to study whether amortized autoregressive transformers can internalize constrained optimization structure.
AI.method: ToR-OT is a transformer trained via autoregressive token regression on a large synthetic corpus of OT instances to decode sparse primal transport plans without test-time optimization.
AI.result: On low-dimensional discrete OT problems, ToR-OT generalizes zero-shot to unseen distribution pairs and heterogeneous cost metrics, producing accurate approximate plans that compare favorably with per-instance neural OT baselines.
AI.conclusion: While not yet replacing classical solvers, ToR-OT demonstrates that autoregressive transformers can learn sparse, constrained optimization structures in an amortized, zero-shot manner.

title: What Does Weight-Space Programming Add to Diffusion Editing? Program Construction versus Score-Guided Refinement
summary: Weight-space programming (WSP) lets a language model construct executable weight updates for another network. We study diffusion concept editing through an interface in which programs define training contexts, preservation constraints and update directions, while a shared numerical fitter selects their coefficients. We compare generated programs with published editors, a shared-panel hand-written baseline and budget-matched search over conventional edits on 24 TIMED test edits for Stable Diffusion 1.4. The preregistered rewrite pipeline shows no advantage over the strong baseline. In an exploratory comparison, one-shot Astra programs improve fresh-scene VLM joint success, which requires subject presence together with whole-image target matching, by +10.0 points over the shared-panel baseline, while CLIP relative match shows no detectable change. These programs organise adjustable directions around protected text-state subspaces. Probing and rewriting the Astra programs then raises CLIP by +6.2 points while joint success changes by -9.7. On a fixed 144-image sample, five additional evaluators give point estimates in the same directions under whole-image target matching; checks of subject-local change give less decisive differences. Together, these results identify useful behaviour in complete generated programs and show that score-guided revision need not preserve it: program construction and revision should be evaluated as distinct stages of a WSP pipeline.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates Weight-Space Programming (WSP) for diffusion concept editing on Stable Diffusion 1.4, comparing one-shot LLM-generated edit programs against score-guided rewrites and baselines. One-shot Astra programs improve VLM joint success by +10.0 points, whereas score-guided rewriting degrades it.
AI.motivation: Weight-space programming lets LLMs construct executable weight updates, but it is unclear what program construction versus score-guided refinement contributes to diffusion editing.
AI.method: On 24 TIMED test edits for Stable Diffusion 1.4, the authors compare LLM-generated programs (using a shared numerical fitter) against published editors, a shared-panel hand-written baseline, and budget-matched search, and test probing/rewriting of one-shot Astra programs.
AI.result: While the preregistered rewrite pipeline shows no advantage over the strong baseline, one-shot Astra programs improve fresh-scene VLM joint success by +10.0 points over the shared-panel baseline (with no CLIP change); probing and rewriting those programs raises CLIP by +6.2 points but drops joint success by -9.7 points.
AI.conclusion: Program construction and score-guided revision behave differently in WSP pipelines and should be evaluated as distinct stages.

title: Spatially local mini-batching for implicit neural representations
summary: Neural surrogates based on implicit neural representations (INRs) are typically trained on mini-batches spread over the whole domain, since a generic INR loses accuracy when every point of a batch lies in one small region. We show that low-rank neural representations (LRNRs), INRs whose weight matrices are products of shared bases with coefficients emitted by a small hypernetwork, can be trained with spatially local mini-batches. Each step uses the points of one time snapshot of an adaptive-mesh numerical solution inside one small cell, with snapshots and cells drawn according to the refinement of the mesh. We posit that such training is enabled by the structural property of LRNRs, as a local step reaches the shared bases only through the $r$ coefficients of each layer, and keeps one cell from rewriting the network. By a Kolmogorov-width argument, we show that when restricted to a small cell, the hidden states of LRNRs lie close to a low-dimensional subspace, which suggests the local steps only affect low-rank subspaces of the shared bases. On six hyperbolic-conservation-law problems with solutions computed using adaptive mesh refinement, one local training recipe reaches 1.1-2.3% relative $L^2$ error with a tenth of the parameters of a dense network of the same width. Finally, we provide a comparison by training a hypernetwork-SIREN, a DeepONet, and a Fourier neural operator (FNO) of the same size with the same local batches and training budget. We observe that these baselines reach 16-78% where the LRNR reaches 4.9%. Interestingly, we also observe that local training has a significant effect on the per-cell low-dimensional structure even in a wide generic hypernetwork-SIREN.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that low-rank neural representations (LRNRs) can be trained effectively with spatially local mini-batches on adaptive-mesh numerical solutions, achieving 1.1-2.3% relative L2 error with one-tenth the parameters of a dense network.
AI.motivation: Generic implicit neural representations (INRs) lose accuracy when trained on spatially local mini-batches because a local step overwrites the global network, forcing surrogates to use domain-wide mini-batches.
AI.method: The authors train LRNRs, whose weight matrices are products of shared bases and hypernetwork-emitted coefficients, using points from a single time snapshot inside one small adaptive-mesh cell, and analyze the mechanism via a Kolmogorov-width argument.
AI.result: Across six hyperbolic-conservation-law problems, local LRNR training reaches 1.1-2.3% relative L2 error with 10x fewer parameters than a dense network, and achieves 4.9% error where hypernetwork-SIREN, DeepONet, and FNO baselines reach 16-78%.
AI.conclusion: The structural low-rank decomposition of LRNRs confines local gradient updates to low-dimensional subspaces of the shared bases, enabling accurate, parameter-efficient local mini-batch training of neural surrogates.

title: PCGRL for Complex Platformers: Synthesizing Playable and Diverse Levels via Inflated Envelopes and Forward Curricula
summary: Procedural Content Generation via Reinforcement Learning (PCGRL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for automated game development. However, existing PCGRL frameworks still suffer from severe exploration bottlenecks and scaling limitations when faced with long-sequence generation tasks governed by strict rigid-body rules and non-linear kinematic boundaries (e.g., platformer constraints). Consequently, traditional approaches frequently fail to maintain reliable level solvability on large-scale canvases. To address these challenges, we present a physics-aware, curriculum-guided PCGRL framework. First, we construct an "Inflated Volume Envelope" mechanism, which provides a physics-constrained representation that incorporates continuous kinematic feasibility into the discrete state space of the MDP. Second, to alleviate the sparse reward challenge induced by extremely long decision sequences, we introduce intermediate state-transition feedback and a multi-stage forward extension curriculum learning framework, enabling informative value estimation and stable credit assignment over long-horizon trajectories. Finally, to resolve the issue where deterministic policies after convergence generate highly monotonous map paths with a lack of diversity, we activate high-entropy stochastic inference during the synthesis phase, regularized by a post-hoc parallel rejection filtering mechanism. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework significantly enhances structural diversity while maintaining high physical playability across multi-scale environments. Comparative evaluations across multi-scale canvases demonstrate that our framework maintains superior convergence stability and dimensional scalability, reliably synthesizing solvable levels where traditional PCGRL baselines degrade.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a physics-aware, curriculum-guided PCGRL framework for complex platformers that improves structural diversity and maintains high physical playability across multi-scale canvases.
AI.motivation: Existing Procedural Content Generation via Reinforcement Learning (PCGRL) frameworks suffer from exploration bottlenecks, sparse rewards over long horizons, and monotonous converged policies when generating large-scale platformer levels with strict kinematic constraints.
AI.method: The framework introduces an Inflated Volume Envelope to encode continuous kinematic feasibility into the discrete MDP state space, intermediate state-transition feedback with a multi-stage forward extension curriculum, and high-entropy stochastic inference with post-hoc parallel rejection filtering.
AI.result: Comparative evaluations across multi-scale environments show that the framework improves structural diversity, convergence stability, and dimensional scalability while reliably synthesizing solvable levels where traditional PCGRL baselines degrade.
AI.conclusion: Combining physics-constrained state representations, forward curriculum learning, and filtered stochastic inference makes PCGRL scalable and reliable for complex, long-horizon platformer level generation.

title: Perception into Imagination: Executable Memory for World Models
summary: Physical agents must use what they previously saw or touched after visibility or contact is lost. Their actions change the implications of these remembered facts. We introduce executable perceptual memory (EPM), a world-model framework that advances explicit perceptual state alongside neural latent dynamics during imagination. Its evolving read-out informs reward prediction, value estimation and policy learning. We align reward inputs with the transitions that produced them and supervise the reward head on open-loop rollouts of recorded actions. On Memory Maze $13\times13$, EPM reaches 30.37 return at 1M interactions, compared with 23.37 when the same evolving read-out informs only policy and value on a common perceptual front end: a gain of 7.00 [3.80, 10.21]. The complete method also improves control on $9\times9$ and in MiniWorld. Probes of remembered, out-of-view arrivals show stronger reward anticipation in both visual implementations. Concentration, tactile recovery and real tactile frames demonstrate complementary roles of remembered facts in imagined-policy training, motion-dependent decisions and sensory-content retention. EPM connects persistent perception to the predicted consequences and learning signals of a world model for Physical AI.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Executable Perceptual Memory (EPM), a world-model framework that advances explicit perceptual state alongside neural latent dynamics during imagination to improve reward prediction, value estimation, and policy learning.
AI.motivation: Physical agents must reason about previously seen or touched objects after visibility or contact is lost, as their actions alter the implications of those remembered facts.
AI.method: EPM maintains an evolving explicit perceptual read-out alongside latent dynamics during imagination, aligns reward inputs with the transitions that produced them, and supervises the reward head on open-loop rollouts of recorded actions.
AI.result: On Memory Maze 13x13 at 1M interactions, EPM reaches 30.37 return versus 23.37 when the read-out informs only policy and value (a gain of 7.00), and also improves control on Memory Maze 9x9, MiniWorld, and tactile tasks.
AI.conclusion: Connecting persistent explicit perception to imagined reward, value, and policy learning strengthens world models for Physical AI in partially observable settings.

title: Similar Is Not Useful: Selecting In-Context Demonstrations by Closed-Loop Utility
summary: Retrieval-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) policies fill their context with the demonstrations whose frames look most like the current observation under frozen DINOv2 embeddings. We ask whether visual similarity selects the demonstrations that make the policy succeed. For a frozen retrieval-augmented VLA (RICL on $\pi_0$-FAST, LIBERO), we make the demonstration pool swappable at run time and score each demonstration's utility by regressing the closed-loop success of 60 fixed-size pools on their membership. On initial states disjoint from those used for scoring, pools of the five highest-utility demonstrations succeed on 66.4% of 760 paired episodes across 19 tasks, pools of the five most similar on 55.7%, and random pools on 55.5%. Utility beats similarity by 10.8 points ($p=3.2\times10^{-6}$; positive on 15 of 18 untied tasks), including on 12 tasks the policy was never primed on, and similarity-selected pools do no better than random ($+0.1$ points). Within a task, a pool's visual similarity to the test scenes tracks its success at Spearman 0.10; across tasks, similarity separates tasks whose scenes differ and falls to chance when two tasks share a scene. The gain comes from on-task closed-loop evidence: best-of-ten direct search over pools recovers two-thirds of it with 100 rollouts. Against the shipped 20-demonstration pool, utility-curated pools of five lead by 7.0 points over 560 paired episodes from two evaluation runs ($p=0.006$), and utility-ordered retrieval inside the full pool leads by 4.5 points ($p=0.055$).

AI.tldr: This paper shows that selecting in-context demonstrations by closed-loop utility rather than visual similarity substantially improves retrieval-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) policy success on LIBERO.
AI.motivation: Retrieval-augmented VLA policies typically select demonstrations whose frames are most visually similar under frozen DINOv2 embeddings, without verifying whether visual similarity actually improves closed-loop task execution.
AI.method: For a frozen RICL policy on pi0-FAST, the authors swap demonstration pools at run time and regress the closed-loop success of 60 fixed-size pools on their membership to score each demonstration's utility.
AI.result: Across 760 paired episodes on 19 LIBERO tasks, top-5 utility pools achieve 66.4% success compared to 55.7% for top-5 visual similarity and 55.5% for random pools (p = 3.2e-6), while similarity correlates weakly with within-task success (Spearman 0.10).
AI.conclusion: Closed-loop execution evidence is a far more reliable criterion than visual similarity for curating and ordering in-context demonstrations in retrieval-augmented VLA policies.

title: BQ-LoRA: Binary-Quantized Low-Rank Adapters as Implicit Regularizers for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 20 pages, 4 figures, 21 tables
summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning of quantized large language models is dominated by QLoRA, which combines 4-bit weight quantization with FP16 low-rank adapters. We ask whether the FP16 adapter precision is necessary. Replacing it with a single binary bit per adapter parameter, combined with a learned per-layer scale $s$ and a Scaled Straight-Through Estimator, reduces adapter storage by 13-16x. We introduce two variants -- NormScale, which binarizes under a norm-preserving scale with a clipped STE, and LearnThresh, which makes the binarization threshold learnable -- unified under a framework we call BQ-LoRA. Our main theoretical contribution is a tight characterization of the BQ-LoRA hypothesis class: it has bounded entrywise norm, a typical-set spectral norm bound that is $\Theta(r)$ times sharper than the worst case, a full-rank, near-isotropic update, and consequently a Rademacher complexity that yields an explicit $\tilde{O}(s_{\max}\alpha\sqrt{d_{out}/(rn)})$ generalization bound. FP16 LoRA has no comparable a priori norm or isotropy control. On Qwen2.5 (1.5B-72B), BQ-LoRA exceeds QLoRA's benchmark averages at every scale by 0.8-3.5 points; on LLaMA-2 (7B/70B) it remains competitive at the same storage reduction but does not uniformly lead the strongest FP16-adapter baselines (LoftQ at 7B, QLoRA at 70B). On Qwen2.5-7B the binary adapter preserves the 4-bit base WikiText-2 PPL within 0.06 (9.86 vs. 9.80) while QLoRA worsens it by 0.59. The reduction applies to inference-time adapter storage and serving; training memory matches QLoRA and step time rises by under 4%. We translate the storage saving into a deployment study, BQ-SGMV, by extending Punica's SGMV kernel with a binary inner-product primitive: the same A100-80GB holds 15.6x more adapters in HBM, and our research prototype eliminates cache misses under a skewed synthetic workload.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces BQ-LoRA, which replaces FP16 LoRA adapters with 1-bit binary-quantized adapters and a learned per-layer scale, reducing adapter storage by 13-16x while matching or exceeding QLoRA on Qwen2.5.
AI.motivation: Standard QLoRA combines 4-bit base weights with FP16 low-rank adapters, leaving open whether full FP16 adapter precision is necessary for parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
AI.method: BQ-LoRA binarizes adapter parameters with a Scaled Straight-Through Estimator via two variants (NormScale with clipped STE and LearnThresh with learnable thresholds), and extends Punica's SGMV kernel (BQ-SGMV) for multi-adapter serving.
AI.result: On Qwen2.5 (1.5B-72B), BQ-LoRA outperforms QLoRA by 0.8-3.5 points on benchmark averages and preserves 4-bit Qwen2.5-7B WikiText-2 perplexity within 0.06 (9.86 vs. 9.80), while holding 15.6x more adapters in A100-80GB HBM with under 4% training step-time overhead.
AI.conclusion: Binary-quantized low-rank adapters act as implicit regularizers with provable Rademacher complexity bounds, enabling massive inference-time storage and serving gains without sacrificing fine-tuning quality.

title: Scaling Laws for Vision-Language Fusion
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have emerged as central foundation models combining multimodal perception with text comprehension. While VLMs are traditionally built via late fusion by continued pre-training an off-the-shelf language model on multimodal (image-text) data, mixing modalities from the start of pre-training (early fusion) has recently gained traction. However, the fundamental trade-offs between these paradigms remain poorly understood, resulting in expensive and heuristic-driven training recipes. In this paper, we systematically analyze the learning dynamics of these multimodal pre-training processes, showing that validation losses during vision-language fusion can be modeled by separating the base learning trajectory, where different data types contribute at distinct rates, from a distribution shift driven by the competition between modalities. We derive a scaling law that unifiedly describes these dynamics, enabling accurate loss predictions across mixture ratios, training steps, and model sizes. Crucially, our law characterizes the trade-off between early and late fusion: under a fixed data budget, early fusion preserves text performance while late fusion favors vision performance, yielding a trade-off that increasingly tilts toward early fusion as model size scales. Extensive experiments confirm that our scaling law reliably captures multimodal learning dynamics and governs fusion decisions.

AI.tldr: This paper derives a scaling law for vision-language fusion that models validation loss across mixture ratios, training steps, and model sizes, explaining the trade-off between early and late fusion.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models are built via either late fusion or early fusion, but the fundamental trade-offs between these paradigms are poorly understood, leading to expensive, heuristic-driven training recipes.
AI.method: The authors model multimodal validation loss by separating the base learning trajectory, where data types contribute at distinct rates, from a distribution shift driven by cross-modal competition.
AI.result: Experiments confirm that the scaling law accurately predicts loss across mixture ratios, steps, and model sizes, showing that under a fixed data budget early fusion preserves text performance while late fusion favors vision performance, with the trade-off tilting toward early fusion at larger scales.
AI.conclusion: The proposed scaling law provides a principled, predictive foundation for choosing between early and late fusion and designing multimodal pre-training recipes.

title: Fair Bubble Sort: Provably Optimal Fair Ranking with Continuous Sensitive Attributes
comment: 35 pages, 9 figures, 4 tables. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Code: this https URL
summary: Most fair-ranking methods assume categorical protected attributes, requiring continuous attributes such as age or income to be discretized into groups. This introduces arbitrary thresholds, loses fine-grained information, and ignores the natural ordering of the attribute. In this paper, we study the problem of fair ranking with continuous protected attributes without relying on thresholding. We introduce Continuous Pairwise Parity (CPP), a fairness notion based on Kendall correlation between ranking positions and the protected attribute, and seek rankings that satisfy a prescribed CPP constraint while minimizing their Kemeny distance from an initial score-based ranking. To solve this problem, we propose Fair Bubble Sort (FBS), an efficient post-processing algorithm based on targeted adjacent swaps. We prove that FBS is exactly optimal for the unweighted Kemeny distance and provide approximation guarantees for the score-weighted setting. FBS is output-sensitive, with running time determined by the number of swaps required to meet the fairness constraint. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that FBS is scalable and consistently outperforms discretization-based baselines, achieving a superior fairness-accuracy Pareto front.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Fair Bubble Sort (FBS), an output-sensitive post-processing algorithm for fair ranking with continuous sensitive attributes that is provably optimal for unweighted Kemeny distance.
AI.motivation: Existing fair-ranking methods assume categorical protected attributes and discretize continuous attributes like age or income, introducing arbitrary thresholds and losing ordering information.
AI.method: The authors define Continuous Pairwise Parity (CPP) using Kendall correlation between ranking positions and the continuous attribute, and design FBS to minimize Kemeny distance from an initial ranking via targeted adjacent swaps.
AI.result: FBS is proven exactly optimal for unweighted Kemeny distance with approximation guarantees for score-weighted Kemeny distance, and experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show it scales well and outperforms discretization baselines on the fairness-accuracy Pareto front.
AI.conclusion: Formulating continuous fair ranking via Kendall correlation and adjacent swaps avoids discretization artifacts and yields provably optimal, scalable post-processing.

title: InfuseLoop: Cross-Trajectory Latent Injection for Scalable Parallel Looped Transformers
summary: Parallel Looped Transformers (PLTs) use otherwise idle decoding compute by overlapping recurrent iterations. However, vanilla PLTs scale poorly with depth: they exhibit training-loss spikes, and their quality gains shrink as more loops are added. The benefit of additional loops depends on the information available to each iteration, so we examine whether the existing computational dependencies limit effective depth scaling. We find that only the preceding in-trajectory state is passed across loop boundaries, even though completed cross-trajectory representations are already available. Based on this finding, we propose InfuseLoop, a cross-trajectory latent injection mechanism. It aggregates causally available hidden states from later prediction trajectories through lightweight attention residuals. This design preserves token-parallel training and concurrent loop execution, and requires only $O(Rd)$ additional hidden-state storage. Experiments show that InfuseLoop eliminates training-loss spikes and improves validation-loss scaling up to eight loops. At eight loops, InfuseLoop reduces perplexity by 3.4--17.1% relative to vanilla PLTs and by 10.5--37.3% relative to the non-looped baseline. It also improves average downstream accuracy by 0.84 and 1.99 percentage points over these two baselines. InfuseLoop incurs only 0.3% decoding time over vanilla PLTs and 23.3% over the non-looped baseline, while keeping the same logical KV-cache footprint as vanilla PLTs.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes InfuseLoop, a cross-trajectory latent injection mechanism for Parallel Looped Transformers (PLTs) that eliminates training-loss spikes and improves depth scaling up to eight loops.
AI.motivation: Vanilla PLTs pass only the preceding in-trajectory state across loop boundaries, causing training-loss spikes and diminishing quality gains as more loops are added.
AI.method: InfuseLoop aggregates causally available hidden states from later prediction trajectories using lightweight attention residuals, preserving token-parallel training and concurrent loop execution with O(Rd) extra hidden-state storage.
AI.result: At eight loops, InfuseLoop reduces perplexity by 3.4-17.1% over vanilla PLTs and 10.5-37.3% over non-looped baselines, improves average downstream accuracy by 0.84 and 1.99 percentage points, and adds only 0.3% decoding time over vanilla PLTs with the same logical KV-cache footprint.
AI.conclusion: Injecting causally available cross-trajectory latent states unlocks effective depth scaling in Parallel Looped Transformers at negligible runtime and memory overhead.

title: Encoding, Decodability, and Use: A Five-Layer Framework for Benchmark Measurement Audits with Evidence from UAV Intent Recognition
summary: Benchmark accuracy is routinely read as evidence that a model understands the construct the benchmark measures. We propose and instantiate on AeroIntent a five-layer framework that decomposes that reading into observation, representation, decoding, use, and behaviour. The framework separates encoding, decodability, and use as distinct levels. In the instantiation, the observation layer is unreliable on 7 of the 20 Drone programs and floors the direct visual correlate of radial velocity at a 0.26\% scale change. The representation layer exposes two task-designed RGB features with nominal signals. RAFT flow radial bias reaches $r=+0.257$ ($p=0.030$), and bounding-box optical-flow divergence reaches $r=+0.203$ ($p=0.029$). No multi-feature readout gives a fold-mean test correlation above the cluster minimum detectable effect (MDE), and the largest positive global out-of-sample correlation is $r=+0.080$. The decoding layer sets the MDE at $|r|=0.599$ at the multi-feature Bonferroni threshold ($\alpha=0.00714$, power 0.80), and the observed $r=+0.080$ has power 0.00. Two injection experiments establish the MDE's condition from both sides: aligned injections are detected at or above the simulated power, and orthogonal injections are not detected. The use layer finds accuracy consistent with program memory (program-identity 0.937/0.597/0.210) and multi-region static cues. The behaviour layer is consistent with accuracy not requiring a radial-velocity readout (appearance 0.6552 vs bounding-box trajectory 0.4080, cluster-level paired $\Delta=+0.2471$, $p=0.0132$).

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a five-layer benchmark measurement audit framework (observation, representation, decoding, use, and behaviour) and applies it to AeroIntent to show that accuracy does not require radial-velocity readout.
AI.motivation: High benchmark accuracy is often assumed to prove that a model understands the target construct, without verifying whether the construct is actually observable, decodable, or used.
AI.method: The authors decompose construct validity into observation, representation, decoding, use, and behaviour layers, testing AeroIntent with optical-flow features, cluster minimum detectable effect (MDE) bounds, aligned/orthogonal injection experiments, and appearance vs. trajectory ablations.
AI.result: On AeroIntent, observation fails on 7 of 20 Drone programs, the largest positive out-of-sample multi-feature correlation is r = +0.080 (below the MDE of |r| = 0.599, power 0.00), and appearance-only accuracy exceeds bounding-box trajectory accuracy (0.6552 vs. 0.4080, p = 0.0132).
AI.conclusion: Separating encoding, decodability, and use exposes when benchmark accuracy relies on static appearance cues and program memory rather than the intended physical construct.
