title: Eyes in the Update? Learning Where Rewards Land in Multimodal Reasoning
summary: Multimodal post-training has moved from broad instruction tuning toward reinforcement learning for image and video reasoning, where outcome rewards can improve final-answer accuracy. Yet these rewards are assigned to complete generated trajectories, while visual evidence is used only at sparse and uneven positions inside the response. Recent work has begun to make multimodal RL more token-sensitive through grounding signals or external token-level weighting. We ask a more specific question: can the allocation of the same trajectory-level reward be inferred from the model's own multimodal computation, rather than from an auxiliary annotator, perception module, or process label? We propose Gaze-RL, a representation-driven policy optimization method that redistributes completion-level advantage through a latent reward landing field. The field is computed from internal cross-modal geometry and local predictive uncertainty, assigning larger update weight to positions that are both visually anchored and decision-bearing while remaining mean-one, so the total credit of each rollout is preserved and only its positionwise allocation changes. Gaze-RL requires no process supervision, auxiliary perception module, or architectural modification, and improves both Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3.5 across a broad range of image and video benchmarks.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Gaze-RL, a representation-driven policy optimization method that redistributes trajectory-level rewards to visually anchored and decision-bearing tokens without external annotators or process labels.
AI.motivation: Multimodal RL for image and video reasoning assigns outcome rewards uniformly to entire trajectories, even though visual evidence is used sparsely and unevenly across generated tokens.
AI.method: Gaze-RL computes a mean-one latent reward landing field from the model's own internal cross-modal geometry and local predictive uncertainty, reweighting completion-level advantage per position while preserving total rollout credit.
AI.result: Across a broad range of image and video reasoning benchmarks, Gaze-RL consistently improves both Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3.5 without process supervision, auxiliary perception modules, or architectural changes.
AI.conclusion: Inferring token-level credit assignment directly from internal multimodal computation offers a lightweight, annotation-free way to make multimodal RL more visually grounded.

title: How Many Training Labels Are Wrong? Auditing a Fitted Model through Gradient Allocation
summary: How many labels in a training set are wrong, and which ones? The usual answers read a held-out set or the model's outputs. A held-out reading depends on how the held-out set was drawn, and an output-based reading fails once the model has fitted its wrong labels, because the loss of a fitted wrong label is small and the prediction agrees with it. We read the answer from the per-example gradients of a single trained model. Each example, together with its label, asks the network to change in a particular way. We normalise the magnitudes of its gradient into a gradient allocation and compare it with the mean allocation of every class. An example is flagged when relabelling it as its nearest other class makes its allocation fit better than under its own label, and the share of flagged examples is the reading of the noise rate. The rule has no threshold and needs no clean data, no held-out set and no further training. After the model has fitted 99-100% of its wrong labels, the allocation still separates wrong from right labels with an AUC of 0.94-0.96 on the noisiest human labels of CIFAR-10N, where a feature-space margin falls to 0.79-0.84 and the loss, the gradient norm and the self-influence of an example to 0.73-0.76. On such a fitted model, readings of the noise rate from predictions or feature margins fall to 0-6% at true rates of 8-58% on CIFAR-10 with ViT-S, while the audit reads 54-96% of the true rate, and at least 93% of the examples it counts carry wrong labels. On a briefly trained model, before the wrong labels are fitted, the reading lies within 1.7 percentage points of the true noise rate on CIFAR-10 from 0% to 58% noise. Confident learning, which trains four further models, separates wrong labels about as well (AUC 0.925-0.998 against 0.900-0.995) and mostly reads the noise rate more closely, at a lower precision. An audit of 5,000 examples takes 14 to 27 seconds on one GPU.

AI.tldr: This paper audits mislabeled training data in a single fitted model using normalized per-example gradient allocations, achieving 0.94-0.96 AUC on CIFAR-10N even after 99-100% of wrong labels are fitted.
AI.motivation: Output-based and margin-based label-noise detectors fail once a model memorizes its wrong labels, while held-out methods depend on held-out sampling and multi-model methods like confident learning require retraining.
AI.method: Each example's gradient magnitudes are normalized into a gradient allocation and compared against class-mean allocations; an example is flagged if relabeling it to its nearest other class improves the fit, requiring no thresholds, clean data, or retraining.
AI.result: On CIFAR-10N after fitting 99-100% of wrong labels, gradient allocation achieves 0.94-0.96 AUC versus 0.79-0.84 for feature margins and 0.73-0.76 for loss, gradient norm, and self-influence, while auditing 5,000 examples in 14-27 seconds on one GPU.
AI.conclusion: Per-example gradient allocations preserve a clear signal of label noise even after complete memorization, enabling fast, threshold-free auditing of fitted models.

title: Escaping Latent Traps by Remembering: Training-Free Episodic Kernel Repulsion for World-Model Planning
summary: Latent world models plan towards a goal image by minimising the distance between predicted and goal latents. This distance is not geodesic: it has local minima, latent traps, behind walls, at corners and in dead ends, and memoryless receding-horizon replanning keeps the agent in them, revisiting states far from the goal. We propose Episodic Kernel Repulsion (EKR), a training-free cost term that penalises candidate plans by a top-$k$ Gaussian kernel to a novelty-gated memory of the latents the agent has actually visited, rescaled by the current base cost so that its strength is comparable across models. Across two JEPA world models and four benchmarks, EKR raises average success from 31.8% to 46.7% (LeWM) and from 54.7% to 64.0% (H-JEPA) with the same model, planner and budget. Same-memory counterfactuals show that, in most settings, EKR pushes plans away from visited states, in navigation, often at a higher base cost; stuck episodes and revisits drop accordingly. In seven of eight settings it matches or exceeds $4\times$ samples at $0.8$--$1.5\times$ compute. Without tuning, it transfers to DINO-WM with CEM: $+6.7$ and $+19.3$ points on official and longer-goal Wall tasks, and from 44.7% to 100.0% and from 21.0% to 32.0% on long-horizon PointMaze and Push-T.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Episodic Kernel Repulsion (EKR), a training-free cost term for latent world-model planning that penalizes revisiting previously visited latent states to escape local-minimum traps.
AI.motivation: Minimizing latent distance to a goal image suffers from local minima behind walls, at corners, and in dead ends, causing memoryless receding-horizon planners to get stuck revisiting the same states.
AI.method: EKR adds a top-k Gaussian kernel penalty against a novelty-gated episodic memory of visited latents, rescaled by the current base cost so its strength transfers across models without tuning.
AI.result: EKR raises average success from 31.8% to 46.7% on LeWM and 54.7% to 64.0% on H-JEPA across four benchmarks, matches or exceeds 4x-sample baselines at 0.8-1.5x compute in 7 of 8 settings, and transfers to DINO-WM with CEM (e.g., 44.7% to 100.0% on long-horizon PointMaze).
AI.conclusion: Training-free episodic repulsion in latent space effectively prevents receding-horizon planners from getting trapped in non-geodesic local minima.

title: Right Labels, Wrong Reasons: Signed Feature Attribution for Multi-Label Explainability
comment: 7 pages, 1 figure, 5 tables. Accepted at the 2027 IEEE Symposium Series on Computational Intelligence (IEEE SSCI 2027), Gold Coast, Australia, February 2027
summary: When a multi-label classifier assigns the right labels, it may do so for the wrong reasons. Diffuse feature combinations may vary across classifier families and lack a dominant feature. This paper proposes FLEX (Fisher LDA Explainer), a global surrogate that fits a single direct multi-label Fisher LDA over the full binary label matrix, producing signed feature attribution lists for each label in a single coherent coordinate system. Across the evaluated benchmarks and classifier families, FLEX reproduces the black box's predictions with consistently high fidelity. Pooling covariance across labels outperforms a per-label alternative on most datasets, with the advantage growing largest where labels are numerous and positive examples are scarce. FLEX's fidelity-complexity Pareto curve is monotonically increasing, giving practitioners a predictable path to higher-fidelity explanations as more features are used, and its in-sample fidelity matches or leads Binary Relevance alternatives once a modest feature budget is allowed. The magnitude of each discriminant weight vector bounds its label's separability, flagging labels that may be predicted correctly for the wrong reasons. The evaluated classifiers largely agree on which predictions to make, but reach those decisions through different feature subsets when no single feature dominates.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes FLEX (Fisher LDA Explainer), a global multi-label surrogate that produces signed feature attributions in a single coherent coordinate system and flags labels predicted correctly for the wrong reasons.
AI.motivation: Multi-label classifiers can assign correct labels using diffuse, model-dependent feature combinations, making it hard to compare explanations or detect spurious reasoning across label sets.
AI.method: FLEX fits a direct multi-label Fisher LDA over the full binary label matrix, pooling covariance across labels and using discriminant weight magnitudes to bound label separability.
AI.result: Across evaluated benchmarks and classifier families, FLEX reproduces black-box predictions with high fidelity, outperforms per-label covariance on most datasets (especially with many labels and scarce positives), and yields a monotonically increasing fidelity-complexity Pareto curve.
AI.conclusion: A unified multi-label Fisher LDA surrogate provides predictable, high-fidelity signed attributions and diagnoses when classifiers agree on predictions for different underlying reasons.

title: Testing World Models on Actions They Have Never Seen: Held-Out Plans, Forecast Accuracy and Price Rules in Retail
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Companion to arXiv:2611.20811
summary: A world model is trusted to answer "what if": how its world responds to an action it has never seen. We give a test of that trust for any action-conditioned world model: actions held out of training by design and scored against a known answer; whether forecast accuracy predicts accuracy on those actions; and the same structure given to simpler models. We run it in retail, where the action is a price and promotion plan, across 2,853 fitted models. First, forecast accuracy is a fair guide between kinds of model (rank correlation with error on new plans 0.32 to 0.66) and a poor guide between versions of one world model: where merchants plan into high-demand weeks the link reverses, down to -0.69. Second, training the world model to learn the effect of actions (JEPA pretraining, a latent consistency check, adaptation at the plan date) leaves its error on new plans unchanged. Third, in generated worlds the recorded regular price and three price rules improve it. Given the same rules, a log-linear model is best when its curve can match the truth; in a world whose curve lies outside the rules, the world model with the rules is ahead of the log-linear model with the rules in 36 of 40 worlds, and does as well without its recurrent cell. On real data (Breakfast at the Frat, The Complete Journey and M5) the rules lower the world model's error on pure price cuts deeper than any it saw (0.63 to 0.56 on the Frat; 0.45 to 0.44, within chance, on The Complete Journey), but not on lasting price moves. Fourth, a small share of random test plans helps every model a little. In a generated dosing world, a stress test in a second domain, the first finding repeats, and the built-up drug level lowers the world model's error (2.86 to 1.91) though it still predicts only 0.12 to 0.32 of the true gain. The test carries to any domain where a world model is asked about actions outside its history.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a held-out-action evaluation protocol for action-conditioned world models and tests 2,853 models in retail, showing that forecast accuracy is an unreliable guide to performance on unseen plans.
AI.motivation: World models are trusted to answer counterfactual "what-if" questions about unseen actions, yet standard forecast accuracy may not reflect accuracy under held-out action plans.
AI.method: The authors hold out price and promotion plans by design against known answers across real retail datasets (Breakfast at the Frat, The Complete Journey, M5) and generated retail and dosing worlds, comparing world models with simpler baselines given the same price rules.
AI.result: Forecast accuracy correlates fairly across model families (0.32 to 0.66) but poorly or negatively (-0.69) within a world model family on high-demand weeks; JEPA pretraining and adaptation leave new-plan error unchanged, whereas adding price rules lowers error on deep price cuts (0.63 to 0.56 on Frat) and beats log-linear baselines in 36 of 40 nonlinear generated worlds.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating world models requires holding out structured actions rather than relying on forecast accuracy, and domain structure like price rules matters more than generic pretraining for unseen-action generalization.

title: Physically Admissible Generative Flow Matching for Sparse Flow Reconstruction
summary: Reconstructing full fluid velocity fields from sparse, localized observations is a severely ill-posed inverse problem: most of the spatial domain remains unobserved, discrete conservation laws must hold strictly, and predictive uncertainty must be reliable. Existing generative models typically enforce physical constraints only at the terminal output or via soft penalties, leaving intermediate generative trajectories unconstrained. We introduce Feasible Subspace Consistency (FSC), a framework that preserves physical admissibility as an invariant of continuous generative dynamics: tangent-space matching confines the entire ODE trajectory to the discrete conservation manifold, while mass-orthonormal coordinates preserve the kinetic-energy metric. Sparse reconstruction then reduces to amortized posterior transport in the latent space of a frozen FSC prior, ensuring every posterior sample inherits incompressibility and boundary conditions without per-sample projection loops. We validate FSC on a periodic Kolmogorov flow, where exact spectral projection isolates path tangency and metric isometry, and a wall-bounded cylinder wake with immersed obstacles, realized via matrix-free iterative projection. FSC prevents the mode-coverage collapse induced by terminal projection (increasing mode coverage from $0.000$ to $0.790$) while eliminating high-wavenumber spectral distortion. In sparse reconstruction, amortized FSC reduces global relative error by $50\%$ and $46\%$, and sensor residuals by $63\%$ and $55\%$, relative to the unconditioned prior, while delivering calibrated, spatially heterogeneous uncertainty.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Feasible Subspace Consistency (FSC), a generative flow-matching framework that confines the entire ODE trajectory to discrete physical conservation manifolds for sparse flow reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Existing generative models for fluid reconstruction enforce physical constraints only at the terminal output or via soft penalties, causing mode collapse, spectral distortion, or constraint violations along intermediate trajectories.
AI.method: FSC uses tangent-space matching to keep the continuous ODE trajectory on the discrete conservation manifold and mass-orthonormal coordinates to preserve the kinetic-energy metric, reducing sparse reconstruction to amortized posterior transport in a frozen FSC prior's latent space.
AI.result: On periodic Kolmogorov flow and a wall-bounded cylinder wake, FSC prevents terminal-projection mode collapse (raising mode coverage from 0.000 to 0.790), eliminates high-wavenumber spectral distortion, and cuts global relative error by 50% and 46% and sensor residuals by 63% and 55% over the unconditioned prior.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing physical admissibility as an invariant of the generative flow trajectory yields calibrated, conservation-exact sparse flow reconstruction without per-sample projection loops.

title: ReMaRL: Learning to Unmask and Remask in Frozen Diffusion Language Models
summary: Masked diffusion language models generate tokens in parallel, and the order in which tokens are unmasked affects final-answer accuracy. Several methods learn unmasking policies from task rewards, but these policies cannot remask earlier predictions. Remasking lets the model correct those predictions using newly generated context. Heuristic rules guide both unmasking and remasking, while supervised remaskers learn to detect token errors. Neither approach directly optimizes these decisions for final-answer correctness. To address this gap, we introduce ReMaRL (Remasking with Reinforcement Learning), a lightweight policy that learns which tokens to unmask, retain, or remask. We train this roughly 0.3M-parameter policy with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) from final-answer rewards while keeping the diffusion model frozen. With LLaDA-8B-Instruct, ReMaRL achieves the highest scores among the compared unmasking and remasking policies within the tested inference budgets of 4-32 model calls on math and 8-16 calls on code.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ReMaRL, a lightweight 0.3M-parameter reinforcement-learning policy that learns which tokens to unmask, retain, or remask in frozen masked diffusion language models.
AI.motivation: Existing unmasking policies for masked diffusion language models cannot remask earlier predictions to fix errors, while heuristic or supervised remaskers do not directly optimize for final-answer correctness.
AI.method: ReMaRL trains a roughly 0.3M-parameter policy using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) from final-answer rewards while keeping the underlying diffusion language model frozen.
AI.result: With LLaDA-8B-Instruct, ReMaRL achieves the highest accuracy among compared unmasking and remasking policies within 4-32 model calls on math and 8-16 calls on code.
AI.conclusion: Learning joint unmask-and-remask policies via final-answer RL significantly improves the accuracy-compute trade-off of frozen masked diffusion language models.

title: Lost in the Funnel: Selection-Induced Miscalibration in Ranking and Decision Systems
summary: Modern ranking and decision systems combine components with divergent objectives, and scores calibrated at the model boundary are used as calibrated probabilities throughout the funnel, across filtering, reranking, business-rule enforcement, and auctions. Yet calibration is typically validated only where the score is produced, so its breakdown where the score is used is routinely overlooked. We ask when calibration survives this selection, how inherited error differs from selection effects, and what can fail for a perfectly calibrated score at a component boundary. We study these questions through a boundary-wise diagnostic framework of residual identities. We target rubric-judged relevance rather than presentation-dependent metrics such as CTR, so calibration is measurable at every funnel layer of interest. We first present an industry-wide case study that applies our diagnosis to settings where calibration deteriorates at decision time, tracing the degradation to selection rather than model error. This diagnosis motivates Funnel-Aware Recalibration (FAR): post-hoc, selection-policy-aware recalibration at the boundary where scores drive decisions. In a live two-region production A/B test, FAR cuts decision-time expected calibration error (ECE) by 60-80% and improves auction efficiency. We further adapt two public datasets to simulate industry settings, providing additional evidence for the mechanism. We plan to release the adapted datasets and their generation pipeline to support further research. Finally, we distill these findings into practical operating principles for calibrating multi-stage scoring systems.

AI.tldr: This paper diagnoses selection-induced miscalibration across multi-stage ranking and decision funnels and introduces Funnel-Aware Recalibration (FAR), which cuts decision-time ECE by 60-80% in a live production A/B test.
AI.motivation: Ranking systems validate score calibration only at the model boundary where scores are produced, overlooking how downstream filtering, reranking, and business rules break calibration where scores are actually used.
AI.method: The authors develop a boundary-wise diagnostic framework using residual identities against rubric-judged relevance, and propose FAR, a post-hoc selection-policy-aware recalibration applied at the decision boundary.
AI.result: An industry case study traces decision-time miscalibration to selection rather than model error, and in a live two-region production A/B test FAR reduces decision-time expected calibration error (ECE) by 60-80% and improves auction efficiency, supported by two adapted public datasets.
AI.conclusion: Multi-stage decision systems require selection-aware recalibration at downstream decision boundaries rather than relying solely on upstream model calibration.

title: DLS: Dual-Logic Graph Neural Networks with Chaos-Fuzzy Residuals for Robust Link Prediction
comment: Submitted to World Wide Web (Springer Nature) on January 5, 2026. Preprint version, currently under peer review
summary: Link prediction is a fundamental task in graph mining, critical for applications ranging from biological interaction discovery to recommender systems. While Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs) have achieved state-of-the-art results, they are fundamentally limited by the inadvertent suppression of high-frequency signals, as the recursive aggregation that stabilizes structural learning inherently leads to over-smoothing, rendering node representations indistinguishable in deep layers. This limitation is particularly severe in heterophilous graphs, where structural proximity does not imply feature similarity. In this paper, we propose DLS (Dual-Logic SAGE), a novel inductive framework designed to break the over-smoothing barrier via a "controlled instability" mechanism. Unlike conventional methods relying on static structural heuristics, DLS introduces a dynamic residual pipeline. First, a Chaotic Injection Module utilizes the Logistic Map to diversify the feature manifold, exploiting sensitivity to initial conditions to separate topologically similar but semantically distinct nodes. Second, to mitigate the aleatoric uncertainty introduced by chaotic dynamics, a Fuzzy-Logic Gating Mechanism applies soft-thresholding to filter noise and retain only high-confidence signals. Experimental results on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that DLS effectively balances feature discrimination with robustness, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in heterophilous settings while maintaining competitive efficiency on standard homophilous graphs.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes DLS (Dual-Logic SAGE), an inductive graph neural network using chaotic feature injection and fuzzy-logic gating to overcome over-smoothing in heterophilous link prediction.
AI.motivation: Message Passing Neural Networks suppress high-frequency signals and suffer from over-smoothing in deep layers, which severely degrades link prediction on heterophilous graphs where connected nodes differ in features.
AI.method: DLS introduces a dynamic residual pipeline combining a Chaotic Injection Module (using the Logistic Map to diversify node representations) with a Fuzzy-Logic Gating Mechanism (soft-thresholding to filter chaotic noise and retain high-confidence signals).
AI.result: Experiments on diverse benchmarks show that DLS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on heterophilous link prediction while maintaining competitive efficiency on homophilous graphs.
AI.conclusion: Combining controlled chaotic diversification with fuzzy noise filtering effectively breaks the over-smoothing barrier for inductive link prediction.

title: AlignedHPO: Efficient Surrogate-Guided Loss Hyperparameter Optimization
summary: Modern deep learning losses involve multiple hyperparameters, such as weights, scales, and margins, typically tuned manually or through expensive black-box optimization despite their differentiability. We propose AlignedHPO, an efficient framework for tuning differentiable loss hyperparameters using gradient alignment and surrogate validation objectives. Our method employs Jacobian-vector products to reduce hypergradient computation time and memory, while differentiable metric surrogates guide optimization toward task-specific evaluation criteria. We address gradient magnitude ambiguity and stochastic instability through normalized alignment and gradient smoothing. Experiments with generalized Focal Loss and ArcFace demonstrate effective adaptation across long-tailed classification and open-set face recognition. AlignedHPO achieves competitive or improved performance compared to implicit differentiation, with nearly 12x faster hypergradient computation. These results highlight the potential of efficient surrogate-guided loss hyperparameter optimization.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes AlignedHPO, a gradient-alignment framework for tuning differentiable loss hyperparameters that achieves nearly 12x faster hypergradient computation than implicit differentiation.
AI.motivation: Deep learning losses contain multiple differentiable hyperparameters (weights, scales, margins) that are still typically tuned manually or via expensive black-box search.
AI.method: AlignedHPO uses Jacobian-vector products, differentiable metric surrogates, normalized gradient alignment, and gradient smoothing to optimize loss hyperparameters toward task-specific evaluation criteria.
AI.result: On long-tailed classification with generalized Focal Loss and open-set face recognition with ArcFace, AlignedHPO matches or outperforms implicit differentiation while computing hypergradients nearly 12x faster.
AI.conclusion: Normalized gradient alignment with surrogate objectives makes online, gradient-based loss hyperparameter optimization practical and fast.

title: CULypso: A Clustered Federated Unlearning paradigm for Vehicular Ad-Hoc Networks
summary: Unlearning has emerged as an essential security and privacy-preserving solution in Machine Learning, enabling networks to support their clients' rights for data erasure, as mandated by data protection regulations. Introducing such a non-trivial task to an edge, highly mobile and time-sensitive vehicular network is an even greater, largely unexplored challenge. This article argues that a hierarchical Federated Unlearning approach could be aptly integrated into vehicular ad-hoc networks (VANETs), leveraging topology and movement to reduce communication, resource and time costs, while effectively forgetting a client's influence on the global model updates. In order to achieve this, we propose CULypso, an approximate, surgical, hierarchical unlearning algorithm tailored for clustered VANETs. Inspired by the nymph in Greek mythology, Calypso, whose name translates to 'she who conceals the knowledge', CULypso, with the capital letters referencing \textbf{C}lustered \textbf{U}n\textbf{L}earning, aims to achieve exactly what its name suggests: conceal, erase or forget in our case, knowledge it contains. Extensive experiments uphold the potency of our paradigm with it performing approximately 65\% better than FedEraser in terms of time, server storage load, and unlearning fidelity while utterly outperforming baseline full retraining.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes CULypso, a hierarchical clustered federated unlearning algorithm for vehicular ad-hoc networks (VANETs) that outperforms FedEraser by roughly 65% in time, server storage, and unlearning fidelity.
AI.motivation: Supporting data-erasure rights via federated unlearning in highly mobile, time-sensitive edge VANETs is challenging due to dynamic topology and tight communication and resource constraints.
AI.method: CULypso performs approximate, surgical, hierarchical unlearning tailored to clustered VANETs, exploiting network topology and vehicle movement to erase a client's influence on global updates.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show CULypso performs approximately 65% better than FedEraser in time, server storage load, and unlearning fidelity, while substantially outperforming full retraining baselines.
AI.conclusion: Topology-aware hierarchical unlearning provides a practical, low-overhead mechanism for privacy-compliant data erasure in vehicular networks.

title: HADVQ: Hessian Aware Directional Vector Quantization
summary: Ultra-low-bit quantization of large language models is a challenging task because aggressive compression severely distorts model parameters and disproportionately harms a small number of highly sensitive channels. We present a vector quantization method tailored for this regime. Our approach begins with random preconditioning, which regularizes the weight space and makes it more amenable to quantization. We then represent weights in polar coordinates and decouple the quantization of directions and magnitudes. To quantize directions, we leverage the structure induced by random preconditioning and design a structured codebook based on the $E_8$ lattice, yielding a compact yet expressive representation. To further reduce degradation, we detect extremely important channels using a proxy Hessian and preserve them with an additional cost of only 0.16 bits. Together, these components provide an effective quantization pipeline for LLMs in the extremely low-bit regime. Empirical results demonstrate improved accuracy, highlighting the benefit of combining geometric structure, lattice-based codebooks, and selective channel preservation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents HADVQ, an ultra-low-bit vector quantization method for LLMs that combines random preconditioning, polar-coordinate decoupling with an E8 lattice codebook, and Hessian-aware channel preservation.
AI.motivation: Ultra-low-bit quantization severely distorts LLM weights and disproportionately degrades a small subset of highly sensitive channels.
AI.method: HADVQ applies random preconditioning to regularize weights, decouples magnitudes and directions in polar coordinates, quantizes directions with a structured E8 lattice codebook, and preserves critical channels detected by a proxy Hessian at an extra cost of 0.16 bits.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations demonstrate improved LLM accuracy in the extremely low-bit regime compared to existing quantization approaches.
AI.conclusion: Pairing geometric lattice codebooks with selective Hessian-based channel preservation enables accurate ultra-low-bit compression of large language models.

title: LoopPrune: Recurrent Pruning for Looped Diffusion Transformers
summary: Looped diffusion Transformers reuse shared blocks to deepen computation and match larger models with fewer parameters, reducing storage and deployment burdens. Yet repeated attention and MLP computations remain costly. Pruning reduces storage and computation by removing redundant parameters or units. Training-free methods struggle to resolve recurrent contributions, while training-based methods lack explicit constraints on position-specific errors affecting later inputs and final outputs. We propose LoopPrune, a pruning and recovery framework addressing these requirements. Recurrent importance estimation combines shared-removal effects and position variation to select a shared structure; shared reconstruction pools recurrent input statistics to compensate weights. Loop-position recovery compares complete denoising predictions at identical student states and matches text guidance, updating all student parameters against a fixed dense teacher. Extensive experiments across four open-source models, six benchmarks, and three pruning paradigms demonstrate effectiveness. At 30% structured parameter pruning, Looped-DiT B/16 retains 93.14% of dense six-benchmark average accuracy, exceeding the best baseline by 9.49%. Across PyTorch, vLLM-Omni, and SGLang Diffusion, pruned SDXSv3 reduces peak allocated GPU memory by 34.36-44.64% and accelerates denoising 1.46-1.74x over dense models.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes LoopPrune, a recurrent pruning and loop-position recovery framework for looped diffusion Transformers that retains 93.14% of dense accuracy at 30% structured pruning and speeds up denoising by 1.46-1.74x.
AI.motivation: Looped diffusion Transformers save parameters by reusing shared blocks, but repeated attention and MLP passes remain costly, and existing pruning methods fail to account for recurrent, position-specific error propagation.
AI.method: LoopPrune combines recurrent importance estimation (measuring shared-removal effects and position variation), shared reconstruction from pooled recurrent input statistics, and loop-position recovery that aligns student denoising predictions and text guidance with a dense teacher.
AI.result: Across four models and six benchmarks, 30% structured pruning of Looped-DiT B/16 retains 93.14% of dense accuracy (+9.49% over the best baseline), and pruned SDXSv3 cuts peak GPU memory by 34.36-44.64% and accelerates denoising 1.46-1.74x across PyTorch, vLLM-Omni, and SGLang Diffusion.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for recurrent loop dynamics during both pruning and teacher-guided recovery enables substantial memory and speed gains in looped diffusion Transformers.

title: PANO: Parallel Latent Space Neural Operator for Solving PDEs
summary: Aggregating observations into a limited number of latent tokens and learning physical interactions in the latent space has emerged as an effective approach for Transformer-based neural operators to solve Partial Differential Equation (PDE) problems involving large-scale observations. However, existing methods typically compress observations using a single aggregation pattern, making physical information not retained by that pattern invisible to the latent space and thereby constraining physical interactions within it. To address this limitation, we propose PArallel Latent Space Neural Operator (PANO), a novel neural operator for solving PDEs that formulates physical interactions among observations as an additive combination of interaction results from parallel latent spaces with shared parameters. Specifically, PANO transforms observations into multiple distinct compressed representations through independent mappings, learns physical interactions in parallel based on these representations, and finally fuses the decoded results to predict the target physical field. Within PANO, we further propose Coupled Assignment Projection (CAP) to construct bidirectionally consistent encoding and decoding mappings, and Pairwise Latent Space Attention Layer (PaLA) to jointly update latent representations of each latent space through adaptive cross-space interactions. Extensive experiments on nine benchmarks spanning diverse physical systems, geometries, and observation scales demonstrate that PANO achieves state-of-the-art performance. Notably, PANO reduces equivalent plastic strain prediction errors on Unilateral Stamping by 28.3% (or more) and lift-coefficient prediction errors on AirCraft by 21.4% (or more) compared with existing methods. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes PANO, a Parallel Latent Space Neural Operator for solving PDEs that learns physical interactions across multiple parallel latent spaces and cuts prediction errors by over 21-28% on key benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing Transformer-based neural operators compress observations into a single latent space, causing physical information missed by that single aggregation pattern to become invisible to latent interactions.
AI.method: PANO maps observations into multiple distinct latent representations with shared parameters, updates them via Coupled Assignment Projection (CAP) for bidirectional consistency and Pairwise Latent Space Attention (PaLA) for cross-space interaction, and fuses the decoded outputs.
AI.result: Across nine PDE benchmarks, PANO achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, reducing equivalent plastic strain error on Unilateral Stamping by at least 28.3% and lift-coefficient error on AirCraft by at least 21.4%.
AI.conclusion: Parallelizing latent-space projections with bidirectional coupling and cross-space attention prevents information bottlenecks in neural PDE solvers.

title: Virtual Double Oracle: Faster Convergence by Leveraging Strategies That Were Watching All Along
summary: Double Oracle (DO) and PSRO approximate Nash equilibria in two-player zero-sum games by iteratively expanding a strategy population with best responses supplied by an oracle. Online Double Oracle (ODO) interleaves multiplicative weights updates (MWU) with population discovery and obtains an $O(\sqrt{k\ln k/T})$ rate, where $T$ is the number of learning rounds and $k$ is the larger of the two players' final population sizes. We identify the reinitialisation step as an underexplored design choice: at each expansion, MWU-based methods reset newly discovered strategies to a uniform prior. We introduce Virtual Double Oracle (VDO), which exploits a bilinear identity (a strategy's full hindsight loss history collapses to its utility against the time-averaged opponent) to initialise each new strategy with the MWU weight it would have had from the start. We prove that VDO achieves $O(\sqrt{k/T})$ exploitability over the discovered population as it grows, provided the cumulative cost of adding strategies is at most linear in $k$, a condition supported by our empirical measurements. Discounted VDO (dVDO) moderates historical preferences to reduce over-concentration at reinitialisation. Experiments across matrix games, poker, and Goofspiel show that, with a suitable discount, dVDO can substantially reduce finite-horizon exploitability relative to both VDO and uniform-reset ODO, and can improve the discovered strategy populations.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Virtual Double Oracle (VDO) and Discounted VDO (dVDO), which initialize newly discovered strategies with their hindsight multiplicative-weights prior to achieve faster convergence in two-player zero-sum games.
AI.motivation: Online Double Oracle (ODO) resets newly discovered strategies to a uniform prior at each population expansion, discarding historical payoff information and slowing convergence.
AI.method: VDO uses a bilinear identity—showing a strategy's hindsight loss history equals its utility against the time-averaged opponent—to initialize new strategies with the MWU weight they would have accumulated from the start, while dVDO discounts historical preferences to avoid over-concentration.
AI.result: The authors prove an O(sqrt(k/T)) exploitability rate for VDO under linear strategy-addition cost, and experiments on matrix games, poker, and Goofspiel show dVDO substantially reduces finite-horizon exploitability over VDO and uniform-reset ODO.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging hindsight utility at reinitialization removes the uniform-reset bottleneck in Online Double Oracle and improves both convergence speed and discovered strategy populations.

title: SilverSpoon-KD: A General-Purpose Toolkit for Knowledge Distillation
comment: 28 pages, 10 figures, 11 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Knowledge distillation transfers deep learning representations from a teacher model to a student model, typically reducing model size or inference cost. However, knowledge distillation tooling has not kept pace with the breadth of research methods: existing toolkits typically support only a limited subset of techniques and use cases. We present SilverSpoon-KD, an open-source PyTorch toolkit that unifies different distillation paradigms and architectural relationships across workloads and applications behind a single API. Moreover, SilverSpoon-KD offers the first general-purpose blockwise knowledge distillation implementation with unique scalability features. We validate its versatility across vision, masked language model, and causal language models on tasks spanning homogeneous, heterogeneous, and quantization distillation across paradigms. We also evaluate SilverSpoon-KD by comparing its performance, including throughput and GPU memory usage, with existing toolkits. Despite extensive support for convenience, metric calculation, and tracking, we have found SilverSpoon-KD's performance to be on par with or better than existing toolkits.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SilverSpoon-KD, an open-source PyTorch toolkit that unifies diverse knowledge distillation paradigms and offers general-purpose blockwise distillation behind a single API.
AI.motivation: Existing knowledge distillation toolkits support only narrow subsets of techniques and architectures, lagging behind the breadth of modern distillation research.
AI.method: SilverSpoon-KD provides a unified PyTorch API supporting homogeneous, heterogeneous, quantization, and scalable blockwise knowledge distillation, along with built-in metric calculation and experiment tracking.
AI.result: Validated across vision, masked language models, and causal language models, SilverSpoon-KD matches or exceeds existing toolkits in throughput and GPU memory efficiency despite its broader feature set.
AI.conclusion: A unified, scalable distillation toolkit lowers engineering friction and accelerates experimentation across diverse model families and distillation paradigms.

title: WATERFALL: Workflow for Adaptive Training with Evolutionary Reward Formulation and Automated Learning Loops
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (poster). 78 pages, 13 figures, 19 tables. Code: this https URL OpenReview: this https URL
summary: Reward design remains a central bottleneck in reinforcement learning (RL), particularly in sparse-reward, long-horizon and partially observable settings requiring dependency chaining, memory, and deceptive affordance disambiguation. While recent foundation-model approaches reduce manual reward engineering, most assume goal-conditioning, task descriptions, expert demonstrations, or ground-truth metrics. These assumptions are problematic in partially observable environments, where task-relevant objectives, affordances, and dynamics must be discovered through interaction rather than disclosed a priori. We formalise this problem setting by introducing WATERFALL, an iterative population-based workflow for automated reward discovery under the strict observability constraints inherent in POMDP environments. WATERFALL achieves this by (i) synthesising diverse programmatic reward candidates via persona-conditioned generation, (ii) evaluating candidate behaviour from raw visual rollouts utilising a Swiss-system evolutionary tournament judged by vision-language models to identify elites, and (iii) leveraging longitudinal assessment histories to iteratively mutate, escalate, or prune candidates. We evaluate WATERFALL across fully observable and reveal-gated partially observable environments ranging from discrete to continuous, comparing against sparse-reward RL, intrinsic-motivation and foundation-model reward-synthesis baselines. Our results indicate that WATERFALL discovers and refines reward programs without access to privileged information, outperforming baselines that retain their native information advantages, most clearly in the POMDP regime. Extensive ablations substantiate that visual evidence, tournament-based selection, and iterative refinement are jointly important. Enforcing this contract is what separates autonomous reward discovery from benchmark-privileged reward shaping.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces WATERFALL, an evolutionary reward-discovery workflow that uses persona-conditioned generation and VLM-judged visual tournaments to learn reward programs in partially observable environments without privileged information.
AI.motivation: Existing foundation-model reward-synthesis methods assume goal-conditioning, task descriptions, expert demos, or ground-truth metrics, which are unavailable in partially observable (POMDP) settings where objectives must be discovered through interaction.
AI.method: WATERFALL generates diverse programmatic reward candidates via persona-conditioned synthesis, evaluates raw visual rollouts in a Swiss-system tournament judged by vision-language models, and iteratively mutates, escalates, or prunes candidates using longitudinal histories.
AI.result: Across fully observable and reveal-gated POMDP benchmarks, WATERFALL discovers effective reward programs without privileged information and outperforms sparse-reward RL, intrinsic-motivation, and foundation-model baselines that retain their native information advantages.
AI.conclusion: Combining evolutionary tournaments with VLM visual judgment enables autonomous reward discovery under strict partial observability.

title: Path-Aligned Constraint Equivariance
summary: Learned super-resolution of physical fields must satisfy structural constraints---such as divergence-free flow ($\nabla\cdot u=0$), curl-free fields ($\nabla\times u=0$), and pointwise sum-to-one normalization ($1^\top p=1$)---that standard training objectives do not enforce. Soft penalties trade fidelity against satisfaction via a scalar hyperparameter $\lambda$ but cannot drive the residual to zero; hard-constrained regression eliminates the residual by construction yet converges to the conditional mean, losing small-scale spectral structure. We observe that in Conditional Flow Matching with linear paths, a linear constraint $Ax=c$ is preserved along the entire transport trajectory whenever the velocity field is compatible ($Av_\theta=0$) and the initial noise is consistent ($Ax_0=c$); along the trajectory, the latter two conditions are also necessary. We term this the path-equivariance principle and instantiate it in PACE (Path-Aligned Constraint Equivariance), a framework that enforces these conditions through a null-space parameterization of the velocity field and a constraint-respecting noise sampler, with no modification to the loss function or the ODE integrator. Across three constraint families, PACE reduces the mean constraint residual by one to five orders of magnitude relative to unconstrained baselines, matching the residual level of the data-generation pipeline itself. The proposed framework requires only a closed-form parameterization onto the null space of $A$; within this scope, it offers exact constraint enforcement while recovering the spectral content and predictive diversity that conditional-mean regression systematically loses, all under a single unified recipe.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces PACE (Path-Aligned Constraint Equivariance), a Conditional Flow Matching framework that enforces linear physical constraints exactly along the entire transport trajectory without modifying the loss or ODE integrator.
AI.motivation: Soft penalties cannot drive physical constraint residuals to zero, while hard-constrained regression collapses to the conditional mean and loses small-scale spectral detail in physical field super-resolution.
AI.method: PACE enforces the path-equivariance principle for linear constraints Ax = c by parameterizing the velocity field onto the null space of A and sampling initial noise from a constraint-respecting distribution.
AI.result: Across three constraint families (divergence-free, curl-free, and sum-to-one), PACE reduces mean constraint residuals by one to five orders of magnitude relative to unconstrained baselines—matching data-generation precision—while preserving spectral content and predictive diversity.
AI.conclusion: Null-space velocity parameterization and consistent noise sampling provide a unified, exact way to enforce linear physical constraints in flow-matching super-resolution.

title: Beyond Attribute-Centric Fairness: Modelling and Mitigating Unified Bias Representation in Omni-modal Large Language Models
summary: Omni-modal large language models (OLLMs) provide joint multimodal understanding and generation capabilities, making them well-suited to complex environments and promising backbones for next-generation AI. Despite these advances, the harmful stereotypes encoded in such models manifest in increasingly diverse forms, leading to broader and more severe societal consequences. Existing debiasing methods typically impose separate fairness objectives for each sensitive attribute and modality to minimise demographic-dependent variations. However, in omni-modal settings, this attribute-centric paradigm struggles to jointly address diverse social biases with distinct fairness objectives and to generalise beyond predefined attributes. To this end, we propose OmniDebias, one of the first methods for promoting fairness in OLLMs, which employs a bias-centric formulation to extract and mitigate a shared bias representation across attributes and modalities while preserving attribute-related knowledge. Specifically, we exploit activation inconsistencies of a given attribute (e.g., gender) across semantic contexts (e.g., occupations) to disentangle bias from legitimate knowledge. We further consolidate multiple extracted biases into a shared representation, formulating a unified objective that captures the underlying structure across social biases and generalises to unseen attributes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that eliminating unified bias with both post-hoc editing and fine-tuning can consistently improve fairness across diverse attributes and modalities in OLLMs while maintaining favourable utility.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes OmniDebias, a bias-centric debiasing framework for omni-modal large language models (OLLMs) that extracts and mitigates a shared bias representation across attributes and modalities.
AI.motivation: Existing debiasing methods apply separate fairness objectives per sensitive attribute and modality, failing to jointly address diverse stereotypes or generalize to unseen attributes in OLLMs.
AI.method: OmniDebias exploits activation inconsistencies of an attribute across semantic contexts (e.g., occupations) to disentangle bias from legitimate attribute knowledge, and consolidates extracted biases into a shared representation for post-hoc editing or fine-tuning.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that removing this unified bias representation consistently improves fairness across diverse attributes and modalities—including unseen attributes—while maintaining favorable model utility.
AI.conclusion: Modeling a shared, bias-centric representation rather than per-attribute objectives enables generalizable fairness improvements in omni-modal LLMs.

title: Who Pays for Byzantine Robustness? Validity, Data-Share Dictatorships, and Fairness When Only a Few Hospitals Collaborate
comment: 12 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Clinical federated learning (FL) collaborations typically connect only three to six hospitals, yet Byzantine-robust aggregation rules are designed and benchmarked on synthetic partitions across dozens of equal-sized clients. We conduct an empirical audit of eight standard aggregation rules: FedAvg, coordinate-wise median, trimmed mean, Krum, Multi-Krum, Bulyan, geometric median (GeoMed), and Centered Clipping (CC). We evaluate both unweighted and sample-size-weighted variants across three cross-silo medical datasets from the FLamby benchmark: Fed-Heart-Disease ($n = 4$ hospitals), Fed-TCGA-BRCA ($n = 6$ regions), and Fed-ISIC2019 ($n = 6$ centres). We execute 54,214 training runs across enumerated attacker coalitions ($f \in \{1, 2\}$) paired with exact-twin leave-out controls that decompose performance drops into honest data loss versus adversarial attack damage. We report three findings. First, client-count validity checks fail to capture breakdown in skewed medical consortia: while $n = 6, f = 1$ satisfies every count condition except Bulyan's, assigning sample-size weights turns median and GeoMed into a clean-model dictatorship whenever a single hospital holds more than half the training data, and causes weighted median, GeoMed, and CC to collapse when that dominant centre attacks. Second, exact-twin leave-out controls reveal that when the largest hospital attacks, the apparent failure of count-based robust rules is predominantly caused by the loss of honest training data (7.5 to 10.4 points on ISIC) rather than adversarial perturbation (2.3 to 3.8 points on ISIC). Conversely, weight-dependent rules suffer large true attack damage (16.1 to 25.1 points on ISIC). Third, unweighted robust rules consistently discount whichever institution generates the most atypical parameter updates, penalizing the smallest hospital on Heart but penalizing larger institutions on TCGA and ISIC.

AI.tldr: This paper audits eight Byzantine-robust federated learning aggregation rules across 54,214 runs on cross-silo medical datasets, showing that skewed hospital data sizes break standard validity checks and create data-share dictatorships.
AI.motivation: Byzantine-robust FL rules are designed for dozens of equal-sized clients, whereas real clinical collaborations involve only three to six hospitals with highly skewed data volumes.
AI.method: The authors evaluate unweighted and sample-size-weighted FedAvg, median, trimmed mean, Krum, Multi-Krum, Bulyan, GeoMed, and Centered Clipping on FLamby datasets (Fed-Heart-Disease, Fed-TCGA-BRCA, Fed-ISIC2019) under enumerated attacker coalitions and exact-twin leave-out controls.
AI.result: Assigning sample-size weights turns median and GeoMed into a dictatorship when one hospital holds over half the data (causing 16.1-25.1 point attack damage on ISIC when it attacks), while unweighted robust rules lose 7.5-10.4 points primarily from discarding honest data rather than adversarial perturbation (2.3-3.8 points) and systematically penalize institutions with atypical updates.
AI.conclusion: Standard Byzantine-robust aggregation rules are ill-suited to small, skewed clinical consortia, where client-count validity checks mask severe fairness and robustness failures.

title: Action-outcome coupling: a pre-investment feasibility audit for offline reinforcement learning in supply chain operations
summary: Prescriptive analytics initiatives in logistics, such as offline reinforcement learning and next-best-action systems, are often funded before anyone verifies that the available historical logs can support an improved decision policy. We formalise this pre-investment feasibility question via action-outcome coupling: a total-effect variance index measuring how much expected outcomes change with the logged action. Coupling provides an algorithm-independent upper bound on any policy's achievable value, expressed in monetary units per decision for both single-step and discounted sequential objectives. We also analyse the asymptotic false-licensing risk of an invalid workflow: fitting a value model and evaluating the model's greedy policy on the same data. The false-licence rate is driven mainly by the number of state cells over which selection is performed, rising from the nominal test level with one cell to near certainty with a few dozen, while overlap has a smaller effect. We then propose an audit that assigns logs to four tiers of decision support, separately for fixed and contextual policies, and returns an explicit stopping rationale. On a randomised e-commerce log, the audit endorses a fixed recommendation policy, certifying gains equal to 30 per cent of the theoretical ceiling; the remaining gap reflects bound looseness under an 80-action design. Two public logistics logs fail at different checkpoints: one because the target is an accounting identity of the action, and another because, with 27 clusters, estimated coupling stays below the design's detectability threshold even though a conservative offline learner certifies an improvement in 29 of 30 seeds.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces action-outcome coupling, an algorithm-independent pre-investment audit that bounds achievable offline RL policy value in monetary units before funding analytics initiatives.
AI.motivation: Organizations often fund offline RL and next-best-action projects before verifying whether historical logs contain enough signal to support an improved decision policy, and risk false licensing by evaluating greedy policies on the same data used to fit value models.
AI.method: The authors define action-outcome coupling as a total-effect variance index bounding single-step and sequential policy value, analyze how state-cell count drives false-licensing risk, and build a four-tier audit for fixed and contextual policies.
AI.result: On a randomized e-commerce log, the audit certifies gains equal to 30% of the theoretical ceiling for a fixed policy; on two public logistics logs, it catches an accounting-identity target in one and flags below-threshold detectability across 27 clusters in the other.
AI.conclusion: Pre-investment coupling audits prevent wasted analytics spending by quantifying achievable policy value and exposing spurious targets or low-power designs upfront.

title: Projected Penalty-Gradient Tracking for Communication-Efficient Byzantine-Resilient Federated Learning
summary: We investigate communication-efficient federated learning over heterogeneous datasets in the presence of Byzantine adversaries capable of uploading arbitrary information. Penalty-based methods bound the influence of each worker through the bounded gradient of a penalty function; however, the bound is lost once the uploads are compressed, since a Byzantine worker can accumulate an unbounded state at the server. To retain the Byzantine resilience under compressed uploads, we propose a projected penalty-gradient tracking framework, where each honest worker uploads a compressed residual of its penalty gradient and the server projects each reconstructed state onto the known penalty-gradient ball. The framework accommodates any contractive compressor and yields two algorithms: fault-resilient proximal gradient with consistent sparsification (FRPG-CS), whose shared mask is protected by freshly drawn reserve rows, and lazily aggregated FRPG (LAG-FRPG), whose uploads are event-triggered. For smooth and strongly convex losses, we establish a finite-time bound on the expected objective gap, where the Byzantine error floor is independent of the compressor and the compression error decays faster than the optimization error. We also bound the expected number of lazy uploads and derive certificates that separate the finite-penalty model bias from the optimization error. Experiments on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST show that the proposed algorithms attain the highest accuracy among twelve methods under the Min-Max attack, whereas a compressed-momentum benchmark and a local-update benchmark remain preferable in attack-free accuracy and total traffic, respectively.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a projected penalty-gradient tracking framework (FRPG-CS and LAG-FRPG) that preserves Byzantine resilience in communication-efficient federated learning under arbitrary contractive compression.
AI.motivation: Penalty-based Byzantine-resilient FL methods rely on bounded penalty gradients, but this bound is lost when uploads are compressed because Byzantine workers can accumulate unbounded state at the server.
AI.method: Honest workers upload compressed residuals of their penalty gradients and the server projects each reconstructed state onto the known penalty-gradient ball, yielding FRPG-CS (consistent sparsification with reserve rows) and LAG-FRPG (event-triggered lazy uploads).
AI.result: For smooth strongly convex losses, the authors prove finite-time bounds where the Byzantine error floor is independent of the compressor, and on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST under the Min-Max attack the proposed methods achieve the highest accuracy among twelve baselines.
AI.conclusion: Server-side projection of reconstructed compressed states restores provable Byzantine resilience without sacrificing communication efficiency.

title: A Transformer-Derived Iterative Preconditioner
summary: Transformers trained on in-context prediction problems can learn known numerical algorithms, e.g., gradient descent. We go further, showing that their internal computations can reveal new algorithms with provable guarantees. A softmax-attention transformer trained to solve linear systems $Xw=y$ implicitly improves matrix conditioning. Tracing $XX^\top$ reveals an iterative preconditioning primitive, which we develop into RAPID, a standalone algorithm requiring no learned components. RAPID is an anytime preconditioner for symmetric positive definite (SPD) matrices, using randomized mixing and sparse local corrections to improve conditioning. Proof-of-concept experiments on synthetic and real-world problems consistently improve conditioning and reduce conjugate gradient iterations needed to reach a target accuracy. For a Haar-mixing idealization, we prove convergence to any fixed target condition number regardless of spectral distribution, with only logarithmic dependence on initial conditioning. Together, these results show how a transformer can discover a broadly applicable numerical algorithm.

AI.tldr: This paper derives RAPID, a standalone randomized iterative preconditioner for symmetric positive definite (SPD) matrices, by tracing the internal computations of a transformer trained to solve linear systems in context.
AI.motivation: While transformers are known to learn existing algorithms like gradient descent in context, it has been unclear whether their internal representations can reveal new numerical algorithms with provable guarantees.
AI.method: By tracing XX^T in a softmax-attention transformer trained on Xw = y, the authors extract an iterative preconditioning primitive and formalize it as RAPID, an anytime SPD preconditioner using randomized mixing and sparse local corrections without learned weights.
AI.result: On synthetic and real-world SPD problems, RAPID consistently improves matrix conditioning and reduces conjugate gradient iterations, and for a Haar-mixing idealization it is proven to converge to any target condition number with only logarithmic dependence on initial conditioning.
AI.conclusion: Inspecting trained transformers can uncover novel, provably convergent numerical algorithms that operate independently of neural networks.

title: The Kernel Reality Check: Benchmarking and Distilling Efficient Attention at Scale
summary: Kernelized attention methods, which aim to replace the $O(N^2)$ complexity of softmax attention with $O(N)$ alternatives, have been the focus of intense research in the last five years. Despite growing interest, systematic evaluations and fair comparisons across approaches and scales are still missing. We analyze kernelized attention in two halves and highlight prominent limitations on each. On efficiency, FlashAttention achieves lower memory consumption and faster wall-clock time than SOTA kernelized methods during training and in vision transformers across most sequence lengths (with inference-time memory in causal language models the only clear exception), contradicting the core assumption for pure kernelized attention used as a drop-in replacement for softmax. We also discover that reported efficiency gains often fail to reproduce against modern baselines. On quality, current kernelized methods leave gaps of 2-10 points relative to softmax under a unified distillation protocol, and model scala alone does not close these gaps. We show this gap is not intrinsic to kernelization: LARA++, a principled extension of LARA that approximates softmax via importance sampling with adaptive proposal distributions, recovers up to 99% of softmax accuracy. We establish that the gap is closable; however, the computational overhead remains substantial, leaving the efficiency wall intact. Code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks kernelized linear-time attention against softmax attention at scale, finding that FlashAttention is faster and more memory-efficient in most training/vision settings, while LARA++ closes the accuracy gap at high computational cost.
AI.motivation: Kernelized O(N) attention is widely assumed to be a drop-in replacement for O(N^2) softmax attention, but systematic, fair comparisons against modern baselines like FlashAttention across scales are lacking.
AI.method: The authors benchmark SOTA kernelized attention methods against FlashAttention on speed and memory, evaluate quality under a unified distillation protocol, and test LARA++, an adaptive importance-sampling extension of LARA.
AI.result: FlashAttention achieves lower memory and faster wall-clock time than SOTA kernelized methods during training and in vision transformers (with causal LM inference memory the only clear exception); existing kernelized methods lag softmax by 2-10 points regardless of scale, while LARA++ recovers up to 99% of softmax accuracy with substantial computational overhead.
AI.conclusion: Pure kernelized attention currently faces both an efficiency wall against FlashAttention and a quality-compute trade-off, challenging its role as a drop-in softmax replacement.

title: ResoLUT: Distilling Residual Networks into Lookup-Table Networks
summary: Logic networks built from Boolean gates or lookup tables (LUTs) promise efficient hardware inference, but training them at depth and learning their connectivity remain difficult. We do not train logic as logic. Instead, ResoLUT distills a trained residual network (ResNet) layer by layer into LUT trees, preserving its multi-bit residual stream and BatchNorm while extracting connectivity from the teacher rather than learning it. To our knowledge, ResoLUT is the first convolutional logic network in computer vision to retain a ResNet-style multi-bit residual stream. Hard LUT decisions are used throughout training and inference, avoiding a discretization gap in the logic. ResoLUT-20 reaches 95.66% on CIFAR-10 with twice the trees, and ResoLUT-56 reaches 78.87% on CIFAR-100 and 53.69% on ImageNet at 64px, the best results of logic and lookup-table networks on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, showing that LUT networks can scale in depth. We explore and quantify the role of the residuals and the tree budget and shape. The most optimized model, a ResoLUT-8 with one eighth of the trees and further optimizations, fits on an FPGA and reaches 90.04% at 189k images per second, the highest throughput among the compared models above 85% on CIFAR-10.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ResoLUT, which distills trained ResNets layer by layer into lookup-table (LUT) trees while preserving a multi-bit residual stream, achieving state-of-the-art logic-network accuracy and 189k images/s on FPGA.
AI.motivation: Boolean and LUT-based logic networks promise fast hardware inference, but training them at depth and learning their connectivity directly remains difficult.
AI.method: Instead of training logic from scratch, ResoLUT extracts connectivity and distills a trained ResNet layer by layer into LUT trees using hard LUT decisions throughout training and inference, while retaining a multi-bit residual stream and BatchNorm.
AI.result: ResoLUT-20 reaches 95.66% on CIFAR-10 and ResoLUT-56 reaches 78.87% on CIFAR-100 and 53.69% on ImageNet-64px (best among logic/LUT networks on CIFAR-10/100), while a compressed ResoLUT-8 fits on an FPGA at 90.04% accuracy and 189k images/s.
AI.conclusion: Layer-wise distillation from ResNets with preserved multi-bit residuals enables deep, high-accuracy LUT networks suitable for ultra-high-throughput FPGA deployment.

title: DDSL: Iterative Self-Labeling for Financial Market States
comment: 17 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Conference version published in ICAIF 2026. Code available at this https URL
summary: Financial market states lack a unique ground truth and must therefore be constructed from price data. Conventional labeling methods typically define states independently of the downstream classifier, leaving unresolved whether the resulting labels can be recovered from information available at prediction time. We propose DDSL, an iterative self-labeling framework that couples a price- and grammar-guided Viterbi labeler with a Transformer classifier through model feedback. DDSL constructs a nine-state representation that jointly encodes current and future market trends while retaining structured price emissions and temporal constraints throughout refinement. Experiments on SSE50, CSI300, CSI500, and NASDAQ100 show that DDSL increases held-out joint-state macro F1 by 78%-96% over single-pass dynamic-programming labeling. An independent GRU classifier that never participates in the labeling loop reproduces the same trend, while label entropy and class coverage remain stable, indicating that the gain transfers across architectures and is not caused by label collapse. We further show that learnability is controlled by both iteration and the model-feedback weight $\beta_{\mathrm{model}}$. Iterative gains diminish as successive label systems converge, whereas stronger feedback increasingly widens the performance gap between the feedback Transformer and the independent GRU. Increased learnability is accompanied by declining segment-level price-feature separation after an initial improvement. Finally, a non-anticipative event study provides partial external validation: refinement strengthens a conditional BEAR$\rightarrow$BULL reversal signal on the three A-share datasets, while the corresponding effect has the opposite sign on NASDAQ100. These results position DDSL as a structured framework for constructing market-state labels whose learnability can be explicitly controlled and evaluated.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes DDSL, an iterative self-labeling framework that couples a Viterbi market-state labeler with a Transformer classifier via model feedback, boosting held-out joint-state macro F1 by 78-96%.
AI.motivation: Financial market states lack unique ground truth, and conventional labeling methods define states independently of the downstream classifier, leaving learnability at prediction time unresolved.
AI.method: DDSL constructs a nine-state representation encoding current and future trends and iteratively refines labels by coupling a price- and grammar-guided Viterbi labeler with a Transformer classifier weighted by model feedback beta_model.
AI.result: On SSE50, CSI300, CSI500, and NASDAQ100, DDSL increases held-out joint-state macro F1 by 78-96% over single-pass dynamic programming, transfers to an independent GRU without label collapse, and strengthens a conditional BEAR-to-BULL reversal signal on the three A-share indices.
AI.conclusion: Coupling structured dynamic-programming labeling with classifier feedback produces market-state labels with controllable, architecture-transferable learnability.

title: High-Dimensional Black-Box Optimization via Guidance Sampling of Diffusion Models
summary: Many real-world optimization problems involve optimizing black-box objectives for which only a limited number of evaluations are available. Bayesian optimization (BO) is a powerful framework for such problems, but its effectiveness often deteriorates in high-dimensional spaces. Recent work leverages diffusion models for black-box optimization, often through pre-training a reward-conditioned score network to steer generation towards high-reward samples. Alternatively, gradient-based guidance methods assume access to a differentiable reward function from which guidance gradients are queried. However, these approaches either require large amounts of labeled data for offline training or access to exact reward gradients, limiting their applicability in black-box settings. We propose BReaD (Black-box Reward-guided Sampling of Diffusion Model), a guidance sampling framework for optimizing black-box rewards without assuming access to a labeled dataset or reward gradients. The proposed method uses a Gaussian process (GP) as a differentiable surrogate for the unknown objective and actively queries labels for the generated samples. We provide a theoretical analysis of the total-variation distance between the generated distribution and the target distribution. Using Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) as guidance signals, our method balances exploration and exploitation during generation and enables the discovery of high-reward regions in the data space. Numerical experiments on scientific discovery and image generation tasks demonstrate that our framework can effectively optimize black-box rewards in low-data scenarios.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes BReaD, a guidance sampling framework for high-dimensional black-box optimization that uses a Gaussian process surrogate and UCB guidance to steer diffusion models without labeled datasets or reward gradients.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion-based black-box optimizers require either large offline labeled datasets to train conditional score networks or access to exact differentiable reward gradients.
AI.method: BReaD fits a Gaussian process (GP) as a differentiable surrogate to the unknown black-box objective, actively queries labels for generated samples, and uses Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) gradients to guide diffusion sampling, backed by a total-variation distance bound.
AI.result: Numerical experiments on scientific discovery and image generation tasks show that BReaD effectively optimizes black-box rewards in low-data regimes without prior labeled data or reward gradients.
AI.conclusion: Combining active GP surrogates with UCB-guided diffusion sampling enables data-efficient black-box optimization in high-dimensional spaces.

title: NVIDIA Kumo Tabular: Pushing the Accuracy$\unicode{8211}$Efficiency Frontier for Tabular Prediction
summary: We introduce Kumo Tabular, a family of open tabular foundation models for classification and regression, in three sizes: Kumo Tabular-S (27M parameters), Kumo Tabular-M (61M), and Kumo Tabular-L (214M). Pretrained only on artificial tables from the Kumo prior, they can make predictions on new tables without any training. In our approach, a table encoder compresses each row into an embedding, and an in-context learning transformer predicts the unlabeled rows from the labeled ones. Kumo Tabular introduces architectural innovations that improve both training stability and predictive performance, enabling the model to scale up to 150M cells on modern GPUs. Kumo Tabular-L ranks first on eight benchmarks: TabArena, TALENT, BeyondArena, ScoringBench, STRABLE, MulTaBench, RamanBench, and TabBench-Bio. These cover probabilistic regression, tables with over 1M rows or 100K columns, and tables with strings, text, or images. Accuracy improves with model size in all tested comparisons. All three sizes lie on the accuracy-speed frontiers of TabArena and BeyondArena. Kumo Tabular-L predicts faster than the runners-up, LimiX-2 on TabArena (36 times) and TabPFN-3.5 on BeyondArena (1.7 times). Weights and pretraining code are released under OpenMDW-1.1 and Apache 2.0, respectively.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces NVIDIA Kumo Tabular (27M, 61M, and 214M parameters), a family of open tabular foundation models pretrained on synthetic tables that ranks first on eight benchmarks and predicts up to 36x faster than runners-up.
AI.motivation: Tabular prediction models need to generalize across diverse schemas, modalities, and scales up to millions of rows without task-specific training while remaining fast at inference.
AI.method: A table encoder compresses each row into an embedding and an in-context learning transformer predicts unlabeled rows from labeled ones, pretrained solely on artificial tables from the Kumo prior and scaling up to 150M cells on modern GPUs.
AI.result: Kumo Tabular-L (214M) ranks first on all eight evaluated benchmarks (including TabArena, TALENT, and BeyondArena), all three sizes sit on the accuracy-speed frontier, and Kumo Tabular-L predicts 36x faster than LimiX-2 on TabArena and 1.7x faster than TabPFN-3.5 on BeyondArena.
AI.conclusion: Pretraining scalable row-encoded in-context transformers on synthetic priors pushes both the accuracy and inference-speed frontiers for zero-shot tabular prediction.

title: Variance Restoration over Covariance Rank: Memory-Budgeted Analytic Continual Learning
summary: Analytic continual learning replaces iterative gradient updates with closed-form ridge regression over frozen pre-trained representations, summarizing all past sessions in two running sufficient statistics: the feature autocorrelation matrix $\Sigma_t$ and the class cross-correlation matrix $\Gamma_t$. Lifting backbone features into a wide random code of dimension $M \gg D$ substantially improves linear separability across tasks, but forces $\Sigma_t$ to grow quadratically as $\mathcal{O}(M^2)$. Under a fixed persistent memory envelope $\Bcal$, a learner faces a fundamental structural trade-off: store exact pairwise co-activations inside a narrower feature code, or expand to a wide code while compressing cross-coordinate interactions. We observe that the coordinate self-variances $v_t = \diag(\Sigma_t)$ and class statistics $\Gamma_t$ grow only linearly with $M$, whereas off-diagonal interactions dominate memory. We introduce \method (\textbf{Co}ordinate-\textbf{Re}stored \textbf{A}nalytic \textbf{C}ontinual \textbf{L}earning), which retains $(v_t, \Gamma_t)$ exactly, maintains off-diagonal co-activations through a streaming rank-$q$ factor $F_t$, restores exact diagonal variances via $\Sighat_t = F_t^\top F_t + \Diag(v_t - \diag(F_t^\top F_t))$, and solves the full $M\times C$ normal equations via the Woodbury identity. Across five class-incremental benchmarks on frozen ViT-B/16, \method matches dense full-covariance readouts within $0.09$ points while cutting persistent state by $90.7\%$ ($35.9$ vs.\ $385.3$ MiB). Under equal memory envelopes of $16$--$80$ MiB, prioritizing expansion width $M$ over covariance rank $q$ outperforms exact narrow readouts in $17$ of $18$ configurations by up to $+2.19$ points.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CoReACL, a memory-budgeted analytic continual learning method that stores exact diagonal variances and class statistics alongside a low-rank off-diagonal factor, cutting persistent memory by 90.7% within 0.09 points of full-covariance readouts.
AI.motivation: Analytic continual learning lifts frozen features to a wide dimension M for linear separability, but storing the full M x M autocorrelation matrix grows quadratically and exceeds tight memory budgets.
