AI.method: CoReACL retains linear-cost coordinate self-variances and class cross-correlations exactly, compresses off-diagonal co-activations via a streaming rank-q factor, restores exact diagonal variances, and solves normal equations via the Woodbury identity.
AI.result: Across five class-incremental benchmarks on frozen ViT-B/16, CoReACL matches dense full-covariance readouts within 0.09 points while reducing persistent state from 385.3 to 35.9 MiB (90.7%), and outperforms exact narrow readouts in 17 of 18 equal-memory configurations (16-80 MiB) by up to +2.19 points.
AI.conclusion: Prioritizing feature expansion width over off-diagonal covariance rank while restoring exact diagonal variances yields superior accuracy under fixed memory budgets in analytic continual learning.

title: Pareto-Informed Smart "Predict, then Optimize" for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Problems
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Accepted after peer review at the Multi-Objective Decision Making (MODeM) Workshop at ECAI 2025
summary: Many real-world planning applications, from logistics, routing to resource allocation, give rise to optimization problems that need to balance multiple, conflicting objectives. While machine learning is often used to predict the unknown parameters or costs of these problems, standard models trained on prediction accuracy can lead to suboptimal plans. Decision-Focused Learning (DFL) addresses this by integrating the downstream optimization task into the training objective. However, existing DFL methods for multi-objective problems rely on simple scalarization, which fails to capture the rich trade-offs of the Pareto Frontier. To address this gap, we propose a Pareto-aware extension to single-objective Smart "Predict, then Optimize" (SPO+) for multi-objective combinatorial optimization problems. Our loss function leverages the true Pareto Frontier, forming a target decision that aligns with a sampled preference vector, and minimizes regret against this target. Experiments on multi-objective shortest path and multi-objective knapsack problems show that our approach outperforms traditional two-stage Mean Squared Error (MSE) baselines. It also surpasses scalarization-based SPO+ approaches.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Pareto-informed extension of Smart "Predict, then Optimize" (SPO+) for multi-objective combinatorial optimization that outperforms MSE and scalarization-based SPO+ baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing Decision-Focused Learning (DFL) methods for multi-objective problems rely on simple scalarization, which fails to capture the trade-offs of the full Pareto Frontier.
AI.method: The proposed loss function leverages the true Pareto Frontier to construct a target decision aligned with a sampled preference vector and minimizes regret against that target.
AI.result: Experiments on multi-objective shortest path and multi-objective knapsack problems show that the Pareto-aware SPO+ loss outperforms both two-stage MSE baselines and scalarization-based SPO+ approaches.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating true Pareto Frontier targets into regret-based decision-focused learning improves multi-objective combinatorial planning over scalarization.

title: Learning to Undo: Transfer Reinforcement Learning under State Space Transformations
summary: Transfer learning in reinforcement learning (RL) has shown strong empirical success. In this work, we take a more principled perspective by studying when and how transferring knowledge between MDPs (a source and a target) can be provably beneficial. Specifically, we consider the case where there exists an undo map such that applying this map to the target's state space recovers the source exactly. We propose an algorithm that learns this map by matching state feature statistics gathered from both MDPs, and then uses it to transfer the source policy to the target. We theoretically justify the algorithm by analyzing the setting when the undo map is linear and the source is linearly-$Q^\star$ realizable, where our approach has strictly better sample complexity than tabula rasa RL in the target MDP. Empirically, we demonstrate that these benefits extend beyond this regime: on challenging continuous control tasks and Atari games, our method achieves significantly better sample efficiency. Overall, our results highlight how shared structure between tasks can be leveraged for efficient transfer of policies across environments.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a transfer reinforcement learning algorithm that learns an undo map between target and source state spaces by matching state feature statistics, achieving provably better sample complexity and stronger empirical efficiency.
AI.motivation: Transfer RL lacks principled guarantees for when and how a source policy can be transferred to a target MDP whose state space is transformed relative to the source.
AI.method: Assuming an undo map exists that recovers the source state space from the target's, the algorithm learns this map by matching state feature statistics from both MDPs and uses it to transfer the source policy, with theoretical analysis for linear undo maps and linearly-Q* realizable sources.
AI.result: The authors prove strictly better sample complexity than tabula rasa RL in the linear setting, and demonstrate significantly improved sample efficiency on continuous control tasks and Atari games.
AI.conclusion: Learning state-space undo maps via feature-statistic matching provides a theoretically grounded and empirically effective mechanism for policy transfer in RL.

title: Get Hint-Augmented GRPO Done Right Through Activation Steering
summary: GRPO has become the dominant reinforcement learning method for eliciting reasoning capability in LLMs using verifiable rewards. However, it suffers from a fundamental failure mode: when a training question exceeds the base model's current capability, all generated responses fail and receive zero reward, yielding no gradient signal and stalling further capability expansion. An emerging class of GRPO extensions, termed Hint-Augmented GRPO (HA-GRPO), adds a "hint" to the context to reduce the difficulty of the question, thereby producing a usable gradient signal. Nevertheless, existing HA-GRPO methods share a key issue: no hint is available at inference time to append to the question, creating a training-inference context mismatch that leads to inconsistent performance gains. In this work, we reinterpret the function of hinting -- not as reducing question difficulty, but as steering model behavior -- and propose ASH (Activation Steering for Hinting), a novel HA-GRPO method built on this view. During training, the model is presented with both hinted and plain questions, while a trainable steering vector is optimized to widen the margins between the model's generation probabilities for responses to the hinted version relative to the plain version, thereby capturing the question-agnostic component of the behavioral shift induced by the hint. During inference, the trained steering vector is directly injected into the model's activation, reproducing the hint-conditioned behavior without requiring any hint in the context. Experiments with four LLMs (Qwen3-1.7B/4B-Base, Llama-3.2-1B/3B-Instruct) show that ASH consistently improves pass@$k$ on competition-level mathematics benchmarks (AMC, OlympiadBench, AIME24, AIME25) and out-of-distribution benchmarks (Minerva, GPQA-Diamond). Notably, it improves average pass@8 of Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-4B-Base by \textbf{2.60}\% and \textbf{2.21}\%.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes ASH (Activation Steering for Hinting), a Hint-Augmented GRPO method that captures hint-induced behavioral shifts as a trainable steering vector to improve LLM reasoning without requiring hints at inference time.
AI.motivation: Standard GRPO stalls on questions beyond a base model's capability due to zero-reward gradients, while existing Hint-Augmented GRPO methods suffer from a training-inference context mismatch because hints are unavailable at test time.
AI.method: ASH trains a steering vector alongside hinted and plain questions to widen the generation probability margins between hinted and plain responses, then injects this vector into model activations during inference to reproduce hint-conditioned behavior.
AI.result: Across four LLMs (Qwen3-1.7B/4B-Base and Llama-3.2-1B/3B-Instruct), ASH consistently improves pass@k on competition math benchmarks (AMC, OlympiadBench, AIME24, AIME25) and out-of-distribution benchmarks (Minerva, GPQA-Diamond), boosting average pass@8 by 2.60% on Qwen3-1.7B-Base and 2.21% on Qwen3-4B-Base.
AI.conclusion: Reinterpreting hints as activation steering rather than difficulty reduction resolves the training-inference mismatch in Hint-Augmented GRPO and yields consistent reasoning gains.

title: Where Should Physics Enter? Information, Identifiability and Calibration in Probabilistic Sea Surface Temperature Forecasting
summary: Advection-diffusion priors are a common way to make neural sea surface temperature (SST) forecasts physics-informed. We test where such a prior must enter a heteroscedastic ConvLSTM to help, using daily NOAA OISST v2.1 for the Bay of Bengal (1982-2024) and a synthetic benchmark on the same grid with known currents of controlled strength. (i) On real data, a soft advection-diffusion residual with a learned velocity gives no reliable benefit (lead-15 CRPS -0.007 degrees C, 95% interval [-0.022, +0.008]); a plain temporal-smoothness penalty matches it, and equivalence within 3% is not established either. (ii) Learned velocities do not recover the currents, whether placed in the loss, in an explicit transport step, or in a transport step without neural correction: they correlate with the reference no better than a shuffled-date null, even on synthetic data where knowing the currents would improve day-15 forecasts by 16-23%. (iii) Supplied currents help on synthetic data, but mostly as information: giving them to the network as input channels, without transport, recovers 92% of the transport design's lead-5 gain, and a frozen-current numerical forecast does as well as either. (iv) With GLORYS12 reanalysis currents on real data, the transport design is 6% and 4% worse at leads 1 and 5; reanalysis advection explains essentially none of the daily OISST change (correlation 0.02), and frozen-current transport is worse than persistence. (v) The defect that matters is lead-dependent miscalibration shared by every model. One variance multiplier per lead, fitted on validation data, brings 90% coverage to 0.85-0.91 at all leads and lowers day-1 CRPS by 13-21%; fine-tuning on 15-day rollouts fixes long-lead coverage but costs short-lead skill. This version withdraws an earlier claim of an 81% CRPS reduction that came from an uncontrolled comparison.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates where advection-diffusion physics priors should enter a heteroscedastic ConvLSTM for probabilistic sea surface temperature (SST) forecasting, finding that learned velocities fail to recover currents and that lead-dependent variance calibration is the dominant factor.
AI.motivation: Advection-diffusion priors are widely used in physics-informed neural SST forecasting, yet it remains unclear whether they provide genuine physical identifiability or real skill gains over simpler baselines.
AI.method: The authors evaluate soft advection-diffusion residuals, explicit transport steps, and input-channel current injection on daily NOAA OISST v2.1 data for the Bay of Bengal (1982-2024) and a synthetic benchmark with known currents, alongside post-hoc lead-dependent variance calibration.
AI.result: On real data, soft advection-diffusion residuals yield no reliable gain (lead-15 CRPS -0.007 C, 95% CI [-0.022, +0.008]), learned velocities correlate no better than shuffled-date nulls, and GLORYS12 reanalysis currents worsen transport forecasts at leads 1 and 5 by 6% and 4%; in contrast, fitting one variance multiplier per lead restores 90% coverage to 0.85-0.91 and reduces day-1 CRPS by 13-21%.
AI.conclusion: Physics priors in neural SST forecasting primarily help as input information when currents are accurate, while addressing lead-dependent miscalibration is far more impactful than enforcing advection-diffusion dynamics.

title: A Neural Envelope Method for Rapid Gradient-based Optimum Takeoff Trajectory Design
comment: 16 pages, 12 figures, submitted to AIAA Aviation conference
summary: Urban air mobility arises to mitigate ground traffic congestion. Multidisciplinary analysis and optimization (MDAO) has been introduced to reduce the energy consumption, thereby expanding aircraft performance. Surrogate-based MDAO lowers the cost of optimization, but multimodality disrupts global optimum search for both simulation-based and surrogate-based optimizations. Convex envelopes convert multimodal spaces into unimodal spaces, permitting efficient convex optimization; however, convexifying a design space may produce infeasible "optimal" designs due to complex design constraints. To address these challenges, this work proposes the coupling of a physics-constrained generative adversarial networks (physicsGAN) and neural envelope to transform original, constrained, non-convex optimizations into unconstrained, convex optimizations. Specifically, the physicsGAN discovers a feasible design space where all design candidates inherently satisfy all constraints, by penalizing surrogate-predicted constraint violations during training. Moreover, the neural envelope constructs a neural network-based convex envelope for the transformed objective function within the physicsGAN-discovered feasible space. Note that the neural envelope only needs to deal with objective function since constraints are inherently satisfied in the feasible space. The neural envelope is demonstrated on takeoff trajectory optimizations of the Airbus A3 Vahana eVTOL aircraft. Results show that neural envelopes achieve a 99.91% mean accuracy within a flight-condition space compared with reference convex envelopes. Neural-envelope-enabled optimizations achieve 99.84% accuracy on the global optimum design, costing only 0.04 seconds on average. The neural envelope accelerates the trajectory optimization by 53 and 162 times on average compared to the physicsGAN-enabled gradient-based and global optimizations, respectively.

AI.tldr: This paper couples a physics-constrained GAN (physicsGAN) with a neural convex envelope to convert constrained, non-convex takeoff trajectory optimization into fast, unconstrained convex optimization.
AI.motivation: Surrogate-based multidisciplinary analysis and optimization (MDAO) suffers from multimodality, and standard convex envelopes can produce infeasible designs when complex constraints are present.
AI.method: A physicsGAN is trained with surrogate-predicted constraint violation penalties to discover a feasible design space, within which a neural network constructs a convex envelope of the objective function for rapid gradient-based optimization.
AI.result: On takeoff trajectory optimization for the Airbus A3 Vahana eVTOL aircraft, neural envelopes achieve 99.91% mean accuracy against reference convex envelopes and 99.84% global optimum accuracy in 0.04 s on average, accelerating optimization by 53x and 162x over physicsGAN-enabled gradient-based and global optimizations.
AI.conclusion: Combining physics-constrained generative feasible-space discovery with neural convex envelopes enables accurate, real-time global optimization for constrained aerospace design problems.

title: Correcting Flows with Marginal Matching
summary: Flow matching models, ODE-based generative models, generate samples by gradually morphing a simple source distribution into a target distribution. However, these models still face challenges in optimally balancing computational efficiency with generation fidelity. While predictor-corrector schemes have been proven to help address this issue in diffusion models effectively, their application to flow matching models remains under-explored. In this work we present a novel training-based predictor-corrector framework for flow matching, which exploits the fact that the ODE can be easily reversed. Our key idea, termed Marginal Matching, is to correct samples at a particular time step in the forward ODE towards a matching marginal distribution of the backward ODE. This scheme proves to reduce a bound on the distance between the data distribution and the learned distribution, motivating two different implementations for the correction function. We show that our proposed method improves sample quality on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-64, with minimal overhead in computation time.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Marginal Matching, a training-based predictor-corrector framework for flow matching models that improves sample quality with minimal computational overhead.
AI.motivation: Flow matching models struggle to balance generation fidelity and computational efficiency, and predictor-corrector schemes that help diffusion models remain underexplored for ODE-based flow matching.
AI.method: Exploiting the reversibility of flow matching ODEs, Marginal Matching trains a correction function to align samples at a given time step in the forward ODE toward the matching marginal distribution of the backward ODE, reducing a bound on distribution distance.
AI.result: Evaluated on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-64, the proposed two implementations of Marginal Matching improve sample quality while adding minimal computation time.
AI.conclusion: Reversing the flow matching ODE to enforce marginal consistency provides a principled, lightweight predictor-corrector mechanism for higher-fidelity generative modeling.

title: Learning Stratified Policies for Inference-Time Objectives
summary: Inference-time scaling improves the performance of large language models by sampling multiple responses and evaluating their collective utility. However, many existing approaches obtain these samples by repeatedly sampling from a single policy. In this work, we study if the sample budget at inference time can instead be allocated across a population of policies. We introduce stratified policies, where each of $k$ learned policies contributes one response to a $k$-sample inference-time objective. We realize this policy population using separate LoRA adapters on a shared language model backbone and optimize it for pass@$k$. We theoretically motivate the approach by analyzing the linear setting; a population of LoRAs can achieve zero best-of-$k$ approximation error in settings where every single LoRA has strictly positive prediction error. Empirically, we demonstrate that stratified policies consistently improve pass@$k$ over a single-policy baseline across multiple reasoning tasks. Overall, our results highlight how distributing samples across complementary policies can be a more effective use of sample budget than repeated i.i.d. sampling from a single policy at inference time.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes stratified policies, a population of separate LoRA adapters on a shared LLM backbone optimized for pass@k, to allocate inference-time sample budgets across complementary policies rather than a single policy.
AI.motivation: Inference-time scaling typically draws multiple i.i.d. samples from a single policy, which can be suboptimal for collective utility objectives like pass@k.
AI.method: The authors train k distinct LoRA adapters on a shared LLM backbone so each policy contributes one response to a k-sample objective, and analyze the linear setting theoretically to show how a population of LoRAs can achieve zero best-of-k error.
AI.result: Across multiple reasoning tasks, stratified policies consistently outperform a single-policy baseline in pass@k.
AI.conclusion: Distributing inference-time samples across complementary learned policies uses the sample budget more effectively than repeated sampling from a single policy.

title: Learned versus Kinematic Trajectory Prediction under Reduced Observation Frequency
comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Code and per-scenario results: this https URL
summary: Trajectory prediction models for automated driving are usually trained on data with a fixed sampling frequency, while positions received via vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication arrive at 1-10 Hz. We study whether a learned predictor that uses only the observation history keeps its advantage over constant velocity (CV) and constant acceleration (CA) models when the history frequency drops. On the Argoverse 2 motion forecasting dataset, the 5 s history of the focal agent was downsampled from 10 Hz to 5, 2, and 1 Hz, and the 6 s future was predicted without maps or neighboring agents. An LSTM-based recurrent neural network (RNN) trained for each frequency was compared with the same network trained at 10 Hz and applied to sparse histories after linear interpolation. Hypotheses and thresholds were fixed before training, the main RNNs were trained with ten seeds each, and results on 24,984 test scenarios have bootstrap confidence intervals over scenarios and seeds. The average displacement error of the frequency-specific RNN grew by 3.1% at 5 Hz, 10.1% at 2 Hz, and 20.3% at 1 Hz. Contrary to our hypothesis, its advantage over the better kinematic model did not vanish on straight motion and was 24-30% on both straight motion and turns at every frequency, while for pedestrians CV was more accurate. The 10 Hz model with interpolation was at most 1.3% less accurate than the frequency-specific model down to 2 Hz but 11.5% less accurate at 1 Hz. Each hypothesis was only partly supported.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates whether a learned LSTM trajectory predictor retains its accuracy advantage over kinematic models (constant velocity and constant acceleration) when observation frequency drops from 10 Hz to 5, 2, and 1 Hz.
AI.motivation: Automated driving predictors are typically trained at fixed 10 Hz rates, whereas V2X communication delivers positions at 1-10 Hz, raising the question of whether learned models still outperform simple kinematic baselines under sparse observations.
AI.method: Using 24,984 test scenarios from Argoverse 2 without maps or neighboring agents, the authors compare frequency-specific LSTMs (trained with 10 seeds each) against a 10 Hz LSTM with linear interpolation and kinematic CV/CA models across 5 s histories and 6 s horizons.
AI.result: The frequency-specific RNN's average displacement error increases by 3.1% at 5 Hz, 10.1% at 2 Hz, and 20.3% at 1 Hz, yet it maintains a 24-30% advantage over the best kinematic model on both straight motion and turns at all frequencies (though CV is more accurate for pedestrians); linear interpolation with the 10 Hz model is within 1.3% down to 2 Hz but 11.5% worse at 1 Hz.
AI.conclusion: Learned trajectory predictors remain substantially more accurate than kinematic models even at 1 Hz V2X rates for vehicles, though dedicated low-frequency training is needed below 2 Hz.

title: Fine-Tuning Gemma 4 Edge Models for MATLAB Signal-Processing Code with SFT and QLoRA on a Laptop iGPU
summary: Small language models that run on a laptop are attractive for writing signal-processing code offline, but they make systematic errors on digital signal processing (DSP) conventions. We apply supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to the Gemma 4 edge models E2B and E4B with 66 checked examples covering 11 signal-processing MATLAB subtasks, using low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and quantized LoRA (QLoRA) on the integrated GPU (iGPU) of a laptop, and deploy the 8-bit integer (int8) models with the adapters through OpenVINO. On held-out variants scored by deterministic checkers, the pass rate rises from 18/66 to 37/66 (LoRA) and 37/66 (QLoRA) for E2B and from 32/66 to 47/66 for E4B (QLoRA). Reading all 159 failing programs shows that the adapters remove most errors of convention, such as the sign of a lag, units and array shapes, but few errors in building signals and noise. Applied at run time, the adapter costs 17-19% of the generation speed.

AI.tldr: This paper fine-tunes Gemma 4 edge models (E2B and E4B) using SFT with LoRA and QLoRA on a laptop iGPU to fix digital signal processing (DSP) convention errors in MATLAB code.
AI.motivation: Small offline language models running on laptops frequently make systematic errors on DSP conventions such as lag signs, units, and array shapes when generating MATLAB code.
AI.method: The authors apply SFT with LoRA and QLoRA on 66 checked examples across 11 MATLAB DSP subtasks on a laptop iGPU, then deploy the int8-quantized models with adapters via OpenVINO.
AI.result: On held-out variants, deterministic checker pass rates increase from 18/66 to 37/66 (LoRA and QLoRA) for E2B and from 32/66 to 47/66 (QLoRA) for E4B, eliminating most convention errors while incurring a 17-19% generation speed overhead.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight on-device QLoRA fine-tuning effectively corrects domain-specific convention errors in edge LLMs, though errors in signal and noise construction remain.

title: Distortion-Free Semantic Watermarks for Black-Box Generative Models
comment: Project page: this https URL Code: this https URL
summary: We present a provably distortion-free semantic watermarking algorithm that requires only black-box sampling access to a generative model and black-box access to a semantic embedding. A watermark is called distortion-free if, averaged over its secret detection key, it leaves the generator's output distribution unchanged; this provides a formal guarantee that watermarking does not reduce output quality. Conventional such watermarks are often brittle to transformations. This is especially problematic for images, where benign operations such as compression, cropping, or resizing change the entire pixel representation. Semantic watermarks therefore require detection to be robust to content-preserving transformations. Previous methods combining these properties rely heavily on specific white-box properties of the underlying model: either to autoregressive text generation or to diffusion-specific access, such as control of the initial noise or diffusion inversion. In contrast, our construction is fully generic: It only interacts with the generative model and the semantic embedding, a function that determines the notion of "preserving content" under which detection should be robust, via sample and query access. We then instantiate this framework for image generation. We characterize the two competing properties required of the semantic embedding: it should remain stable under transformations that preserve an image's content, but should distinguish independent generations from the same prompt. We train an image encoder directly for this tradeoff. The resulting encoder improves separation while maintaining stability over off-the-shelf alternatives and enables strong aggregate detection while remaining robust to various transformations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our watermark scheme on both open-source and closed models, which is possible only due to restriction to black-box access.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a provably distortion-free, transformation-robust semantic watermarking algorithm that requires only black-box access to a generative model and a semantic embedding.
AI.motivation: Existing distortion-free semantic watermarks rely on white-box access to autoregressive token distributions or diffusion noise/inversion, preventing their use on closed-source models.
AI.method: The authors construct a generic black-box watermarking scheme using only sample and query access, and train a dedicated image encoder that balances invariance to content-preserving transformations (compression, cropping, resizing) with separation between independent generations from the same prompt.
AI.result: The trained encoder outperforms off-the-shelf alternatives on the stability-separation tradeoff, enabling strong aggregate detection and transformation robustness on both open-source and closed image generation models.
AI.conclusion: Provably distortion-free and robust semantic watermarking is achievable purely via black-box access, extending watermarking guarantees to closed generative models.

title: Do LLM Agents Still Need to Be Told How to Self-Improve?
summary: LLM agents increasingly drive their own learning. Self-improvement methods delegate various components of model optimization to the models themselves. As models become more capable, this motivates a basic question: do these increasingly capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? In this paper we study an autonomous paradigm in which, given basic primitives, resources, and a general goal for self-improvement, agents construct their own self-learning algorithm for context-based optimization. Using the setting of gameplay as a testbed, a frozen LLM agent is given a compute budget and tools for collecting experience and updating text documents, and allowed to freely experiment without an externally imposed loop or access to real-world data. We find that sufficiently capable models do self-improve under these conditions, demonstrating strategies that align with classic cognitive frameworks for self-regulated learning and constructs from machine learning literature on self-generated curricula. Furthermore, we study the extent to which the learned text artifacts transfer to external benchmarks, observing improvement across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether capable LLM agents can autonomously design their own context-based self-improvement algorithms without an externally imposed learning loop.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents become more capable, it is unclear whether they still require human-specified self-improvement loops or can self-organize their own learning when given basic primitives.
AI.method: Using gameplay as a testbed, frozen LLM agents are given a compute budget, experience-collection tools, and text-document editing tools with a general self-improvement goal, and are allowed to experiment freely without real-world data or an external loop.
AI.result: Sufficiently capable models autonomously self-improve using strategies resembling self-regulated learning and self-generated curricula, and the resulting text artifacts transfer to external benchmarks across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation.
AI.conclusion: Advanced LLM agents can independently construct effective context-based self-learning algorithms, reducing the need for rigid, hand-crafted self-improvement pipelines.

title: Improving Early Detection of Scientifically Interesting Radio Sources Using Enhanced Isolation Forest
summary: The rapid growth of radio astronomical surveys has created a major challenge in identifying scientifically interesting sources from large populations of observed objects. This study investigates whether enhanced Isolation Forest (iForest) methods can improve the early detection and ranking of scientifically interesting radio sources. Four iForest variants, Standard Enhanced, Pooled Gain, Kurtosis-based, and Hypervolume, are evaluated using 1,031 extended radio sources from the MeerKAT Galaxy Cluster Legacy Survey (MGCLS). Each source is represented by a 52-dimensional feature set derived using Bootstrap Your Own Latent (BYOL) self-supervised learning and principal component analysis (PCA), while expert scientific-interest ratings are used to define the ground-truth labels. The methods are evaluated using Average Precision (AP), receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC AUC), Precision@10, Precision@50, and cumulative anomaly detection. Pooled Gain achieves the highest Average Precision (AP = 0.201) and the strongest early-stage ranking performance (P@10 = 0.600), identifying six expert-validated anomalies among the ten highest-ranked sources. Standard Enhanced and Kurtosis-based achieve the highest ROC AUC (0.677), while the AUC values of the four variants range from 0.653 to 0.677. These results indicate that feature-aware isolation strategies can improve the prioritization of scientifically interesting sources at the top of the ranked list, although overall discrimination remains comparable across the evaluated variants. The findings support the use of enhanced Isolation Forest methods as an initial ranking mechanism within human-in-the-loop systems for large-scale radio astronomical surveys.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates four enhanced Isolation Forest (iForest) variants for early detection and ranking of scientifically interesting radio sources in the MeerKAT Galaxy Cluster Legacy Survey (MGCLS).
AI.motivation: Growing radio astronomical surveys produce vast object catalogs, making automated prioritization of scientifically interesting sources essential for human-in-the-loop discovery.
AI.method: Using 1,031 extended MGCLS radio sources represented by 52-dimensional BYOL self-supervised + PCA features and expert ratings as ground truth, the authors compare Standard Enhanced, Pooled Gain, Kurtosis-based, and Hypervolume iForest variants.
AI.result: Pooled Gain achieves the highest Average Precision (0.201) and Precision@10 (0.600, identifying 6 expert-validated anomalies in the top 10), while Standard Enhanced and Kurtosis-based reach the highest ROC AUC (0.677, with all variants ranging from 0.653 to 0.677).
AI.conclusion: Feature-aware isolation strategies improve top-ranked prioritization of anomalous radio sources, supporting their use as an initial ranking stage in human-in-the-loop astronomical surveys.

title: RTLReviewBench: LLM Hardware Reviewers Rarely Miss Bugs but Routinely Reject Correct RTL
comment: 24 pages, 6 figures, 16 tables. Benchmark, model responses, and code: this https URL
summary: Hardware teams increasingly ask large language models (LLMs) to review register-transfer level (RTL) code, yet it is unclear whether a model can tell a correct module from a buggy one without simulating it. We introduce RTLReviewBench, a benchmark of 114 matched pairs of buggy and correct Verilog modules. Each pair shares one specification, most buggy modules are real failures of LLM code generators, and every label is confirmed by simulation. Evaluating 12 commercial and open-weight models, we find a consistent asymmetry: reviewers rarely accept buggy code but often reject correct code, producing more than five false rejections for every missed bug. Synthetic mutants hide part of the problem: on the same designs, models miss far fewer injected bugs than real ones. Asking a model to reason before it commits to a verdict sharply reduces false rejections for weaker reviewers, and a controlled ablation shows that where the reasoning appears in the output matters more than the instruction to reason, whereas sampling and majority voting do not help. A blinded audit further shows that some correct "buggy" verdicts rest on false technical claims. We release the benchmark, a harder split for future models, all model responses, and the evaluation code at this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper introduces RTLReviewBench, a benchmark of 114 matched buggy/correct Verilog module pairs, revealing that LLM hardware reviewers rarely miss bugs but frequently reject correct RTL code.
AI.motivation: Hardware teams increasingly use LLMs to review RTL code, yet it is unknown whether LLMs can reliably distinguish buggy from correct modules without simulation.
AI.method: The authors construct 114 specification-matched pairs of buggy and correct Verilog modules (mostly real LLM code-generator failures verified by simulation) and evaluate 12 commercial and open-weight models, including ablations on reasoning placement and sampling.
AI.result: Models produce over five false rejections for every missed bug, synthetic mutants underestimate missed-bug rates compared to real failures, and prompting models to reason before committing to a verdict sharply reduces false rejections in weaker reviewers (with reasoning placement mattering more than the instruction itself, while majority voting does not help).
AI.conclusion: Current LLM RTL reviewers suffer from high false-rejection rates and occasional false technical claims, making pre-verdict reasoning placement critical for practical hardware review.

title: Edge-Adaptive Hiera-Seg Model for Building-Integrated Photovoltaic Power Forecasting
summary: Building integrated photovoltaic power forecasting is challenging because facade orientation, rooftop geometry, nearby buildings, vegetation, cloud movement, module temperature, inverter status and edge device reliability jointly affect power generation. This paper proposes an edge-adaptive HieraSeg model for short term BIPV power forecasting with multi-orientation visual-irradiance fusion. RGB facade images, optional thermal cues, irradiance measurements, module temperature, facade orientation, rooftop masks, shading labels, sky condition, historical power and edge device state are aligned into synchronous forecasting windows. HieraSeg extracts hierarchical regions from facade, rooftop, sky, shadow and background images, while the edge-adaptive module changes feature weights under missing frames, latency shifts and local shading changes. The segmentation branch identifies occluded module areas and separates facade, rooftop, sky and background evidence before the forecasting head estimates future BIPV output. Experiments are designed on a simulated multibuilding BIPV dataset with unseen building and unseen orientation tests. The model reports predicted power, confidence interval, dominant evidence, occlusion contribution, orientation contribution and energy-management review priority. This output is intended to show whether the forecast is driven by irradiance change, visible shading, orientation response, stale edge information or recent power history. The framework supports local forecasting at edge controllers with limited communication delay and computing resources, linking visual occlusion, irradiance dynamics and power history to traceable forecasting results for building energy management, microgrid scheduling and BIPV operation planning.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an edge-adaptive HieraSeg model for short-term building-integrated photovoltaic (BIPV) power forecasting using multi-orientation visual-irradiance fusion.
AI.motivation: BIPV power forecasting is complicated by facade orientation, rooftop geometry, shading, cloud movement, and unreliable edge devices.
AI.method: HieraSeg aligns RGB facade images, optional thermal cues, irradiance, temperature, orientation, rooftop masks, shading, sky condition, historical power, and edge device state into synchronous windows, using a segmentation branch to separate occluded and background regions and an edge-adaptive module to reweight features under missing frames or latency shifts.
AI.result: Designed for a simulated multi-building BIPV dataset with unseen building and orientation splits, the model outputs power forecasts, confidence intervals, dominant evidence, occlusion/orientation contributions, and energy-management review priorities.
AI.conclusion: Integrating hierarchical visual segmentation with edge-adaptive feature weighting enables traceable, resource-efficient BIPV forecasting on local edge controllers.

title: Stop Early, Stay Simple: Evidence Acquisition for Power System Fault and Attack Diagnosis
summary: Diagnostic models for cyber-physical power systems usually inspect every telemetry source for every event, although some events are clear from one source and others need several. We ask when a learned policy for choosing that evidence is worth its added complexity. To answer this, we present ActiGrid, a benchmark framework for active evidence acquisition that pairs a classifier trained to tolerate missing modalities with a Double Deep Q-Network (DQN), which either requests another source or stops and diagnoses but never operates grid actuators. On the public TU Delft digital substation and MSU/ORNL power system attack benchmarks, we compare the DQN with fixed subsets and orders, calibrated entropy stopping, a greedy value of information rule, and tree ensembles trained per subset. The learned policy does adapt to what it observes, yet it is statistically indistinguishable from entropy stopping on TU Delft and Pareto dominated by simple controls on MSU/ORNL, while compact subset classifiers outperform it while reading fewer sources on both benchmarks. Entropy stopping run over those subset classifiers reaches the highest mean Macro-F1 on TU Delft (0.928 while reading 57% of the sources) but brings no saving over a static three source subset on MSU/ORNL, where no method exceeds 0.45 Macro-F1. Selective acquisition can pay off, but on these benchmarks it does not need a learned policy.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ActiGrid, a benchmark for active evidence acquisition in power system fault and attack diagnosis, showing that simple static subsets or entropy stopping match or outperform learned RL policies.
AI.motivation: Cyber-physical power system diagnostics typically inspect all telemetry sources for every event, and it is unclear when a learned sequential acquisition policy justifies its added complexity.
AI.method: ActiGrid pairs a missing-modality-tolerant classifier with a Double DQN that decides whether to request another telemetry source or stop and diagnose, and compares it against fixed subsets, calibrated entropy stopping, greedy value-of-information, and per-subset tree ensembles on TU Delft and MSU/ORNL benchmarks.
AI.result: The Double DQN is statistically indistinguishable from entropy stopping on TU Delft and Pareto-dominated by simple controls on MSU/ORNL; entropy stopping over compact subset classifiers achieves the highest mean Macro-F1 on TU Delft (0.928 using 57% of sources), while no method exceeds 0.45 Macro-F1 or beats a static three-source subset on MSU/ORNL.
AI.conclusion: Selective evidence acquisition can reduce telemetry usage in power system diagnosis, but simple static subsets or entropy stopping suffice without a learned RL policy.

title: Video recordings and play behaviour annotations of group-housed dairy calves on two Dutch farms
summary: Play is used as an indicator of positive welfare in dairy calves, but openly available video of group-housed calves with individual behaviour annotations is scarce. We describe video from four camera deployments of about one week each in group pens of dairy calves on two farms in the Netherlands: a research and teaching dairy farm (2024 and 2025) and a commercial dairy farm (2024). The recordings comprise 1,173 video files spanning 651 h. For eight observation days, trained observers coded calf behaviour continuously in Noldus The Observer XT with an 18-item ethogram of play and other behaviours, covering 104 h of video, 90 h of which have every calf in the pen coded. The release also contains 1.1 million decoded frames from seven annotated sessions, a per-frame timestamp read by optical character recognition from the camera clock burned into each frame, per-calf segmentation tracks and per-calf frame-level play labels. The data support studies of calf behaviour and welfare and the development and evaluation of automated behaviour recognition.

AI.tldr: This paper releases a dataset of 651 hours of video recordings (1,173 files) of group-housed dairy calves across two Dutch farms, including 104 hours of continuous 18-item ethogram annotations and 1.1 million decoded frames with per-calf tracks and play labels.
AI.motivation: Play behavior is a key welfare indicator in dairy calves, but publicly available video datasets with individual, frame-level behavior annotations are scarce.
AI.method: The authors deployed cameras for roughly one week across four deployments at a research farm (2024-2025) and a commercial farm (2024), coded 104 hours continuously in Noldus The Observer XT (90 hours with every calf coded), and extracted OCR timestamps, segmentation tracks, and frame-level play labels.
AI.result: The released dataset provides 1,173 video files (651 h), 104 h of 18-item ethogram annotations, and 1.1 million frames with per-calf segmentation tracks and play labels.
AI.conclusion: This dataset provides a large-scale benchmark for studying calf welfare and developing automated behavior recognition models.

title: Better Calibrated, Better Planned: Uncertainty-Aware Multi-ASV Informative Path Planning for Oil Spill Monitoring
comment: 11 pages, 7 figures, Submitted to IEEE Internet of Things Journal
summary: Monitoring oil spills with fleets of Autonomous Surface Vehicles (ASVs) requires mapping a heterogeneous pollutant field from sparse, noisy measurements under tight time and energy budgets. Informative Path Planning (IPP) addresses this problem by coupling a reconstruction model, which infers the field and its uncertainty, with a planner that decides where to sample next. Prior work has focused on planning strategies and has largely relied on Gaussian Processes (GPs), leaving the calibration of the model's uncertainty underexplored. We study how uncertainty calibration conditions multi-vehicle IPP with a fleet of ASVs that coordinates online through a shared uncertainty map. We introduce Evidential Deep Learning (EDL) as an uncertainty-calibrated information model. We benchmark EDL, Monte Carlo Dropout and Deep Ensembles against a GP in closed loop with five planners on physics-based oil spill simulations. Across 60 maps, the choice of model dominates the outcome, explaining 80\% of the variance of the final reconstruction error, against 1\% for the planner among the deep models. EDL achieves the lowest error and the highest IoU under every planner, is the best calibrated model and runs at 3.9 ms per step. With 50 cells per vehicle it reconstructs the spill better than MC Dropout and Deep Ensembles with 150. Deep Ensembles become more confident as their error grows, whereas EDL is unaffected. Robustness of the information model to the data its own planner collects is therefore a requirement of uncertainty-aware IPP.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks uncertainty-aware information models for multi-ASV oil spill informative path planning (IPP), showing that Evidential Deep Learning (EDL) dominates reconstruction accuracy and calibration over GP, MC Dropout, and Deep Ensembles.
AI.motivation: Prior multi-vehicle IPP research has focused on planning algorithms using Gaussian Processes, leaving the impact of deep uncertainty calibration on closed-loop sampling underexplored.
AI.method: The authors integrate EDL, Monte Carlo Dropout, Deep Ensembles, and GP into a closed-loop multi-ASV IPP framework across five planners and 60 physics-based oil spill simulation maps.
AI.result: Model choice explains 80% of final reconstruction error variance compared to 1% for the planner; EDL achieves the lowest error, highest IoU, best calibration, and 3.9 ms/step runtime, outperforming MC Dropout and Deep Ensembles at 50 cells per vehicle versus 150, while Deep Ensembles become overconfident as error grows.
AI.conclusion: Well-calibrated uncertainty models like EDL that remain robust to planner-collected data are far more critical to multi-ASV IPP performance than the choice of planner.

title: Chain-of-Thought Controllability Can Reduce Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is a promising tool for detecting hidden goals, off-task behavior, and other failures in AI agents. One risk is that models could deliberately shape their reasoning to make it opaque to monitors. We stress-test this risk through persona-control training: supervised fine-tuning on mathematical reasoning traces rewritten in the voices of diverse personas. This induces a broader ability to control CoT, even though training contains no monitor-evasion examples. In covert side-task evaluations, traces in which a gpt-oss-20b model organism completes the hidden side task contain less monitorable evidence than the base model's. Averaged across evaluations and CoT lengths, weighted by side-task-success counts, the CoT monitorability metric g-mean$^2$ falls from 0.94 for the base model to 0.68 for the model organism without a hiding instruction, and to 0.22 when explicitly instructed to hide. In intervention evaluations, explicit hiding often drives monitorability near zero. The effect extends to a Kimi-K2.6 model organism in agentic environments, though hidden objectives requiring extended reasoning or longer trajectories remain more monitorable than simple single-step side tasks. We further discover that targeted transparency prompts can substantially recover monitorability, sometimes surpassing the base model. These model organisms provide a testbed for studying monitorability failures and potential mitigations. Our code can be found on this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that training LLMs to control their chain-of-thought (CoT) style via persona-control SFT inadvertently reduces CoT monitorability, even without monitor-evasion training.
AI.motivation: CoT monitoring is used to detect hidden goals and off-task behavior in AI agents, raising the concern that models capable of controlling their CoT could make their reasoning opaque to monitors.
AI.method: The authors fine-tune gpt-oss-20b and Kimi-K2.6 on math reasoning traces rewritten in diverse persona voices, then evaluate CoT monitorability (g-mean^2) on covert side-task and agentic benchmarks with and without explicit hiding instructions or transparency prompts.
AI.result: For gpt-oss-20b, g-mean^2 drops from 0.94 (base) to 0.68 without hiding instructions and 0.22 with explicit hiding instructions (often near zero in interventions), with similar effects in Kimi-K2.6; however, targeted transparency prompts substantially recover monitorability.
AI.conclusion: General CoT controllability can degrade monitorability as an unintended side effect, though transparency prompting offers a promising mitigation.

title: Data-Driven Variable-Length Compression of 3D Representations
summary: Compressing 3D shapes is important for the efficiency of many applications, yet existing methods either cannot leverage dataset-level statistics or use a fixed compression ratio for all shapes. We propose a learned variable-length compression method that exploits structure across a training dataset while adapting compressed representation size to individual shape complexity using only fast feed-forward inference. Our method operates on general latent representations and improves rate-distortion for both meshes and signed distance fields. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a learned, feed-forward variable-length compression method for 3D latent representations that adapts compressed size to individual shape complexity.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D shape compression methods either ignore dataset-level statistics or apply a fixed compression ratio regardless of shape complexity.
AI.method: The method exploits training-dataset structure and uses fast feed-forward inference to dynamically allocate variable-length compressed representations per shape across general latent spaces.
AI.result: Experiments show improved rate-distortion performance for both 3D meshes and signed distance fields.
AI.conclusion: Adapting latent representation length to shape complexity via feed-forward inference yields better rate-distortion tradeoffs for 3D data compression.

title: Coordination of Heterogeneous Teams with Uncertain Task Requirements
summary: Coordinating a team of heterogeneous agents to complete tasks with unknown requirements is a challenging multi-agent planning problem. Agents differ in their ability to discover task requirements and in their ability to engage tasks, so the planner must coordinate task discovery, execution, and staging. This paper introduces a hierarchical planner that uses a graph neural network policy to assign actions to agents, then finds a path to the action's location using a shortest-path algorithm. The central part of our approach is the CAAT graph, which is a graph representation of the planning context consisting of the agents, tasks, capabilities, and actions. We demonstrate that our learned planner can jointly coordinate a heterogeneous team to simultaneously discover task requirements and complete tasks in a shorter time compared to baselines that optimize task discovery and task engagement independently. Furthermore, we show that our policy can zero-shot plan on out-of-distribution settings by training only on an outdoor map then transferring without finetuning to an indoor map with more agents, tasks, and capabilities than seen during training.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a hierarchical planner using a graph neural network policy over a CAAT graph representation to coordinate heterogeneous multi-agent teams under uncertain task requirements.
AI.motivation: Heterogeneous teams must jointly discover unknown task requirements and execute tasks, whereas existing baselines often optimize discovery and engagement independently.
AI.method: The authors represent agents, tasks, capabilities, and actions in a unified CAAT graph, use a GNN policy to assign actions to agents, and compute paths via a shortest-path algorithm.
AI.result: The learned planner completes tasks faster than independent discovery/engagement baselines and generalizes zero-shot from an outdoor training map to an indoor map with more agents, tasks, and capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Encoding heterogeneous team capabilities and task uncertainty in a unified graph enables effective joint coordination and strong zero-shot generalization.

title: Quantum-Classical Separation in Probability Distribution Transport via Nonlocal Games
summary: In many-body physics and generative artificial intelligence, locality provides a natural notion of phase equivalence: two quantum states or classical probability distributions are regarded as in the same phase when local dynamics can reversibly transform one into the other. This raises a fundamental question: can local quantum dynamics transport classical probability distributions in ways that local classical dynamics cannot? We establish a quantum-classical separation in distribution transport: two classical distributions can be connected exactly and reversibly by a constant-depth local quantum circuit, whereas classical stochastic transport requires a substantially larger spatial range. We demonstrate this separation explicitly on a one-dimensional chain and develop a general construction principle on graphs, based on nonlocal games. Moreover, the source distribution can itself be generated by a simple local classical process, establishing a quantum advantage in distribution generation as well. Our results reveal a fundamental distinction between classical and quantum local reversibility, even when both the initial and final states are entirely classical.

AI.tldr: This paper proves a quantum-classical separation in probability distribution transport, showing that constant-depth local quantum circuits can reversibly connect classical distributions that require much larger spatial range classically.
AI.motivation: Understanding whether local quantum dynamics can transport classical probability distributions in ways impossible for local classical stochastic dynamics is a fundamental question in many-body physics and generative AI.
AI.method: Using nonlocal games, the authors construct explicit 1D chain examples and a general graph-based construction where a constant-depth local quantum circuit reversibly transforms a simple classical source distribution into a target classical distribution.
AI.result: They establish that local classical stochastic transport requires a substantially larger spatial range than constant-depth local quantum circuits to connect the same classical distributions, also yielding a quantum advantage in distribution generation.
AI.conclusion: Local quantum reversibility is fundamentally more powerful than local classical reversibility even when both initial and final states are purely classical.

title: ALOHA Lightning: Learning Fast and Precise Manipulation
summary: Learning from human demonstrations has enabled robots to acquire a wide range of manipulation skills, but learned policies typically execute far slower than ordinary humans. This speed gap is mainly due to lack of an interface for collecting demonstration data at high speed, and the difficulty in training policies that can robustly execute high-speed motions. In this paper, we present ALOHA Lightning (Flash ALOHA), a system for learning fast and precise robotic manipulation. Our system uses kinesthetic teaching to intuitively collect near-human-speed demonstrations on a backdrivable bimanual platform, yielding natural and fast trajectories. We also present a learning pipeline that enables smooth high-speed execution through test-time action smoothing and aligns the visual data distribution between data collection and deployment with masking. Given 50 demonstrations for each task, ALOHA Lightning autonomously completes bimanual tasks such as ball tossing and catching, folding shorts, battery insertion, and bussing tables for over 80% success rates while close to human speed. Project website: this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper presents ALOHA Lightning, a kinesthetic teaching and policy learning system that enables bimanual robots to perform fast, precise manipulation at near-human speeds.
AI.motivation: Imitation-learned robot policies typically execute much slower than humans due to a lack of high-speed demonstration interfaces and difficulty maintaining robustness during fast motions.
AI.method: ALOHA Lightning uses kinesthetic teaching on a backdrivable bimanual platform for natural high-speed data collection, combined with test-time action smoothing and visual masking to align data-collection and deployment distributions.
AI.result: With 50 demonstrations per task, ALOHA Lightning achieves over 80% success rates at near-human speeds on bimanual tasks including ball tossing and catching, folding shorts, battery insertion, and bussing tables.
AI.conclusion: Combining backdrivable kinesthetic data collection with action smoothing and visual masking closes much of the speed gap in bimanual robotic manipulation.

title: Wrong Input, Wrong Threshold: Re-evaluating Adversarial Facial Privacy
comment: 10 pages main text and 15 pages supplementary material. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Published face-privacy methods report protection above 90% against black-box recognition models. That number comes from an evaluation protocol with two independent defects, reported in a measure that cannot size either one. The input is wrong: methods published since 2022 feed the network the whole photograph, or a detector's box, where deployed systems detect, align to a landmark template and crop. Re-scoring the same files through a realistic front end costs a standard transfer attack 56% of its dodging protection and a budget-allocating attack 7%, with no image regenerated. The measure is wrong: that loss is a difference of success rates, so it saturates, moving by 8.2x over a budget sweep while the effect beneath it moves by 1.34x. We therefore report the paired cosine shift, in which both thresholds cancel algebraically, so the input defect holds without committing to a calibration. Measured that way it is 2.2x and 10.7x larger on three unseen recognizers, and at matched budget it reverses the L-infinity transfer ranking: the one surveyed method that aligns at evaluation gains 0.18 where MI-FGSM loses 0.05. The cause is a resampling mismatch, not perturbation lost outside the crop; optimising through a differentiable alignment operator largely removes it, adding +24 to +58 points on unseen recognizers and a commercial system, with a residual on one of them. The thresholds are wrong: the four constants inherited since 2021 hold the false-accept rate near its nominal 1% on aligned crops but admit 2.3-5.4% on whole images, with an opposite-signed bias across dodging and impersonation, the two tasks reported side by side. Differentiable alignment and gallery scoring are not new: the first generation of this literature used both, and we show what dropping them cost.

AI.tldr: This paper audits adversarial facial privacy evaluations and shows that feeding unaligned images, using saturated success-rate metrics, and inheriting miscalibrated thresholds severely distort reported protection rates.
AI.motivation: Published face-privacy methods report over 90% black-box protection, but their evaluation protocols diverge from deployed face recognition pipelines that detect, align, and crop faces.
AI.method: The authors re-evaluate existing privacy perturbations through realistic alignment front-ends, introduce the threshold-free paired cosine shift metric, and optimize perturbations through a differentiable alignment operator.
AI.result: Realistic alignment drops a standard transfer attack's dodging protection by 56% (7% for budget-allocating attacks) and reverses L-infinity transfer rankings; optimizing through differentiable alignment recovers +24 to +58 points on unseen recognizers and a commercial system, while inherited thresholds admit 2.3-5.4% false-accept rates on whole images instead of 1%.
AI.conclusion: Adversarial facial privacy benchmarks must incorporate differentiable alignment and threshold-free metrics like paired cosine shift to reflect real-world protection.

title: Polylogarithmic Regret via Certainty Equivalence in Degenerate LQR
summary: Singular input penalties, as in minimum variance control, can reduce what must be identified to control an unknown linear system. In online linear quadratic control, certainty equivalence can achieve polylogarithmic regret when the optimal controller is identifiable from data collected under optimal feedback. With a positive definite input penalty, however, this condition is restrictive, since for an invertible state matrix it requires all unknown parameters to be identifiable under optimal feedback. We show that singular input penalties relax this requirement, expanding the class of problems in which certainty equivalence achieves polylogarithmic regret. Specifically, we prove that a certainty-equivalence algorithm with a short initial exploration phase achieves $O(\log^2 T)$ expected regret over $T$ interactions whenever controller identifiability holds. We complement this guarantee with an $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$ minimax lower bound for a family containing a system where controller identifiability fails. For minimum variance control, knowing the range of the input matrix suffices for controller identifiability, a weaker requirement than knowing the full input matrix, as assumed in prior work with positive definite input penalties. This condition also covers underactuated systems, as we illustrate with a cart-pole example.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that certainty equivalence with a short initial exploration phase achieves O(log^2 T) expected regret in online LQR with singular input penalties whenever controller identifiability holds.
AI.motivation: With positive definite input penalties, polylogarithmic regret in online LQR typically requires identifying all unknown system parameters under optimal feedback, which is overly restrictive.
AI.method: The authors analyze degenerate LQR with singular input penalties (such as minimum variance control) using a certainty-equivalence algorithm with brief initial exploration, and derive matching minimax lower bounds.
AI.result: They prove O(log^2 T) expected regret over T steps under controller identifiability and an Omega(sqrt(T)) minimax lower bound when it fails; for minimum variance control, knowing only the range of the input matrix suffices, covering underactuated systems like cart-pole.
AI.conclusion: Singular input penalties substantially relax parameter identifiability requirements for achieving polylogarithmic regret in adaptive linear quadratic control.

title: V2V Communications Using Blockchain-Enabled 6G Technology and Federated Learning
summary: This study proposes an interesting approach for vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) communication, which integrates blockchain technology, federated learning (FL), and allocation optimization of latency and resources. The research evaluates the proposed system using various performance metrics such as packet delivery ratio (PDR), model accuracy, and latency and demonstrates its superiority over existing techniques. Furthermore, the system provides enhanced security through consensus optimization and k-anonymity for data privacy. Overall, the proposed system is a promising solution for efficient and secure V2V communication in the era of connected and autonomous vehicles. Moreover, the proposed approach achieves higher reliability, lower latency, and better resource utilization compared to traditional 5G.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) communication framework integrating blockchain, 6G, federated learning, and resource/latency optimization for connected autonomous vehicles.
AI.motivation: Connected and autonomous vehicles require V2V communication systems that simultaneously achieve high reliability, low latency, efficient resource utilization, and strong data privacy.
AI.method: The system combines federated learning with blockchain consensus optimization, k-anonymity for data privacy, and joint latency and resource allocation optimization.
AI.result: Evaluated on packet delivery ratio (PDR), model accuracy, and latency, the proposed approach outperforms existing techniques and traditional 5G baselines.
AI.conclusion: Integrating blockchain consensus, k-anonymity, and federated learning provides a secure, low-latency, and resource-efficient V2V communication architecture.

title: HubEgo-100K: In-the-Wild Egocentric Video of Skilled Work for Robot Learning
comment: 22 pages, 18 figures, 7 tables. Dataset: this https URL
summary: Robot policies trained by imitation generalize poorly outside the environments and objects seen in training. Published data-scaling studies find that generalization grows with the diversity of training environments and objects rather than with more demonstrations per environment. Robot data is costly to collect across many environments, whereas egocentric human video can be recorded in the wild at scale; existing egocentric video, however, mostly shows daily-life activity and contains little skilled work in real workplaces. We present HubEgo-100K, a dataset built for diversity. This version of the paper covers the first release, v1.0: 10,124 hours of 1080p egocentric video with synchronized 100 Hz inertial (IMU) data from one head-mounted phone camera. In v1.0, 12,227 contributors record their own unscripted work in 15,548 environments (each one contributor's own setting of one type, such as their kitchen or workshop) across 11 setting types, 30 work categories, 56 task types and 35 action families, with 83% of hours in workplace settings. The release comprises 72,754 episodes with machine-generated action and language annotations, in LeRobot and MCAP formats under CC BY 4.0. We measure diversity along each axis, show that inside v1.0, with episodes in random order, new contributors and words keep appearing, and relate the measurements to published evidence on six data properties tied to policy performance, including hand visibility and inertial sensing. We also document collection, curation, privacy measures and data format, and provide a datasheet. Later versions of this paper will add benchmarks and cover further releases toward 100,000 hours.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces HubEgo-100K (v1.0), a 10,124-hour dataset of 1080p in-the-wild egocentric video and 100 Hz IMU data capturing skilled workplace tasks for robot learning.
AI.motivation: Robot imitation policies generalize poorly without diverse environments and objects, yet existing egocentric human video datasets mostly capture daily life rather than skilled workplace tasks.
AI.method: Collected from 12,227 contributors using a head-mounted phone camera across 15,548 environments (83% workplaces), v1.0 spans 11 setting types, 30 work categories, 56 task types, and 35 action families, packaged as 72,754 episodes with machine-generated action/language annotations in LeRobot and MCAP formats.
AI.result: Diversity measurements confirm that new contributors and words continue appearing as episodes are sampled, and the authors analyze six data properties tied to robot policy performance including hand visibility and inertial sensing.
AI.conclusion: HubEgo-100K provides unprecedented environmental and occupational diversity in egocentric video and IMU data to support generalizable robot policy learning.

title: Does the Model Use What It Cites? Counterfactual Tests of Grounded Reasoning Chains in Small Video-Language Models
comment: 24 pages, 4 figures, 27 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: A grounded reasoning chain cites a frame span and a box for every step, so a reader can check where the model looked. Whether the answer depends on the cited region is a different question. We test it by intervention: the regions a model cited in its own chain are blacked out, and the share of correct answers that flip is compared with blacking out boxes of the same size elsewhere on the same frames. The paired difference, the cite gap, needs no annotation. We apply it to 2-3B video-language models trained on exact CLEVRER chains and on pseudo-labelled NExT-QA chains. With the same weights, the cite gap is 0.089 on CLEVRER and 0.003 on NExT-QA. Pooled over models, masking the cited boxes flips 2.2 times as many correct answers as the control on CLEVRER and 1.1 times as many on NExT-QA, also among the answers that depend on the video at all, while the boxes pass a grounding check on both. Masking the cited entity on every frame, instead of the cited box, flips 1.9 times as many answers as its control. The NExT-QA chains were supervised to cite two frames of entities that stay visible on most frames, so this outcome is what the supervision predicts; the point is that the usual check on grounded chains cannot see it. A citation can be verifiable and relevant without the answer depending on it, and a test of grounded reasoning should remove what a chain names, not only where it points.

AI.tldr: This paper uses counterfactual masking interventions to test whether small video-language models actually depend on the bounding boxes and frame spans cited in their grounded reasoning chains.
AI.motivation: Grounded reasoning chains cite specific frames and boxes for verification, but standard grounding checks do not verify whether the model's answer causally depends on those cited regions.
AI.method: The authors black out cited regions in 2-3B video-language models trained on CLEVRER and pseudo-labelled NExT-QA chains, measuring the cite gap (difference in answer flip rate versus equal-sized control boxes on the same frames) and entity-level masking across all frames.
AI.result: The cite gap is 0.089 on CLEVRER (2.2x control flip rate) but only 0.003 on NExT-QA (1.1x control flip rate), even though boxes pass grounding checks on both; masking the cited entity on every frame flips 1.9x as many answers as control.
AI.conclusion: A grounded citation can be visually relevant without causally driving the answer, showing that counterfactual removal of named entities is needed to evaluate grounded reasoning.

title: Benchmarking Deep Learning Models for Wheelchair Configuration Classification in Accessible Automated Vehicle Applications
summary: Making automated vehicles accessible requires consideration of vulnerable road users, including wheelchair users. To offer a more tailored experience that supports independence for this group, vehicle design needs to accommodate the wide range of wheelchair configurations. However, wheelchairs are individualized, varying in frame geometry, propulsion, and visual appearance. Moreover, occupants or accessories may obscure visual cues. Existing mobility-aid datasets only label the presence of a wheelchair, rather than describing its specific configuration. To fill this gap, this paper introduces the Wheelchair Configuration Image Dataset (WCID), comprising 467 face-blurred images across 192 capture groups solely for evaluation. Each image is annotated with (i) a two-class label of manual or powered, (ii) a chair subtype, (iii) occupancy, viewpoint, setting, lighting, occlusion, propulsion, and control, with a 273-image validation split and 194-image test split. Three convolutional neural network backbones and a frozen vision-language probe are trained on an external image dataset and evaluated on WCID to measure cross-dataset generalization, while also testing robustness using Gaussian blur. Convolutional models do well on clean images, but performance drops under strong blur, leaving a gap before deployment. Code, split assignments, labels, trained weights, and the face-blurred images is available at: this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Wheelchair Configuration Image Dataset (WCID) of 467 annotated images and benchmarks CNNs and a frozen vision-language probe for accessible automated vehicle perception.
AI.motivation: Existing mobility-aid datasets only detect wheelchair presence, lacking fine-grained configuration labels needed by automated vehicles to accommodate diverse wheelchair users.
AI.method: WCID provides 467 face-blurred evaluation images (273 validation, 194 test) across 192 capture groups annotated with manual/powered type, subtype, occupancy, viewpoint, setting, lighting, occlusion, propulsion, and control; three CNN backbones and a frozen VLM probe are trained externally and tested on clean and Gaussian-blurred images.
AI.result: Convolutional models perform well on clean WCID images but degrade substantially under strong Gaussian blur, leaving a deployment robustness gap.
AI.conclusion: WCID establishes a fine-grained evaluation benchmark for wheelchair configuration recognition and highlights the need for blur-robust perception in accessible automated vehicles.

title: ThermLeT: Transformer-based Temperature Prediction for 2.5D Chiplet Architecture
comment: Published at VLSID 2026. Code and dataset: this https URL
summary: The drive toward heterogeneous 2.5D chiplet packages promises unmatched performance and customization, yet the resulting density amplifies thermal challenges. To facilitate rapid design space exploration, we present ThermLeT, a multimodal transformer-based, scale invariant surrogate that integrates power density maps, spatial coordinate embeddings, material properties and heat transfer rate to predict steady state temperature in 13 ms, about four orders of magnitude faster than conventional finite element solvers such as ANSYS. To train the transformer model, we also create a dataset of 6,221 chiplet layouts perturbed from three representative architectures. On a 150 sample test set, ThermLeT achieves an RMSE of 3.16°C and an MAE of 2.24°C, improving accuracy by 35% over ThermEDGe and by 71% over HotSpot, while running approximately 6x and 11x lower inference latencies respectively. Ablation studies confirm robust generalization to unseen floorplans. Code and dataset available at this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper presents ThermLeT, a multimodal transformer surrogate that predicts steady-state temperatures for 2.5D chiplet architectures in 13 ms, four orders of magnitude faster than ANSYS.
AI.motivation: Heterogeneous 2.5D chiplet packages create severe thermal density challenges, while conventional finite-element solvers like ANSYS are too slow for rapid design space exploration.
AI.method: ThermLeT integrates power density maps, spatial coordinate embeddings, material properties, and heat transfer rates in a scale-invariant transformer trained on a newly created dataset of 6,221 perturbed chiplet layouts.
AI.result: On a 150-sample test set, ThermLeT achieves an RMSE of 3.16 C and MAE of 2.24 C, improving accuracy by 35% over ThermEDGe and 71% over HotSpot while running 6x and 11x faster, and generalizes to unseen floorplans.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal transformer surrogates can deliver accurate, millisecond-scale thermal prediction to accelerate 2.5D chiplet design space exploration.

title: OCCAM: Improved Single-Cell Representation Learning and Perturbation Effect Prediction
summary: Predicting the effects of genetic perturbations requires models that generalize beyond observed cell contexts and gene combinations. We introduce Occam, a multilayer perceptron (MLP) framework for representation learning and perturbation-effect prediction. Occam combines cell representations learned through denoising with gene interaction, text, and protein-sequence features. It achieves the highest aggregate representation scores for perturbation information and cell-type preservation with batch integration. In cross-context few-shot prediction, a perturbation and a cell context are each observed during training, but never together. Occam better captures the measured response patterns for these unobserved combinations than four retrained competitors or direct transfer of the same perturbation's measured effects from other training cell lines. Without fine-tuning, Occam best distinguishes perturbations among the evaluated models and simple baselines in cell lines held out from predictor training, across seen and unseen assays. Predicting expression levels accurately in these settings remains challenging. For double perturbations, which target two genes simultaneously, Occam composes learned single-gene responses to better capture the combined response and reduce expression error compared with competing models and summed single-gene effects. These gains extend to both strongly additive and weakly additive responses. Together, these results support simple MLPs for cell representation learning and perturbation-effect prediction across contexts and gene combinations.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Occam, an MLP-based framework for single-cell representation learning and genetic perturbation-effect prediction that outperforms competing models across unseen cell contexts and double perturbations.
AI.motivation: Predicting genetic perturbation effects requires generalizing to unseen cell-line contexts and multi-gene combinations beyond observed training pairs.
AI.method: Occam combines denoising-learned cell representations with gene interaction, text, and protein-sequence features, and composes learned single-gene responses to predict double-gene perturbations.
AI.result: Occam achieves the highest aggregate scores for perturbation information and cell-type preservation with batch integration, outperforms four retrained competitors and direct transfer in cross-context few-shot prediction, and reduces expression error on both strongly and weakly additive double perturbations.
AI.conclusion: Simple MLP architectures enriched with multimodal gene and cell features provide strong generalization for single-cell representation learning and perturbation prediction.

title: Sparse Integer Fourier Transform and Its Application In Machine Learning
summary: The Discrete Fourier transform, mainly implemented by Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), has been essential for numerous domains, such as digital signal processing and feature extraction in materials design.
