However, current FFT methods suffer from extensive non-trivial multiplications and twiddle-factor operations in the big data era. To improve the computational efficiency of FFT, this study proposes Sparse Integer Fourier Transform (SIFT), a method that leverages the fast computing of sparsity and small integers, and applies the Radix-n method to derive an FFT. The 2N-point DFT matrix in Radix-n FFT is decomposed into four sparse integer matrices. A diagonal matrix containing complex twiddle factors is efficiently approximated using an optimization strategy while the remaining matrices retain sparsity and integer entries. For radix-32 FFT, SIFT reduces the estimated arithmetic cost by 75%, with RMSE below $2.3765\times10^{-8}$ and MAPE below 0.01089%. We evaluate frequency extraction in a numerical test and an engineering case. In the numerical test, MAPE and RMSE are below 2.016% and $2.536\times10^{-6}$, respectively. For wind turbine fault diagnosis, SIFT extracts compact spectral features that retain fault information while reducing the classifier's input dimensionality relative to the full time series.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Sparse Integer Fourier Transform (SIFT), which decomposes the Radix-n FFT matrix into sparse integer matrices and an approximated twiddle-factor diagonal matrix to reduce arithmetic cost.
AI.motivation: Conventional FFT implementations incur heavy non-trivial multiplications and twiddle-factor operations in large-scale signal processing and machine learning pipelines.
AI.method: SIFT decomposes the 2N-point DFT matrix in Radix-n FFT into four sparse integer matrices and approximates the complex twiddle-factor diagonal matrix via an optimization strategy.
AI.result: For radix-32 FFT, SIFT reduces estimated arithmetic cost by 75% with RMSE below 2.3765e-8 and MAPE below 0.01089%; in a numerical test, MAPE and RMSE are below 2.016% and 2.536e-6, and in wind turbine fault diagnosis it extracts compact spectral features that reduce classifier input dimensionality.
AI.conclusion: Approximating twiddle factors alongside sparse integer matrix decomposition enables substantial arithmetic savings for FFT-based feature extraction with minimal accuracy loss.

title: Deciding Without Pointing: A Case Study of Whether a Decision Model Localizes the Anomalies It Detects
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, 14 tables. Preprint of the technical part of an MSc thesis (Politecnico di Milano). Code and pre-registrations are held privately until venue submission
summary: Decision models can answer a typed question about an image with a probability per option, without generating text. In our case study of Clef-flash (post-trained Qwen3.5-9B backbone) on industrial inspection benchmarks, we ask whether it localizes the anomalies it detects. We obtained uneven results with zero-shot detection: per-category image AUROC 0.924 on MVTec AD and 0.668 on MVTec AD 2. On the former, the decision head's routing attention produces 0.391 mean per-image pixel AUROC, and hiding the image tokens from it leaves detection unchanged. The multimodal LLM's backbone attention does point at the defect, however it falls below a center prior when we change question. It falls below chance if we remove textual context in the question, partly due to backbone attention leaving the object, while the head's map hardly changes. The backbone's states carry the location when probed with normal images, on the test-split images, however, the decision depends on the defect region. A larger model, Clef, that comes with a post-trained Qwen3.8-27B backbone, gives no useful map in the decision head either. We found that it's possible to recover anomaly location by asking question specifically on an image region, retraining the head or reading the backbone, but none matches dedicated few-shot localizers.

AI.tldr: This case study investigates whether decision models (Clef-flash on Qwen3.5-9B and Clef on Qwen3.8-27B) localize the industrial anomalies they detect, finding that their decision heads do not localize defects.
AI.motivation: Decision models output option probabilities without generating text, but it is unclear whether their internal attention mechanisms actually localize the anomalies driving their predictions.
AI.method: The authors evaluate Clef-flash and Clef on MVTec AD and MVTec AD 2, probing decision-head routing attention, backbone attention under question perturbations, and token-masking interventions.
AI.result: Clef-flash achieves 0.924 image AUROC on MVTec AD and 0.668 on MVTec AD 2, yet its decision head yields only 0.391 pixel AUROC and is unaffected by hiding image tokens; backbone attention points to defects but drops below a center prior when questions change, and region-specific prompting or retraining still lags dedicated few-shot localizers.
AI.conclusion: High image-level anomaly detection accuracy in decision models does not imply spatial localization in the decision head, limiting their out-of-the-box interpretability.

title: On Formal Counterfactual Explanations
summary: Counterfactual explanations are often seen as counterfactual conditionals under closest-world semantics, requiring one to reason over all minimally distant counterexamples. In contrast, formal XAI typically relies on feature-based abductive explanations (AXps) and contrastive explanations (CXps), which admit efficient computation and a minimal hitting-set duality. This paper bridges these perspectives by (i) characterizing closest-world counterfactual explanations explicitly as a disjunctive normal form over all minimally distant counterexample instances, and (ii) introducing conjunctive counterfactual explanations (CFXps), a subclass of counterfactual antecedents restricted to conjunctions of feature literals that guarantee prediction change. The paper establishes structural results connecting CXps, AXps and CFXps: every CXp induces an AXp for its witness instance, and every CXp together with a witness AXp induces a CFXp whose support is precisely determined by that AXp. These theoretical results yield a modular approach for computing CFXps using existing AXp/CXp machinery. Experiments on a representative set of benchmarks using tree ensembles and neural networks show that CFXp extraction is practically efficient. Compared with popular point-based counterfactual explainers, CFXps generally require no more feature changes and can guarantee the counterfactual prediction beyond a single instance.

AI.tldr: This paper bridges closest-world counterfactual explanations and formal XAI (AXps/CXps) by introducing conjunctive counterfactual explanations (CFXps) and showing how to compute them using existing AXp/CXp machinery.
AI.motivation: Closest-world counterfactuals require reasoning over all minimally distant counterexamples, whereas formal XAI relies on abductive (AXp) and contrastive (CXp) explanations with efficient hitting-set duality.
AI.method: The authors characterize closest-world counterfactuals as a disjunctive normal form over minimally distant counterexamples, define CFXps as conjunctions of feature literals guaranteeing prediction change, and prove structural links showing every CXp plus a witness AXp induces a CFXp.
AI.result: Experiments on tree ensembles and neural networks demonstrate that CFXp extraction is practically efficient, requires no more feature changes than point-based explainers, and guarantees counterfactual predictions beyond a single instance.
AI.conclusion: Connecting formal AXp/CXp duality to counterfactuals enables efficient, provably valid conjunctive counterfactual explanations.

title: Computed Permutation Trellis Coding: Near-Optimal Quantization from Two Multiplications and a 64-Byte Table
summary: We propose Computed Permutation Trellis Coding (CPTC), a low-bit quantization format for tensors written once and read many times. Formats that round each value on its own, such as INT4 and FP4, waste a large part of their bits against the information-theoretic ideal. Trellis codes recover this loss by encoding values jointly, but prior decoders either need a large lookup table for their best quality or compute values with a hash that restricts what they can decode. CPTC's decoder multiplies its state by two coefficients and adds the top bits of the products to index a 64-byte table. Because that sum is not uniformly distributed, the rarely used ends of a small table can hold values far out in the tails. One decoder serves every bit width from 1 to 6, reproduces the standard integer and floating-point formats exactly, and comes within 0.07 bits of the ideal at 4 bits. It matches a random-permutation trellis code whose table is thousands of times larger, and exceeds every QTIP codebook. In LLM weight quantization without fine-tuning, CPTC has the lowest KL divergence to the unquantized model at every tested bit width on Llama 3.1 8B and 70B Instruct against QTIP's codebooks (by up to 27%). The decoder has been built into the AWS Trainium 4 AI accelerator, where it runs at the throughput of the native FP4 and FP8 formats for a negligible fraction of the systolic array's area. Fused encoding kernels quantize an 8B model's linear layers in under two minutes on one GPU and, in cycle-level simulation, on one Trainium 4 chip.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Computed Permutation Trellis Coding (CPTC), a low-bit quantization format using two multiplications and a 64-byte table that achieves near-optimal rate-distortion and is implemented in AWS Trainium 4.
AI.motivation: Scalar quantization formats like INT4 and FP4 waste bits relative to information-theoretic limits, while prior trellis decoders require either large lookup tables or restrictive hash functions.
AI.method: CPTC's decoder multiplies its state by two coefficients and sums the top bits of the products to index a 64-byte table, supporting 1 to 6 bits with a single decoder and reproducing standard integer/float formats.
AI.result: CPTC comes within 0.07 bits of the ideal at 4 bits, outperforms all QTIP codebooks (reducing KL divergence on Llama 3.1 8B/70B Instruct by up to 27% without fine-tuning), runs at native FP4/FP8 throughput on AWS Trainium 4, and quantizes an 8B model's linear layers in under two minutes on one GPU.
AI.conclusion: CPTC delivers hardware-friendly, near-optimal trellis quantization for LLM weights with negligible area overhead.

title: A single inference process underlies the behavior and neural circuits of working memory
summary: Working memory holds past inputs online for future behavior. Despite decades of research, accounts of working memory remain divided across levels of analysis, with long-standing debates on whether its capacity reflects discrete slots or continuous resources, how attention improves recall, and whether its representations rely on persistent neural firing or activity-silent states. Here we show that MemGP, a theory that is specified at the computational, algorithmic, and circuit levels of analysis simultaneously, can explain diverse behavioral and neural phenomena in working memory. At the computational level, MemGP casts working memory as probabilistic inference over a continuous function on feature space, with a variational objective that balances memory strength against a Gaussian-process prior. At the algorithmic level, writing, storing, and reading of memories correspond to approximating this posterior with a finite set of inducing points, the resource that all items share. In simulations, MemGP reproduces load-dependent precision loss, attentional benefits during maintenance, and inter-item attraction and repulsion, in each case revealing multiple complex computational dependencies. At the circuit level, the algorithm analytically (without training) maps onto a recurrent circuit, including its architecture and dynamics. Beyond reproducing neural phenomena such as delay-dependent drift, this analytical map deduces center--surround connectivity, a property long assumed in attractor models, and a structured combination of persistent activity and synaptic weights to hold memories. Thus, a single inference objective not only jointly predicts the behavioral and neural signatures of working memory, but also addresses, across several instances and different levels of analysis, existing competing explanations.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces MemGP, a unified theory of working memory that casts memory as Gaussian-process variational inference and analytically maps the algorithm onto recurrent neural circuits.
AI.motivation: Working memory research remains divided across computational, algorithmic, and circuit levels over discrete slots versus continuous resources, attention effects, and persistent versus activity-silent states.
AI.method: MemGP models working memory as probabilistic inference over a continuous function with a Gaussian-process prior, approximates the posterior with a finite set of shared inducing points, and analytically maps this algorithm onto a recurrent circuit without training.
AI.result: In simulations, MemGP reproduces load-dependent precision loss, attentional maintenance benefits, inter-item attraction/repulsion, and delay-dependent neural drift, while analytically deriving center-surround connectivity and a mix of persistent activity and synaptic weights.
AI.conclusion: A single probabilistic inference objective can simultaneously account for behavioral and circuit-level signatures of working memory, reconciling competing theories.

title: Addressing Exogenous Variability in Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
comment: 28 pages. Includes supplementary material. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) often fails under exogenous variability such as shifts in opponents or environment regimes that cannot be controlled by the team but alter the transition dynamics. We formalize this challenge as Exogenous Dec-POMDP (ED-POMDP), in which an episode-level exogenous regime, selected independently of the team, indexes the dynamics, and the global state is partitioned into components that are directly responsive to the current team action and components that are not directly action-responsive at the current step. This formulation exposes mediated influence: while team actions do not directly update the latter at the current step, they can shape their later evolution through induced changes in the former. Based on this, we propose LEICA, a CTDE-compatible algorithm that learns history-conditioned context representations for both components and shapes policy updates using agent-wise, influence-weighted counterfactual intrinsic rewards. Across SMAX benchmarks with opponent strategy shifts, LEICA consistently improves both training performance and generalization to unseen opponents' strategies over existing baselines, supporting the usefulness of influence-weighted shaping under exogenous train-test regime shifts.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes exogenous variability in cooperative MARL as Exogenous Dec-POMDP (ED-POMDP) and proposes LEICA, a CTDE algorithm using influence-weighted counterfactual intrinsic rewards.
AI.motivation: Cooperative MARL agents often fail when uncontrollable episode-level exogenous regimes (such as opponent strategy shifts) alter environment transition dynamics.
AI.method: ED-POMDP partitions global state into action-responsive and non-action-responsive components to expose mediated influence, and LEICA learns history-conditioned context representations for both while shaping policy updates with agent-wise, influence-weighted counterfactual intrinsic rewards.
AI.result: Across SMAX benchmarks with opponent strategy shifts, LEICA consistently improves both training performance and zero-shot generalization to unseen opponent strategies over existing baselines.
AI.conclusion: Modeling mediated influence and shaping rewards via counterfactuals improves cooperative MARL robustness under exogenous train-test regime shifts.

title: MedGuardBench: A Patient-Oriented Benchmark for Personalized Guardrail Development
summary: Safety is personal: the same action can be safe for one person but unsafe for another. Yet current guardrails judge content without considering who is affected. Using medication safety, we introduce \textit{patient-conditioned medication guarding}, which predicts a safety verdict and 17 risk categories from a patient profile and prescription. We release \textbf{MedGuardBench}, a drug-disjoint benchmark of 5{,}001 scenarios across 87 medications. We find that standard guardrails rely on surface cues, such as wording and profile presence, rather than patient facts. To address this, we develop \textit{personalized reasoning guardrails} with three components. \textbf{Personalized Reasoning Distillation} links risks to relevant patient fields. \textbf{Context Unrolling (CU)} makes models check each field themselves, reducing false alarms on most backbones; controls show that providing the check does not yield the same benefit. A \textbf{rule-based reward (guided GRPO)} improves unsafe recall and complex-risk detection, including allergies and adverse reactions, on some backbones, but increases false alarms on others. Our models outperform base models and matched no-profile controls in accuracy, while reducing false alarms relative to no-profile controls. Profile removal and swapping confirm that gains come from patient information, not fine-tuning alone.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces MedGuardBench, a 5,001-scenario medication safety benchmark, and develops personalized reasoning guardrails that condition safety verdicts on patient profiles.
AI.motivation: Existing safety guardrails judge content generically without considering individual patient facts, even though medication safety depends critically on who is affected.
AI.method: The authors release MedGuardBench (5,001 drug-disjoint scenarios across 87 medications and 17 risk categories) and propose personalized reasoning guardrails combining Personalized Reasoning Distillation, Context Unrolling (CU) to check each patient field, and rule-based guided GRPO.
AI.result: Standard guardrails rely on surface cues rather than patient facts; CU reduces false alarms on most backbones, guided GRPO improves unsafe recall and complex-risk detection on some backbones, and the combined models outperform base models and no-profile controls in accuracy while reducing false alarms.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning guardrails on structured patient-field checks and personalized reasoning substantially improves patient-specific medication safety.

title: When AUC Meets Generative Reconstruction: A Unified Principle for Balanced Visual Representation Learning
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) require visual encoders that extract fine-grained visual features while constructing semantically disentangled and discriminative representations. Conventional methodologies encounter a fundamental trade-off: contrastive learning enhances inter-class discrimination by suppressing intra-class variability, whereas generative reconstruction emphasizes perceptual fidelity but lacks explicit comparative supervision. The naive aggregation of these objectives via composite loss functions often induces optimization conflicts and instability due to gradient interference within the shared latent space. To resolve this, we introduce a unified representation-learning paradigm that reformulates generative reconstruction as a discriminative ranking problem within the generative output manifold. Our approach maintains perceptual reconstruction as a supervisory signal and integrates a ranking-based discriminative constraint by systematically ordering matched and mismatched reconstruction outputs. This formulation embeds discriminative information seamlessly into the generative process, alleviating the risk of loss competition. Specifically, we propose AUC Generative Reconstruction (AUCGR), which optimizes the area under the ROC curve (AUC) by ensuring higher scores for matched pairs than for mismatched pairs, and Partial AUC Generative Reconstruction (pAUCGR), which addresses supervision bias by focusing on mismatched comparisons within reliable feature subspaces. The proposed objectives are designed to be plug-and-play, requiring no architectural modifications to existing generative reconstruction frameworks. Theoretical analysis establishes rigorous connections to AUC/pAUC optimization and provides generalization guarantees. Extensive experiments validate that our method advances both discriminative accuracy and fine-grained perceptual representation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes AUC Generative Reconstruction (AUCGR) and Partial AUC Generative Reconstruction (pAUCGR), plug-and-play objectives that reformulate generative reconstruction as discriminative ranking to avoid gradient conflicts.
AI.motivation: Combining contrastive learning and generative reconstruction in MLLM visual encoders often causes optimization conflicts and instability due to gradient interference.
AI.method: AUCGR and pAUCGR maintain perceptual reconstruction while adding a ranking-based constraint that orders matched versus mismatched reconstruction outputs in the generative manifold, optimizing AUC or partial AUC without architectural changes.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis establishes generalization guarantees, and extensive experiments show improvements in both discriminative accuracy and fine-grained perceptual representation.
AI.conclusion: Reformulating generative reconstruction as AUC-based ranking unifies discriminative and perceptual representation learning without loss competition.

title: LoCaR: Localized Canvas Retrieval With Frozen Vision-Language Model
summary: Whole image embeddings can under represent small objects and local attributes that distinguish relevant images for localized queries. We present LoCaR, a training free framework for localized text to image retrieval with frozen vision language models. LoCaR constructs and utilizes independent proposals (SAM2) focusing on the object so as to get a more localized representation that independently encodes each region using the frozen visual encoder. We further study paired-support adaptation as an optional residual that uses matched text region exemplars without updating the underlying encoders. We also introduce LOCFG, a Visual Genome derived benchmark designed to evaluate localized retrieval for smaller and more challenging referents. Across several vision language backbones, our results show that improving the region representation itself is the main source of gain.

AI.tldr: This paper presents LoCaR, a training-free framework for localized text-to-image retrieval using SAM2 object proposals encoded by frozen vision-language models, alongside a new benchmark LOCFG.
AI.motivation: Whole-image embeddings from frozen vision-language models underrepresent small objects and local attributes needed for localized text-to-image retrieval.
AI.method: LoCaR generates independent object proposals with SAM2 and encodes each region separately using a frozen visual encoder, optionally adding paired-support residual adaptation from matched text-region exemplars without updating encoder weights.
AI.result: Evaluated on the newly introduced Visual Genome-derived LOCFG benchmark and across multiple VLM backbones, improving region-level representation is the primary driver of retrieval gains.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling region proposals and encoding them independently with frozen VLMs enables effective, training-free localized retrieval.

title: Flocking Time and Graph Volume in Nonlinear Cucker-Smale Models with Dynamic Networks
comment: 14 pages, 3 figures. Accepted manuscript of the article published in J. Inf. Commun. Converg. Eng. 24(2), 155-164 (2026)
summary: This study proposes a Cucker-Smale model incorporating dynamic networks and the discrete $p$-Laplacian ($p \in (1,2)$) and analyzes the relationship between flocking time constraints and graph connectivity from both theoretical and experimental perspectives. We establish that this model achieves flocking within finite time and derive a quantitative relationship between the lower bound of flocking time and graph volume. Based on these results, we observe that imposing sufficiently small flocking time induces an increase in network volume, and that larger initial velocity variance requires greater volume under the same time constraint. In our experiments, we trained a transformer-based PPO policy to select network structures at each time step. Under the most stringent time constraint, the maximum average number of connections increased sharply, confirming a threshold effect. The negative correlation between convergence time and average number of connections reflects the theoretical results well. This study provides quantitative evidence for the phenomenon that time constraints induce connection mobilization.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes a nonlinear Cucker-Smale flocking model with dynamic networks and the discrete p-Laplacian, deriving a quantitative link between flocking time constraints and graph volume.
AI.motivation: Understanding how strict finite-time flocking constraints drive network connectivity mobilization in multi-agent systems remains underexplored both theoretically and experimentally.
AI.method: The authors prove finite-time flocking for a discrete p-Laplacian (p in (1, 2)) Cucker-Smale model, derive a lower-bound relationship between flocking time and graph volume, and train a transformer-based PPO policy to select network structures at each step.
AI.result: Theoretical bounds and PPO experiments show that tighter flocking time constraints and larger initial velocity variance force higher graph volume, with a sharp threshold increase in average connections under the strictest time constraint.
AI.conclusion: Strict convergence-time constraints quantitatively induce network connection mobilization in nonlinear flocking dynamics.

title: Discovery of new antiviral agents through artificial intelligence: in vitro and in vivo results
comment: Accepted manuscript. 13 pages, 5 figures; supplementary material included (supplementary text, Tables S1-S2, Figures S1-S5). Published in Antiviral Research 222 (2024) 105818
summary: In this research, we employed a deep reinforcement learning (RL)-based molecule design platform to generate a diverse set of compounds targeting the neuraminidase (NA) of influenza A and B viruses. A total of 60291 compounds were generated, of which 86.5% displayed superior physicochemical properties compared to oseltamivir. After narrowing down the selection through computational filters, nine compounds with non-sialic acid-like structures were selected for in vitro experiments. We identified two compounds, DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 that effectively inhibited the NAs of both influenza A and B viruses (IAV and IBV), including H275Y mutant strains at low micromolar concentrations. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed a similar pattern of interaction with amino acid residues as oseltamivir. In cell-based assays, DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 inhibited IAV and IBV in a dose-dependent manner with EC50 values ranging from 0.29 uM to 2.31 uM. Furthermore, animal experiments showed that both DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 exerted antiviral activity in mice, conferring 65% and 85% protection from IAV (H1N1 pdm09), and 65% and 100% protection from IBV (Yamagata lineage), respectively. Thus, these findings demonstrate the potential of RL to generate compounds with promising antiviral properties.

AI.tldr: This paper uses a deep RL molecule design platform to discover two non-sialic acid-like compounds, DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021, that inhibit influenza A and B neuraminidases in vitro and protect mice in vivo.
AI.motivation: Discovering new antiviral agents effective against both influenza A and B viruses, including oseltamivir-resistant H275Y mutants, is an urgent therapeutic need.
AI.method: A deep RL platform generated 60,291 candidate compounds targeting influenza neuraminidase; after computational filtering, nine non-sialic acid-like candidates were tested in vitro, in molecular dynamics simulations, in cell assays, and in mouse infection models.
AI.result: 86.5% of generated compounds showed superior physicochemical properties to oseltamivir; DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 inhibited IAV, IBV, and H275Y mutants with cell-based EC50 values of 0.29-2.31 uM, and conferred 65%/85% protection against IAV (H1N1 pdm09) and 65%/100% protection against IBV (Yamagata) in mice.
AI.conclusion: Deep RL-driven de novo molecule generation can successfully identify novel, in vivo-active antiviral candidates against diverse influenza strains.

title: From Temperature-Limited to Battery-Limited Legged Locomotion
comment: 9 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables. Supplementary video in the ancillary files. Dataset: this https URL
summary: On legged robots, sustained locomotion often ends in thermal shutdown rather than battery depletion: the heat of walking concentrates in a few joint motors, which overheat long before the battery is empty. We train thermally aware locomotion policies by reinforcement learning without ever observing temperature, and demonstrate this on a Unitree Go2 quadruped. We first identify a coupled 13-node lumped RC thermal network, fitted on two runs of a single robot and calibrated against the measured electrical power, that predicts all twelve motor temperatures with a mean RMSE below 1 $^\circ$C across different robot instances, gaits, payloads, and speeds. Under a sustained gait, the temperatures the motors will settle at follow directly from the gait-averaged squared torques and joint speeds. Our core contribution is a reward that drives down the hottest predicted asymptotes: thermal time constants exceed the credit-assignment horizon of reinforcement learning by orders of magnitude, but predicted asymptotes respond to torque and joint speed within a single gait cycle, so the policy learns to lower and spread heat with no temperature input. On the robot, the policy turns sustained locomotion from temperature-limited to battery-limited: with a 5 kg payload at 1 m/s, a learned baseline reaches thermal shutdown after 19 minutes (1.1 km), whereas our policy runs the battery down after 174 minutes (10.0 km) with its hottest motor 14 $^\circ$C below the shutdown threshold in a 26 $^\circ$C room; on an unloaded factory circuit with stairs and ramps, the baseline overheats after 25 laps (6.2 km), while our policy completes 47 (11.2 km) on one battery with 22 $^\circ$C of margin.

AI.tldr: This paper trains thermally aware RL locomotion policies for a Unitree Go2 quadruped without temperature observations by minimizing predicted steady-state motor temperatures from a 13-node RC thermal model, shifting endurance from thermal-limited to battery-limited.
AI.motivation: Legged robots often suffer thermal shutdown in a few joint motors long before battery depletion, and thermal time constants are far too long for standard RL credit assignment.
AI.method: The authors fit a coupled 13-node lumped RC thermal network (under 1 C mean RMSE across robots, gaits, payloads, and speeds) and use a reward penalizing the hottest predicted steady-state motor asymptote, which responds within a single gait cycle to torque and joint speed.
AI.result: On a Unitree Go2 with a 5 kg payload at 1 m/s, the baseline hits thermal shutdown at 19 min (1.1 km) while the policy runs until battery depletion at 174 min (10.0 km) with 14 C thermal margin; on an unloaded factory circuit, it completes 47 laps (11.2 km) on one battery with 22 C margin versus 25 laps (6.2 km) for the baseline.
AI.conclusion: Penalizing predicted steady-state thermal asymptotes enables RL policies to distribute heat and achieve battery-limited endurance without requiring temperature sensors.
